The sūrah has spent thirteen verses describing a group that appears successful — treated as believers, unharmed, given a long rope. It ends the unit by saying that nothing about their position is stable, and the reason is not their behaviour but His capacity.

Maʿārif states the warning directly: *In the course of these parables, the hypocrites have also been warned that they are not beyond the power of Allah, and that He can, as and when He likes, take away their sight and hearing, and even destroy them.*

**What the two parables add up to.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar's summary is the best single sentence available on verses 17–20, and it explains why both pictures were needed:

*The hypocrites are similar to the people in these examples because they receive no benefit from anything. In the example of the fire, all they receive is darkness and a smouldering fire. In the example of the storm-cloud, all they receive is fear and alarm because of the thunder and lightning. Similarly, the hypocrites see nothing in Islam except difficulty and harshness.*

Two different people, one outcome. The first had the light and lost it. The second gets flashes and cannot keep moving. Neither ends up anywhere.

And that is why the sūrah stops here. Verses 8 to 20 were a complete unit — Mujāhid's thirteen verses, recorded by Ibn Kathīr at 2:4 — and verse 21 turns, without transition, to the whole of mankind: *O people, worship your Lord.* The hypocrites are finished with. The address widens.

21.text:
*O humanity! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may become mindful of Him.*

**The address changes, and the change is the point.**

For twenty verses the sūrah has been talking *about* people — the believers, the disbelievers, the hypocrites. Now it talks *to* them. *Yā ayyuhan-nās.* O humanity.

Maʿārif sets out what has just been completed, and it explains why the turn happens here:

*Three verses speak of the true and God-fearing Muslims, who not only accept but also act upon the guidance, and the next two verses of those disbelievers who oppose it openly. Then come thirteen verses dealing with the hypocrites who are hostile to this guidance, but, for the sake of petty worldly interests or in seeking to harm the Muslims, try to keep their disbelief concealed and to present themselves as Muslims.*

Then he draws the conclusion the sūrah has been building toward: *the first twenty verses of the Sūrah, in dividing men into three groups on the basis of their acceptance or rejection of the guidance, indicate that the proper criterion for dividing men into groups is neither race or colour, nor language nor geography, but religion.*

So the three categories were never about identity. They were about what you did with the guidance. And now everybody is addressed at once.

**Who "humanity" is.**

Al-Jalālayn: *O people of Mecca.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives both readings: *O people of Mecca; and it is also said that this refers to the Jews.*

The word itself is unrestricted — *an-nās*, people. The commentators are identifying the immediate audience, not narrowing the text.

**Worship your Lord.**

The command is *ʿbudū*, and the reason attached to it is creation: *Who created you and those before you.*

Ibn Kathīr heads this section *Tawḥīd al-Ulūhiyyah* — the oneness of Allah in being worshipped — and opens it exactly there: *Allah next mentioned His Oneness in divinity and stated that He has favored His servants by bringing them to life after they did not exist.*

Not "worship Me because I am powerful." Worship Me because you were nothing, and now you are not.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās adds a detail about how: *Who hath created you as different lineages beginning from a drop of sperm.*

Al-Jalālayn compresses the whole argument: *Who created you — made you when you were nothing — and created those that were before you; so that you may be fearful of His punishment by worshipping Him.*

**Those before you.**

The phrase is easy to skip and it is doing something. It puts the listener inside a line. You were created; so were the generations behind you; the same one did both.

That quietly disposes of the most common form of inherited religion — "this is what my people do." The verse agrees that there are those before you, and then says the One who made them is the One to be worshipped, not them.

Tazkīrul Qurʾān puts the same idea at the centre of its run over 2:21–24: *The proper course for a man is to take God as his Creator, Master and Sustainer, and not attempt to set up anyone as partner with Him; that is, a man should give himself up entirely to God.*

**So that you may become mindful.**

The last phrase is *laʿallakum tattaqūn*, and Al-Jalālayn makes a grammatical observation about it that changes how it reads:

*Laʿalla — "so that" — is essentially an optative but when spoken by God it denotes an affirmative.*

In ordinary Arabic *laʿalla* expresses hope: perhaps, maybe. Al-Jalālayn says that when Allah uses it, it is not a hope. It is a statement that this is what will happen.

Al-Mukhtaṣar renders the result concretely: *so that you may save yourselves from suffering, by following His instructions and keeping away from what He has prohibited.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *so that you may ward off His wrath and torment, and obey Him.*

Taqwā, then, is not a mood of reverence. It is the condition of someone who has adjusted how they act because they have understood who made them.

**Why worship follows creation.**

Maʿārif explains the logic that carries into the next verse: *once one has understood that, in reality, Allah alone is the Creator and the Provider, one will have also understood that no one else can be worthy of worship and of being associated with Allah as an equal or rival god.*

And then he states what he takes these two verses to be for: *To sum up, these two verses call men to what is the essential purpose of sending down all the Divine Books and all the prophets — tawḥīd, or the affirmation and the worship of the one God.*

Everything from verse 21 to the end of the sūrah — the rulings, the stories, the arguments with the Children of Israel — sits under that heading.

22.text:
*He is the One Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy; and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you. So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah in worship.*

**Four things, then a conclusion.**

The verse lists four acts — settling the earth, roofing the sky, sending water, growing fruit — and then draws one inference from all of them. It does not argue. It shows the work and lets the conclusion be obvious.

**The earth as a place of settlement.**

Al-Jalālayn's gloss on this is the most exact of the six, and it is worth reading slowly:

*He Who assigned to you, created for you, the earth for a couch — like a carpet that is laid out — neither extremely hard nor extremely soft, so as to make it impossible to stand firm upon it.*

That middle clause is the whole observation. Not "the earth is solid." The earth is *the right amount* of solid. Too hard and nothing grows; too soft and nothing stands.

Ibn Kathīr makes the same point with a different image: *He made the earth a resting place for them, just like the bed, stable with the firm mountains.* The mountains are what keep the bed from shifting.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās adds the use: *a place for dwelling and sleeping.*

**The sky as a canopy.**

*Bināʾ* — a structure, a building, a roof. Ibn Kathīr glosses it as *a ceiling* and brings 21:32 alongside it: *And We have made the heaven a roof, safe and well-guarded. Yet they turn away from its signs.*

*Maḥfūẓ* — guarded, protected. The roof does something. It is not decoration.

**Water, and its timing.**

*And sends down rain from the sky.* Ibn Kathīr adds three words that are easy to miss: *meaning, through the clouds, when they need the rain.*

*When they need it.* The rain is not evenly distributed. It arrives in relation to need.

Then: *Hence, Allah caused the various types of vegetation and fruits to grow as a means of sustenance for people and their cattle.* He notes that *Allah reiterated this bounty in various parts of the Qurʾān*, and quotes 40:64 as the closest parallel: *It is He Who has made for you the earth as a dwelling place and the sky as a canopy, and has given you shape and made your shapes good, and has provided you with good things. That is Allah, your Lord.*

Al-Jalālayn catches the grammar of provision: *and sent down from the heaven water wherewith He brought forth all types of fruits for your provision.* The fruit is not an independent event. It is the water arriving in a different form.

**Then the command.**

*So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah in worship.*

Al-Jalālayn supplies the reasoning in a single sentence: *so set not up compeers to God — that is, partners in worship — while you know that He is the Creator, that you create not, and that only One that creates can be God.*

That last clause is the argument. Not "He is greater, so worship Him." Only a creator can be God, and you have just been shown four things you cannot do.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads *while you know* two ways: *when you know that He is the fashioner of all these things. It is also said that "when you know" means: when you know from your own scripture that Allah does not have a son, coequal or peer.*

The second reading matters for the audience. This sūrah is addressing Madinah, where there were Jews and Christians with books. The verse is saying: your own scripture already told you this.

**What Maʿārif thinks tawḥīd actually does.**

Maʿārif treats this as the hinge of the whole revelation, and his description of its reach is unusually concrete:

*Tawḥīd is a doctrine which has an all-pervading and radically transforming impact on every sphere of human life, internal as well as external, individual as well as collective. For, once a man comes to believe that there is only One Being who alone is the Creator, the Lord and Master of the universe, who alone is all-powerful and ordains the slightest movement of the smallest atom, and without whose will no one can harm or do good to another — such a man, rich or poor, in joy or sorrow, would always look only towards that One Being, and gain the insight to discover behind the veil of apparent causes the workings of the same Omnipotence.*

He then makes the sharpest comment in the six sources on this verse:

*If our modern worshippers of "energy" only had some understanding of the doctrine of tawḥīd, they would easily see that power resides neither in steam nor in electricity, but that the source of all powers is [Allah].*

The verse's warning about *equals* is not only about statues. It is about anything you treat as the place where power actually lives.

**Why the verse ends where it does.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān describes the error the verse is aimed at: *since He is invisible, it often happens that man gives importance to some visible object and worships that instead of God. He equates the created with the Creator — sometimes just a part of it and sometimes creation in its entirety, at times calling it by the name of God and at times doing so without taking God's name. Therein lies man's basic error.*

Which is why the four acts are all visible. The earth under you, the sky over you, the rain, the fruit. The verse does not ask you to reason about the unseen. It points at what is already in front of you and asks who made it.

And it closes on the one word that makes the whole thing a charge rather than an invitation: *knowingly.* You know. That is the problem.

23.text:
*And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true.*

**The second proof.**

Maʿārif's framing of these two verses against the two before is the cleanest available:

*The Guidance which the Holy Qurʾān provides to man rests on two basic principles — tawḥīd (the Oneness of God) and risālah (Prophethood). The two preceding verses (21 and 22) affirm the Oneness of God in presenting certain acts peculiar to Allah alone as a proof; these two verses (23 and 24) affirm the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ in presenting the word of Allah as a proof. In both the places, the mode of argument is the same.*

And then he states the parallel precisely: *just as the helplessness of man and other creatures in the matter of creating the sky and the earth is a demonstration of the fact that these are the acts of Allah alone, in the same way the helplessness of all created beings in the matter of producing something equal to or resembling the Word of Allah is a demonstration of the fact that this is the Word of Allah alone.*

Creation and revelation are proven the same way — by showing that nobody else can do it.

**Our servant.**

*ʿAbdinā* — Our servant. Ibn Kathīr glosses it: *meaning, Muhammad ﷺ.*

The word is a title here, not a diminuendo. In a verse about who is qualified to speak for Allah, calling him a servant is the qualification.

**If you are in doubt.**

The verse opens with a conditional, and it is a generous one. It does not say "since you deny." It says *if you are in doubt* — and doubt is treated as a legitimate starting position.

Ibn Kathīr identifies the addressees: *And if you (Arab pagans, Jews, and Christians) are in doubt concerning that which We have sent down to Our servant.*

All three groups. Not one opponent but the whole field.

**Produce a sûrah like it.**

Al-Jalālayn does two things here that matter. First, he defines the unit:

*Bring a sūra like it — that is, also revealed. Min mithlihi: min is explicative — that is, a sūra like it in its eloquence, its fine arrangement and its bestowal of knowledge of the Unseen. A sūra is a passage with a beginning and end made up of a minimum of three verses.*

Three verses. That is the floor of the challenge, and it is very low.

Second, he removes the obvious excuse: *So do this, for you are also fluent speakers of Arabic like him.*

The challenge is not issued to people in another language. It is issued to the poets of Quraysh, in their own idiom, by a man they had known for forty years.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās specifies the benchmark: *produce a surah like the surah of the Cow (al-Baqarah).*

**Call your helpers.**

*Wadʿū shuhadāʾakum* — and there is a real disagreement about who these are. Ibn Kathīr collects three:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās**: *shuhadāʾakum* means **"Aids."**
- **As-Suddī**, reporting **Abū Mālik**: *"Your partners, meaning, some other people to help you in that. Meaning then go and seek the help of your deities to support and aid you."*
- **Mujāhid**: *"People, meaning, wise and eloquent men who will provide the testimony that you seek."*

The three readings are not far apart. Call your gods. Call your experts. Call whoever you think can help.

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps it simple: *to call their helpers, if they are truthful about what they say.*

**The challenge is not new here.**

Ibn Kathīr notes that *Allah challenged the disbelievers in various parts of the Qurʾān*, and quotes two:

28:49 — *Say (to them, O Muhammad ﷺ): "Then bring a Book from Allah, which is a better guide than these two (the Torah and the Qurʾān), that I may follow it, if you are truthful."*

17:88 — *Say: "If mankind and the jinn gathered in order to produce the like of this Qurʾān, they could not produce the like of it."*

That second one widens the challenge beyond humans entirely.

**The verse's real shape.**

It is a conditional that expects a failed condition. *If you are in doubt — then produce one.* The verse is not asking them to try. It is telling them what trying will show.

And the next verse confirms that reading by announcing the result before they have attempted it.

24.text:
*But if you are unable to do so—and you will never be able to do so—then fear the Fire fuelled with people and stones, which is prepared for the disbelievers.*

**The interruption that is the verse.**

Between the condition and its consequence, the verse inserts a statement about the future: *and you will never be able to do so.*

Al-Jalālayn identifies it grammatically — *a parenthetical statement* — and then gives its force: *that is, never will you be able to, because of its inimitability.*

The reason given is not their lack of effort. It is *iʿjāz* — the Qurʾān's inimitability. The failure is a property of the text, not of the audience.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās puts it bluntly: *this you can never do, and if you try you will never succeed.*

So the challenge in verse 23 was never open. It was rhetorical in the strict sense — a question whose answer is already known, asked so that the asking makes the answer visible.

**Fear the Fire.**

*Fattaqū an-nār.* The same root as verse 21's *so that you may become mindful* — *laʿallakum tattaqūn*.

The sūrah has now used taqwā twice in four verses, once as the goal of worship and once as the response to the challenge. In both places it means the same thing: adjust what you do because of what you have understood.

Al-Jalālayn spells out the adjustment: *then fear, through belief in God and belief that this is not the words of a human, the Fire.*

**Fuelled with people and stones.**

This is the hardest image in the sūrah so far, and Al-Jalālayn's explanation of it is the most useful of the six:

*The Fire whose fuel is men — disbelievers — and stones, like their very idols, indicating that its heat is extreme, since it burns with the stones mentioned, unlike the fires of this world that burn with wood and similar materials.*

That is the point of the stones. Not that the fire is big. That it burns something our fires cannot burn.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās specifies the material: *and stones of sulphur.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar draws the consequence that makes it personal: *which burns with people who deserve the torment, and with the idols which they used to worship instead of Allah — punishing both the idol-worshippers and what they worshiped.*

Both. The thing you worshipped is in the fire with you, burning. That is the verse's answer to verse 22's *do not knowingly set up equals to Allah* — and the equals are named as fuel.

**Prepared.**

*Uʿiddat* — it has been prepared. Tanwīr al-Miqbās unpacks the verb: *created, prepared and preordained.*

Not "will be prepared." Already prepared. The tense matters, because the verse is speaking to people who are alive and being offered a way out.

Al-Jalālayn adds a grammatical note on how the clause attaches: *this phrase uʿiddat liʾl-kāfirīn — "prepared for disbelievers" — is either a new sentence or a sustained circumstantial qualifier.* Either way it stands as its own statement.

**Why the order is fear, then fire.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar's summary ties it back: *If they are unable to do so — and they will never be able to do it — they should be mindful of the fire of Hell.*

Maʿārif's structural point completes it. Verses 21–22 established tawḥīd from creation; verses 23–24 establish prophethood from revelation. And the second proof ends not in an argument but in a warning, because at that point the argument is over. They have been asked to do one thing. They cannot do it. What remains is the choice.

25.text:
*Give good news, O Prophet, to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow. Whenever provided with fruit, they will say, "This is what we were given before," for they will be served fruit that looks similar but tastes different. They will have pure spouses, and they will be there forever.*

**The turn from warning to good news.**

The verse before ended on a fire already prepared. This one opens with *bashshir* — give good news.

Ibn Kathīr marks the movement: *After mentioning the torment that Allah has prepared for His miserable enemies who disbelieve in Him and in His Messengers, He mentions the condition of His happy, loyal friends who believe in Him and in His Messengers, adhere to the faith and perform the good deeds.*

And then he explains that this alternation is not incidental but is one of the Qurʾān's names:

*This is the reason why the Qurʾān was called Mathanī, based on the correct opinion of the scholars. Mathanī means to mention faith and then disbelief, or vice versa. Or, Allah mentions the miserable and then the happy, or vice versa.*

So verses 24 and 25 are not two topics. They are one method.

**Gardens under which rivers flow.**

Ibn Kathīr reads the phrase literally and then adds detail from ḥadīth:

*Allah stated that Paradise has rivers that run beneath it, meaning, underneath its trees and rooms. From Ḥadiths it is learned that the rivers of Paradise do not run in valleys, and the banks of al-Kawthar (the Prophet's lake in Paradise) are made of domes of hollow pearls, the sand of Paradise is made of scented musk while its stones are made from pearls and jewels.*

Then two narrations. **Ibn Abī Ḥātim** reported that **Abū Hurayrah** said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *The rivers of Paradise spring from beneath hills, or mountains of musk.* And he reported from **Masrūq** that **ʿAbdullāh** said the rivers of Paradise — the report continues in the same vein.

Al-Jalālayn adds a piece of linguistics on the word itself: *tajrī min tahtihāʾl-anhār — that is, there are waters in it. Al-nahr is the place in which water flows, and is so called because the water carves (yanhar) its way through it; the reference to it as "running" is figurative.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names the four rivers: *rivers of wine, milk, honey and water.*

**"This is what we were given before."**

This is the verse's most interesting line, and the commentators differ on what it means.

Maʿārif sets out both readings: *some commentators say that this concerns only the fruits of Paradise, which would be alike in shape, but each time different in taste. Others say that these fruits would resemble the fruits of the earth in shape alone, but their taste would be totally different.*

Al-Jalālayn takes the first: *whenever they are given to eat from these gardens they shall say, "This is what — that is, the like of what — we were provided with before," that is, before this, in Paradise, since its fruits are similar.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar takes the second: *they will comment on how similar they are to the fruits of the earth, saying, "This is similar to what we had before." They will be given fruits that carry the same name and shape, so that they may recognise and desire them, but they will in fact taste differently.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās agrees with Al-Mukhtaṣar: *this is what we ate before — and it is given to them in resemblance as far as the colour is concerned but not the taste, which is different.*

**Why it is designed that way.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar's phrase *so that they may recognise and desire them* is the key. Recognition produces appetite. You reach for what you know. And then it is not that.

Maʿārif draws the conclusion: *the point is that the believers would have a kind of joy in Paradise they had never known before, and that this joy would keep renewing itself at every moment.*

The familiarity is the mechanism of the surprise. Every time, the same fruit, and every time, better.

**Maʿārif's caution.**

He attaches a footnote here that is worth recording, because it is a direct response to a modern reading:

*Our modernists have for some time been quite fond of asserting that in speaking of the fruits of Paradise and its other joys, the Holy Qurʾān has employed only a metaphysical mode of expression in order to suggest spiritual bliss which, by its very nature, is intangible. We do not mean to rule out the possibility or the desirability of analogical or symbolical interpretations of the verses of the Holy Qurʾān. In fact, many authentic Muslim scholars [have done so]…*

He allows symbolic reading generally. He resists reducing these descriptions *only* to symbols.

**Pure spouses.**

Al-Jalālayn: *and there for them shall be spouses, of houris and others, purified from menstruation and impurities.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *pure from menses or any kind of filth.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar explains what purity means here: *In the Garden they will be paired with their mates, who will not have any unpleasant traits that people have on earth.*

Not only physical. Disposition too.

**Forever.**

*Khālidūn fīhā abadan.* Al-Jalālayn: *dwelling therein forever, neither perishing nor departing therefrom.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *never to die or be banished from it.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar closes on the contrast with everything else: *they will live there in eternal bliss, unlike the bliss of the earth, which is only temporary.*

And that contrast reaches back to verse 22. The earth was made a *place of settlement* — a word that in this world means somewhere you stay for a while. Here the same idea is given without the limit.

Tazkīrul Qurʾān states the connection to what came before: *Those who find God in the word of God are already given a glimpse of the next world. They are the ones who shall be admitted into the gardens of Paradise.*

26.text:
*Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller. As for the believers, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. And as for the disbelievers, they argue, "What does Allah mean by such a parable?" Through this test, He leaves many to stray, and guides many. And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious.*

**The verse answers an actual objection, and Ibn Kathīr records it.**

As-Suddī, in his tafsīr, reported from **Ibn ʿAbbās**, **Ibn Masʿūd** and some Companions:

*When Allah gave these two examples of the hypocrites — "Their likeness is as the likeness of one who kindled a fire," and "Or like a rainstorm from the sky" — the hypocrites said, "Allah is far more exalted than for Him to make such examples." So Allah revealed these verses (2:26–27) up to "they are the losers."*

So this verse is a direct reply to verses 17–20, which were authored three verses ago. Somebody objected to the fire and the storm, and the objection was that such imagery is beneath Allah.

Saʿīd said that **Qatādah** widened the objection to the rest of the Qurʾān:

*Allah does not shy away from the truth when He mentions a matter as a parable, whether this matter is significant or not. When Allah mentioned the flies and the spider in His Book, the people of misguidance said, "Why did Allah mention these things?"*

The flies are 22:73 and the spider is 29:41 — the objection was not local to al-Baqarah.

**Maʿārif states the objection and the answer most clearly.**

*They had been saying that had the Qurʾān been the Word of Allah, it would not have employed contemptible creatures like an ant or a gnat in its parables, for such a thing goes against the sublimity and majesty of Allah, when it would embarrass even a man with some sense of dignity.*

And the reply:

*The Holy Qurʾān points out that when one intends to speak of a detestable thing or person or situation, in a parable, the use of a gnat or something even more contemptible neither transgresses the principles of eloquence or logic, nor does it go against the sense of dignity or modesty, and hence Allah does not feel shy in using such imagery.*

The point is about eloquence, not permission. A parable is judged by whether it conveys the thing. A mosquito conveys smallness and insignificance perfectly. Using a lion instead would be worse writing.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās turns the objection around entirely: *He cannot abstain from coining similes, and how can He disdain mentioning something that, if all created beings were to join forces to create, they would not be able to do so.*

The mosquito is not beneath Allah. Nobody can make one.

**Or what is even smaller.**

Al-Jalālayn's grammatical note on the phrase is dense but it settles a common confusion:

*Even of a gnat — baʿūḍa is the singular of baʿūd, that is, small flies; or anything above it, that is, larger than it, so that this explanation is not affected by the size of the creature with regard to the judgement God is making.*

Size is irrelevant to the point being made. Whether the creature is above or below the mosquito, the parable works the same way.

**The two responses.**

*As for the believers, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. And as for the disbelievers, they argue, "What does Allah mean by such a parable?"*

Al-Jalālayn on the believers: *they know it — the similitude — is the truth, established and given in this instance from their Lord.*

On the question itself he gives the grammar and the tone: *mathalan is a specification, meaning "by this similitude"; mā is an interrogative of rejection and is the subject; dhā means alladhī, whose relative clause contains its predicate — in other words, "what use is there in it?"*

An interrogative of rejection. It is not a question. It is a sneer shaped like one — the same shape as verse 14's *we were only mocking.*

Maʿārif explains why the two groups respond differently: *doubts of this kind arise only in the minds of those whom their disbelief has drained of all power to see things in a proper perspective, while such empty misgivings never touch the minds and hearts of true believers.*

**What the parable does.**

*Through this test, He leaves many to stray, and guides many.*

Al-Jalālayn: *Thereby — that is, by this similitude — He leads many astray from the truth on account of their disbelieving in it, and thereby He guides many believers on account of their belief in it.*

The same object, two opposite effects, and the difference is entirely in the receiver. Al-Mukhtaṣar: *There are many people who are misguided by Allah through these examples, because they refuse to consider them; and there are many whom He guides along the right path, because they learn from them.*

**Only the rebellious.**

*And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious.* Al-Jalālayn: *and thereby He leads none astray except the wicked — those that reject obedience to Him.* Al-Mukhtaṣar: *He does not misguide anyone except those who deserve to be misguided. They are those who do not obey Him.*

This is the same structure the sūrah used for the sealed hearts at 2:7 and the increasing sickness at 2:10. Nobody is taken by surprise. The fāsiq is someone who has already refused.

**What the gnat actually means.**

Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī reported that **Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas** read the mosquito as a parable of this world:

*This is an example that Allah has given for the life of this world. The mosquito lives as long as it needs food, but when it gets fat, it dies. This is also the example of people whom Allah mentioned in the Qurʾān: when they acquire, and collect the delights of, the life of this world, Allah then takes them away.*

The creature objected to as too small turns out to be exactly the right size for the point. A mosquito dies of success.

27.text:
*Those who violate Allah's covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ties Allah has ordered to be maintained, and spread corruption in the land. It is they who are the true losers.*

**What the verse is describing.**

Verse 26 ended by saying that Allah *leaves none to stray except the rebellious* — and this verse defines the rebel. Three acts, then a verdict.

Al-Jalālayn: *They the ones thus described shall be the losers, since they shall end up in the Fire made everlasting for them.*

**Which covenant.**

There are three answers in the sources, and they are not really in competition.

Al-Mukhtaṣar takes it back to the beginning of everything, and quotes 7:172: *Those who break the promise they made with God to serve Him alone and follow His way. This is in the verse, "He made them testify concerning themselves: 'Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yes, we bear witness!'" He affirmed this by sending the prophets and the scriptures.*

So there is a covenant made before birth, and it was *affirmed* — the verse's *baʿda mā waththaqah* — by everything that came after: prophets, books, and the world itself.

Al-Jalālayn identifies the covenant historically: *the contract He made with them in the revealed Books, to belief in Muhammad ﷺ, after its solemn binding — after it has been confirmed with them.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās narrows it to one person: *Those who break the covenant of Allah regarding this Prophet ﷺ, after ratifying it — after sanctioning, confirming and vouchsafing it.*

All three readings share a structure. Something was agreed. It was documented. It was witnessed. And then broken.

**Breaking the ties.**

This is the middle clause, and Maʿārif's treatment of it is the most useful thing written on the verse. He reads it as a statement about what Islam actually is:

*The cutting asunder of what Allah has commanded should be joined includes all kinds of relationships — the one between Allah and His servant, the one between a man and his parents and relatives, between him and his neighbours and friends, between one Muslim and another, between one man and another. Actually, Islam means fulfilling one's obligations with regard to all these relationships. And this is also the way to follow the Sharīʿah. Deficiency in fulfilling these obligations produces all kinds of disorder among men, and thus the transgressors end up by being destructive for others and for themselves.*

Read that alongside verse 11 — *Do not spread corruption in the land* — and the two verses meet. Verse 11 accused the hypocrites of corruption and they denied it. This verse says what corruption consists of: broken relationships.

Al-Jalālayn lists the categories: *such as cut what God has commanded should be joined — of belief in the Prophet, of kinship, and other matters.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *of oaths and kinsfolk relations.*

**Corruption in the land.**

The third act. Tanwīr al-Miqbās makes it specific to the historical situation: *by preventing people from the Religion of Muhammad ﷺ and the Qurʾān.*

Tazkīrul Qurʾān generalises it and states the principle: *The message of truth seeks to harmonize man with his own nature: those who prevent others from receiving it are guilty of spreading corruption in the land.*

Which is a demanding claim. It means that obstructing a message is not a neutral act of disagreement. It is damage.

**The three acts are one sequence.**

Notice the order: a promise is broken, then relationships are cut, then corruption spreads. Each follows from the last.

Al-Mukhtaṣar connects them causally: *Those who do not take their promises with God seriously are those who cut off from things which God instructed not to, such as blood relations, and they work to spread corruption on earth through their wrongdoing.*

Not taking the promise seriously is the cause. Cutting ties is what that looks like. Corruption is what it produces.

**The losers.**

*Hum al-khāsirūn.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās explains the word: *the duped, in that they lose both this world and the Hereafter.*

Maʿārif closes on the same note: *It is these, the Holy Qurʾān says, who are the losers — in this world as in the other.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *They are the losers in this world and the next.*

The word *khāsir* is commercial again, like verse 16's failed trade. This sūrah keeps returning to the language of loss and profit, because that is how the people it is addressing thought about value. Verse 16 said their trade was profitless. This verse says they are the ones who lost it.

And the sūrah has now used the phrase *spread corruption in the land* twice — at 2:11 as an accusation the hypocrites denied, and here as a description of what they actually did. Verse 12 said *they fail to perceive it.* They still do not see it. The reader does.

28.text:
*How can you deny Allah? You were lifeless and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life, and then to Him you will all be returned.*

**The question that opens the verse.**

*Kayfa takfurūna billāh.* How can you disbelieve in Allah?

Al-Jalālayn explains what kind of question this is, and it is not a request for information: *the interrogative here is either intended to provoke amazement at their persistent unbelief despite the evidence established, or intended as a rebuke.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās agrees: *how astonishing that you disbelieve in Allah.*

It is astonishment, not inquiry. The verse is not asking *why* you disbelieve. It is saying that there is no available answer.

Al-Mukhtaṣar makes the absurdity explicit: *How can you disbelieve the Oneness of Allah when you can see the signs of His power in your own existence?*

**The four stages.**

Dead. Given life. Caused to die. Brought to life again. And then returned.

Al-Jalālayn locates each one: *you were dead — semen inside loins — and He gave you life in the womb and in this world by breathing Spirit into you… then He shall make you dead after your terms of life are completed, then He shall give you life at the Resurrection, then to Him you shall be returned after resurrection, whereupon He shall requite you according to your deeds.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives the same four with the same precision: *when you were dead — sperm drops in the loins of your fathers — and He gave life to you in the wombs of your mothers. Then He will give you death when your lifespan ends, then life again for the Resurrection, and then unto Him ye will be returned in the Hereafter.*

**Ibn ʿAbbās on what "dead" means.**

Ibn Jarīr reported from **ʿAṭāʾ** that **Ibn ʿAbbās** said: *You did not exist beforehand. You were nothing until Allah created you; He will bring death to you and then bring you back to life during Resurrection.*

Then Ibn ʿAbbās connected it to another verse himself: *This is similar to Allah's statement, "They will say: 'Our Lord! You have made us to die twice and You have given us life twice'" (40:11).*

That is the verse's own cross-reference, supplied by a Companion. Two deaths, two lives.

Ibn Kathīr supports the same reading with two more verses: 52:35–36 — *Were they created by nothing? Or were they themselves the creators? Or did they create the heavens and the earth? Nay, but they have no firm belief* — and 76:1: *Has there not been over man a period of time, when he was not a thing worth mentioning?*

*Not a thing worth mentioning.* Lam yakun shayʾan madhkūrā. Before that there was a stretch of time in which you did not count as a thing anyone would mention.

**The argument inside the verse.**

The four stages are arranged to make resurrection unremarkable. You have already been through the hard part.

You were nothing, and something came from that. Death is a smaller step than non-existence was. And if the first life happened once, the second is not a new kind of event.

Ibn Kathīr puts the point as a testimony: *Allah testifies to the fact that He exists and that He is the Creator and the Sustainer Who has full authority over His servants.*

**Maʿārif's harder conclusion.**

He draws an inference from the verse that is worth recording because it is uncomfortable:

*Verse 28 shows that a man who does not apparently deny Allah, but refuses to accept the Holy Prophet ﷺ as the Messenger of Allah, and the Holy Qurʾān as the Book of Allah, would still be counted among those who do not believe in Allah.*

That follows from the verse's grammar. It does not say "how can you deny resurrection." It says *how can you deny Allah* — and treats the denial as already established by the refusal in front of them.

He also notes what the verse does not cover: *Verse 28 mentions only one kind of life which is to follow one's physical death — that is, the life which will begin on [the Day of Resurrection]*, and he sets out the intervening state, the barzakh, separately.

**Why this verse sits here.**

Maʿārif explains the placement: *These two verses speak of the blessings which Allah has showered on man, pointing out that all the same there are men who do not recognize the bounty of Allah and persist in their denial — the suggestion being that if they do not want to take the trouble of considering the arguments which have been advanced by the Holy Qurʾān in the earlier verses, they should, as every man with an undistorted nature must, at least be grateful to their benefactor, for even this would be a way of realizing why they should be obedient to Allah.*

Verses 21–26 argued. These verses stop arguing and simply list what was given.

And the verse's last line closes the account: *then to Him you will all be returned.* Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the consequence: *Then you will return to Him and be held accountable.*

Tazkīrul Qurʾān draws the practical conclusion: *This state of affairs demands that he devote himself entirely to God; that he remember and obey God throughout his life, forever remaining His humble servant.*

29.text:
*He is the One Who created everything in the earth for you. Then He turned towards the heaven, forming it into seven heavens. And He has perfect knowledge of all things.*

**Everything, for you.**

*Mā fī al-arḍ jamīʿan* — all that is in the earth, all of it.

Al-Jalālayn states the purpose: *the earth and all that is in it, so that you may benefit from and learn lessons from it.*

Two purposes, not one. Benefit and lesson. The earth is both a resource and an argument.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās lists what that includes: *of beasts, plants and other things, as a blessing from Him.* He uses the phrase *made subservient for you* — musakhkhar, put at your disposal.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *the countless rivers, trees and so on, from which you benefit and enjoy.*

Maʿārif notes how much is packed into the phrase: *This small phrase comprehends all kinds of benefits which accrue to him from the earth and its produce.*

**Then He turned to the heaven.**

*Thumma istawā ilā as-samāʾ.* Maʿārif works through the word *istawā* carefully, because it is the same word that appears in the Throne verses and is often read the same way:

*The Holy Qurʾān uses the Arabic word istawā, which initially means "to stand upright, to climb," and thence signifies "to turn or pay attention to something," and, in a wider sense, "to take a straight and firm decision which nothing can hinder." The implication here is that Allah being Omniscient and Omnipotent, it was not at all difficult for Him to create the universe, once He had decided to do so.*

Ibn Kathīr gives the straightforward sense: *meaning, He turned towards the heaven.*

Al-Jalālayn adds the sequence: *then, after creating the earth, He turned — that is, He made His object — heaven.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *He turned to the creation of the heaven.*

**Seven heavens — and the grammar that proves it.**

Al-Jalālayn's note here is the tightest piece of syntax in the six sources:

*And levelled them — fa-sawwāhunna. The pronoun -hunna refers to "heaven," since it, heaven, is implicit in the import of the sentence attributed to it the pronoun — that is to say, He made them thus, as He says in another verse, fa-qadāhunna, "so He determined them" (41:12) — seven heavens.*

The pronoun is feminine plural. The word before it, *as-samāʾ*, is singular. So the plurality has to be coming from somewhere — and it is coming from what the verse says next: seven.

**Ibn Kathīr's detailed parallel.**

He says plainly that *this verse (2:29) is explained in detail in Sūrat as-Sajdah* — and then, unusually, he actually quotes 41:9–12 in full:

*Say: "Do you verily disbelieve in Him Who created the earth in two Days? And you set up rivals with Him? That is the Lord of all that exists. He placed therein firm mountains from above it, and He blessed it, and measured therein its sustenance for its dwellers in four Days… Then He turned to the heaven when it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: 'Come both of you willingly or unwillingly.' They both said: 'We come willingly.' Then He finished them as seven heavens in two Days and He made in each heaven its affair. And We adorned the nearest heaven with lamps to be an adornment as well as to guard."*

And then he draws the structural conclusion: *These verses indicate that Allah started creation by creating earth, then He made heaven into seven heavens. This is how building usually starts, with the lower floors first and then the top floors, as the scholars of tafsīr reiterated.*

The earth was built first because it is the ground floor.

**Why the sūrah mentions creation here at all.**

Ibn Kathīr states the purpose: *After Allah mentioned the proofs of His creating them, and what they can witness in themselves as proof of that, He mentioned another proof that they can witness, that is, the creation of the heavens and earth.*

Verse 28 used the listener's own life as the evidence. Verse 29 uses the world around them. Both are visible.

Al-Jalālayn makes the inference explicit, and it points forward to the resurrection argument: *so do you not then think that the One who has the power to create this to begin with — which is much greater than what you are — also has the power to bring you back after death?*

**Knowledge of all things.**

The verse ends abruptly, on knowledge rather than power. *Wa huwa bi-kulli shayʾin ʿalīm.*

Ibn Kathīr: *His knowledge encompasses all His creation, just as He said in another verse, "Should not He Who has created know?" (67:14).*

That question is the verse's closing argument. The one who built it knows it. Which means the creation is not an accident and it is not abandoned — and it means the One addressing you now is the One who made the ground you are standing on.

Al-Jalālayn specifies the scope: *He has knowledge of all things, in their totality and in their individual detail.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās ties the knowledge back to the making: *regarding the creation of the heavens and earth.*

And the three clauses of the verse line up: He made the earth for you. He built the sky over it. He knows all of it. Which is verse 22's argument again — earth, sky, provision — restated with creation and knowledge added, immediately before the sūrah turns to the story of the first human being.

30.text:
*Remember when your Lord said to the angels, "I am going to place a successive human authority on earth." They asked, "Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood, while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness?" Allah responded, "I know what you do not know."*

**Why the story starts here.**

Maʿārif explains the transition from the blessings to the story of Ādam:

*Blessings are of two kinds — tangible and intangible. Food, water, money, houses, or lands are some of the tangible blessings; while honour, happiness or knowledge are intangible ones. The earlier verses were concerned with blessings of the first kind; these verses speak of those of the second kind — that is to say, how Allah bestowed the gift of knowledge on Ādam, made the angels prostrate themselves before him to show their respect, and gave men the honour of being his sons.*

And he marks the unit: *ten verses, beginning with the 30th, tell the story of the father of mankind.*

**Khālīfah — the word the verse turns on.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān defines it: *The literal meaning of "khalīfah" or "caliph" is "one who takes another's place" — a successor. In the age of hereditary rule, it was generally used for a monarch who took the place of his predecessor. According to this usage, the word came to refer to one invested with power.*

Ibn Kathīr reads it as plural and successive rather than as one man, and supports it with four verses: 6:165 — *And it is He Who has made you generations coming after generations, replacing each other on the earth*; 27:62 — *And makes you inheritors of the earth*; 43:60 — *And if it were Our will, We would have made angels to replace you on the earth*; and 7:169 — *Then after them succeeded an evil generation.*

*Meaning people reproducing generation after generation, century after century.*

Then he makes the argument that settles it: *It appears that Allah was not referring to Ādam specifically as khalīfah, otherwise he would not have allowed the angels' statement, "Will You place therein those who will make mischief therein and shed blood."*

One man could not do that. A species could.

**How the angels knew.**

This is a real question, and the sources give three answers.

Ibn Kathīr's first: *The angels knew of this fact, according to their understanding of human nature, for Allah stated that He would create man from clay.*

His second: *Or, the angels understood this fact from the word khalīfah, which also means the person who judges disputes that occur between people, forbidding them from injustice and sin, as al-Qurṭubī said.* A judge presupposes wrongdoing.

Al-Jalālayn gives a third, which is a historical report: *just as the progeny of the jinn did, for they used to inhabit it, but when they became corrupted God sent down the angels against them and they were driven away to islands and into the mountains.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās agrees the angels had been there: *when your Lord said unto the angels, who were already on the earth.*

**The angels were not objecting.**

Ibn Kathīr is firm on this, because it matters:

*The statement the angels uttered was not a form of disputing with Allah, nor out of envy for the Children of Adam, as some mistakenly thought. Allah has described them as those who do not precede Him in speaking, meaning that they do not ask Allah anything without His permission.*

And then he explains what the question was: *This is only a question for the sake of learning about the wisdom of that, as if they said, "Our Lord! What is the wisdom of creating such creatures, since they will cause trouble in the earth and spill blood? If the wisdom behind this action is that You be worshipped, we praise and glorify You — we never indulge in mischief — so why create other creatures?"*

Al-Jalālayn catches the grammar that carries the implied claim: *the lām of laka — "You" — is extra, and the sentence wa-nuqaddisu laka, "We sanctify You," is a circumstantial qualifier, the import being "thus we are more entitled to be Your vicegerents."*

The words are a question. The structure is an argument.

Ibn Kathīr records a reading that takes this further — that it was *their request that they should be allowed to inhabit the earth instead of the Children of Adam* — and attributes it to ar-Rāzī and others.

**"I know what you do not know."**

Ibn Kathīr's main reading is an answer, not a refusal to answer:

*Meaning, "I know that the benefit of creating this type of creature outweighs the harm that you mentioned, that which you have no knowledge of. I will create among them Prophets and send Messengers. I will also create among them truthful, martyrs, righteous believers, worshippers, the modest, the pious, the scholars who implement their knowledge, humble people and those who love Allah and follow His Messengers."*

Tazkīrul Qurʾān makes the same point with an image that is worth keeping:

*If many human beings were to be corrupted by their power, there would also be a substantial number who, in spite of their power and freedom on earth, would acknowledge God's greatness and their own helplessness. Such people would, of their own free will, adopt the path of submission and obedience to God. Although comparatively few in number, they would be specially prized above all others. They would be just like the food grains at harvest time, which, although greatly outweighed in bulk by chaff and straw, are the truly valuable part.*

The angels counted the chaff. Allah was counting the grain.

**Ibn Kathīr's illustration.**

He brings a ḥadīth to show the answer being enacted:

*The Ṣaḥīḥ recorded that when the angels ascend to Allah with the records of the servant's deeds, Allah asks them, while having better knowledge, "How did you leave My servants?" They will say, "We came to them while they were praying and left them while they were praying." This is because the angels work in shifts with mankind, and they change shifts during the Fajr and ʿAṣr prayers.*

Then he gives the Prophet's ﷺ words: *The deeds of the night are elevated to Allah before the morning, and the deeds of the morning before the night falls.*

And he ties it back to the verse: *the angels' statement, "We came to them while they were praying and left them while they were praying," explains Allah's statement, "I know that which you do not know."*

The angels predicted bloodshed. What they actually report, twice a day, is prayer.

**What the verse was later used to establish.**

Al-Qurṭubī, as Ibn Kathīr records, took the verse into law:

*Al-Qurṭubī, as well as other scholars, said that this verse proves the obligation of appointing a khalīfah to pass judgements on matters of dispute between people, to aid the oppressed against the oppressor, to implement the Islamic penal code and to forbid evil. There are many other tasks that can only be fulfilled by appointing the Imām, and what is necessary in performing an obligation is an obligation itself.*

He then sets out how succession works, with the precedents named: by the Prophet ﷺ naming a successor, as with **Abū Bakr**; by the current khalīfah naming the next, *as Abū Bakr did with ʿUmar*; by leaving it to a consultative council, *just as ʿUmar did*; or by the people of authority gathering around one person and giving him the pledge of allegiance.

**What verse 30 sets up.**

The angels asked a question. The answer was not given to them in full. Verse 31 begins *And He taught Ādam the names of all things* — and the rest of the story is the answer being demonstrated.

31.text:
*He taught Adam the names of all things, then He presented them to the angels and said, "Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true?"*

**The answer to verse 30's question.**

The angels asked what the wisdom was. This verse does not answer in words. It demonstrates.

Ibn Kathīr states the purpose directly: *Allah stated the virtue of Ādam above the angels, because He taught Ādam, rather than them, the names of everything.*

And he explains the ordering, because the prostration in verse 34 actually happened before this: *This occurred after they prostrated to him. This discussion precedes that event here, only to show the importance of his position, and the absence of the angels' knowledge about creating the khalīfah when they asked about it.*

**Which names.**

Ad-Daḥḥāk said that **Ibn ʿAbbās** commented: *the names that people use, such as human, animal, sky, earth, land, sea, horse, donkey, and so forth, including the names of the other species.*

Then Ibn Kathīr records an exchange that is almost comic in its plainness. **Ibn Abī Ḥātim** and **Ibn Jarīr** reported that **ʿĀṣim ibn Kulayb** narrated from **Saʿīd ibn Maʿbad** that **Ibn ʿAbbās** was questioned: *Did Allah teach him the names of the plate and the pot?* He said, *Yes — and even the terms for breaking wind!*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives the same domestic list: *the names of all the beasts and other things, including a cooking pot, a plate and saucer.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the scope: *their pronunciation and meanings.* Not just the labels. What they mean.

Al-Jalālayn narrows it differently: *the names of things named, all of them, by placing knowledge of them into his heart… these names, the majority of which concerned intellectual beings.*

Ibn Kathīr's summary covers all of it: *Allah taught Ādam the names of everything, their proper names, the names of their characteristics, and what they do.*

**Why names are the test.**

Maʿārif records the conclusion one school drew from this verse, and it is larger than the story:

*This episode, according to Imām al-Ashʿarī, shows that language as such has been created by Allah Himself, and not invented by man — its use by different kinds of men has later on produced the many forms of language.*

Language is not a human technology. It was given. Which is why knowing the names is the qualification for the khalīfah — the vicegerent has to be able to name things, sort them, decide between them. That is what judging means.

**A detail in the wording that Maʿārif catches.**

*One should note a subtle suggestion here in the use of two words. In asking the angels for the names of things, Allah said anbiʾūnī — "Tell Me." But in commanding Ādam to do so, He said anbiʾhum — "Tell them." The difference in the mode of expression shows that Ādam was given the rank of a teacher, and the angels that of pupils. It is thus an indication of his superiority over them.*

The angels were asked to report upward. Ādam was told to teach outward.

And he draws a second inference: *an increase or decrease is possible in the degree of knowledge the angels possess, for they were given, through Ādam, at least a primary knowledge about a thing which they did not know before.*

Angels can learn. That is not usually assumed.

**"If what you say is true."**

Al-Jalālayn identifies what is being referred back to, and it is verse 30:

*Said to them in reproach: "Now tell Me, inform Me, the names of these things named, if you speak truly" — in your claim that I would not create anything more knowledgeable than you, or that you are more deserving of this vicegerency.*

The angels never said this in words. Verse 30 recorded their question. Al-Jalālayn is reading the implication of *while we glorify Your praises* — which he had already noted carries the sense *thus we are more entitled to be Your vicegerents.*

So the challenge in this verse answers an argument nobody stated aloud.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *if ye are truthful in your first claim.* Al-Mukhtaṣar: *if they were telling the truth when they said that they were a nobler and better creation than Ādam.*

**Tazkīrul Qurʾān's reading.**

Tazkīrul reads the demonstration differently, and it connects the verse back to the angels' fear of bloodshed:

*The mixture of good and evil in mankind became evident when God, in His omnipotence, brought all the progeny of Ādam before their first father. He said to the angels, "Look, these are the progeny of Ādam. Can you give me the name of each one of them, and say what sort of people they will be?" The angels, having no knowledge of them, were unable to answer. Then God told Ādam their names and characteristics, and then commanded him to pass the knowledge on to the angels. When Ādam had explained to them the nature of the human race, they realized that, besides the wicked and the corrupt, there would also be among their number great, righteous and pious souls.*

On this reading, verse 31 is where the angels finally see the grain among the chaff.

**Where this verse goes.**

Ibn Kathīr quotes **al-Bukhārī** explaining this verse with a report from **Anas ibn Mālik**, in which the Prophet ﷺ describes the Day of Judgement: the believers go to Ādam for intercession and say, *You are the father of mankind. Allah created you with His Own Hand, made the angels prostrate to you, and taught you the names of everything — so intercede for us with your Lord.*

Ādam's three distinctions, listed by the Prophet ﷺ, are the three things these four verses describe.

32.text:
*They replied, "Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise."*

**The shortest verse in this story, and the one that undoes verse 30.**

The angels had implied that they were more deserving. Here they withdraw it, and they do it in three movements: exalt Allah, admit the limit, affirm the two names.

**Glory be to You.**

Al-Jalālayn glosses *subḥānaka* as *exalting You above that any should object to You.*

Not "forgive us for asking." Something stronger — the act of questioning is placed outside what is fitting, and Allah is declared above it.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads it as repentance: *Be glorified! We repent to you of what we said.*

That reading depends on the previous verse having been a fault. Ibn Kathīr's position was the opposite — that *the statement the angels uttered was not a form of disputing with Allah.* Both readings are in the sources, and the verse does not settle it.

**We have no knowledge except what You have taught us.**

This is the verse's centre, and it is a statement about angels, not about people.

Maʿārif's inference from the whole episode was that *an increase or decrease is possible in the degree of knowledge the angels possess.* This verse is the angels saying it themselves. Their knowledge has a boundary, and the boundary was set by teaching rather than by nature.

Al-Mukhtaṣar expands the admission: *Recognising their shortcomings and that everything comes from Allah, they said that they acknowledged that His judgement and sacred law could not be doubted, and that they had no knowledge except for the knowledge He had given them.*

Al-Jalālayn keeps it tight: *We know not except what You have taught us.*

**The two names.**

*Innaka anta al-ʿalīmu al-ḥakīm.* Al-Jalālayn notes the emphasis: *innaka anta emphasises the preceding suffixed pronoun kāf.* You — and only You — are the Knower, the Wise.

Then he defines each: *from whose knowledge and wisdom nothing escapes.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar separates them: *accepting that He is the Knowing, from Whom nothing is hidden, and the Wise in His decrees and laws.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās applies each name to the situation in front of them: *Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Knower — of us and of them — the Wise — regarding our matters and theirs.*

Us and them. Angels and humans. That is the whole dispute in four words.

**Why the two names are the right two.**

The angels had questioned a decision. Their answer affirms knowledge and wisdom — the two qualities a decision requires.

They are not saying "You are powerful, so we submit." They are saying "You know what we do not, and what You do is wise." Which is exactly what verse 30's reply had asserted: *I know what you do not know.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar's phrase *His judgement and sacred law could not be doubted* states the outcome. The question from verse 30 is closed.

And the verse does something else, quietly. In admitting that their knowledge was taught, the angels accept the possibility that someone else could be taught something they were not. That is precisely what verse 33 is about to show.

33.text:
*Allah said, "O Adam! Inform them of their names." Then when Adam did, Allah said, "Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?"*

**Tell them.**

*Anbiʾhum.* Maʿārif's observation, noted at verse 31, lands here: the angels were told *anbiʾūnī* — tell Me. Ādam is told *anbiʾhum* — tell them.

*The difference in the mode of expression shows that Ādam was given the rank of a teacher, and the angels that of pupils. It is thus an indication of his superiority over them.*

The verse does not narrate a test being passed. It narrates a lesson being given.

**What Ādam actually said.**

Al-Jalālayn's account is the fullest: *so he named each thing by its appellation and mentioned the wisdom behind its creation.*

Two things, not one. The name, and the reason it exists. That is more than a vocabulary test — it is the work of a vicegerent, who has to know what things are *for* in order to rule between them.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *When Ādam told the angels the names of things, as he had been taught.*

**Did I not tell you.**

*Alam aqul lakum.* The verse refers back to 2:30's *I know what you do not know* — and treats it as something already said, which it was.

Ibn Kathīr had already explained the function of that earlier reply: *So Allah informed the angels that He knows what they do not know, and then He mentioned this to show them Ādam's superiority over them in knowledge.*

Now the demonstration is complete and the earlier statement is confirmed.

**The secrets of the heavens and the earth.**

*Ghayb as-samāwāti wa al-arḍ.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *the unseen that will take place in the heavens and on the earth.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *everything hidden in the heavens and the earth.*

Note the scope. Not "the unseen in Ādam." In the heavens and the earth — everything, everywhere, including what the angels themselves were about to say.

**What you reveal and what you conceal.**

This is the sharpest line in the verse, and Al-Jalālayn identifies both halves precisely:

*And I know what you reveal — what you manifested when you said, "What will You appoint therein…" — and what you were hiding — what you were keeping secret when you were saying that God would not create anything more knowledgeable or more noble in His eyes than us.*

So the *revealed* part is verse 30's question, which is in the Qurʾān for everyone to read. The *concealed* part is the implication Al-Jalālayn had already drawn out of it — that they considered themselves more entitled.

The verse is telling them: I heard the part you did not say.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives a second reading, and it is a different pair: *And I know that which ye disclose — what you show to your Lord in terms of your obedience to Ādam — and that which ye hide — of this obedience. It is also said that this refers to what Satan disclosed and kept hidden from them.*

On that reading the concealment belongs to Iblīs, and the verse is foreshadowing verse 34.

**Why the verse is addressed to the angels after Ādam has spoken.**

The sequence matters. Ādam teaches. Then Allah turns back to the angels.

He does not congratulate Ādam. He reminds them. Which means the lesson was never for Ādam — he already knew the names. It was for them.

Maʿārif sums up what they had just learned: *The episode recounted in the foregoing verses has shown how the angels came to learn that Ādam was superior to them in so far as he possessed the forms of knowledge necessary for the function of divine vice regency, while they themselves did not, nor did the jinns.*

Tazkīrul Qurʾān adds the moral the episode carries into the rest of the sūrah, connecting it back to the corruption and bloodshed of verse 30:

*Man's greatest crimes, after the denial of his Lord, are spreading corruption and causing bloodshed in the world. Neither an individual nor a group has God's permission to indulge in such actions as may disrupt the order of nature established by God… In short, preserving the system of nature is "to reform" it, while upsetting this system is equal "to spreading corruption."*

That is the definition the whole sūrah will use. Verse 11 accused the hypocrites of spreading corruption in the land. Verse 27 defined it as broken ties. And here, at the origin of the human story, the standard is set.

**What the verse closes.**

Verse 30's question — *will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood?* — is now answered three ways. The angels have seen that Ādam was given what they were not. They have admitted their knowledge has limits. And Allah has told them He knew what they did not say out loud.

The next verse stops arguing entirely and gives an order.

34.text:
*And remember when We said to the angels, "Prostrate before Adam," so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful.*

**The honour made visible.**

Maʿārif explains what the verse adds to the three before it:

*Now, Allah willed to manifest this superiority in a visible and concrete form. So, He commanded the angels to prostrate themselves before Ādam in his honour.*

Verses 31–33 established superiority in knowledge. This verse enacts it in the body.

Ibn Kathīr: *This verse mentions the great honor that Allah granted Ādam, and Allah reminded Ādam's offspring of this fact.*

Reminded. The verse is addressed to the readers, not only narrated at the angels.

**The obedience and the direction.**

**Qatādah** commented: *The obedience was for Allah and the prostration was before Adam. Allah honored Adam and commanded the angels to prostrate before him.*

That distinction is the whole ruling. The act was directed at Ādam; the worship was for Allah.

Ibn Kathīr records the other reading: *Some people said that this prostration was just a prostration of greeting, peace and honor*, and he supports it with 12:100, where Yūsuf's parents and brothers fall prostrate before him: *And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell before him in prostration. And he said, "O my father, this is the explanation of my vision of before."*

Al-Jalālayn agrees: *a prostration that is a bow of salutation.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *a prostration of salutation.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the purpose: *out of recognition and respect.*

**Why Iblīs was included.**

This is the verse's hardest question, and Ibn Kathīr handles it directly under the heading *Iblīs was among those ordered to prostrate before Ādam, although he was not an angel*:

*When Allah commanded the angels to prostrate before Ādam, Iblīs was included in this command. Although Iblīs was not an angel, he was trying — and pretending — to imitate the angels' behavior and deeds, and this is why he was also included in the command.*

Then he points forward to the verse that settles it, 18:50: *Except Iblīs. He was one of the jinn; he disobeyed the command of his Lord.*

**ʿAzāzīl.**

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported that **Ibn ʿAbbās** said:

*Before he undertook the path of sin, Iblīs was with the angels and was called ʿAzāzīl. He was among the residents of the earth and was one of the most active worshippers and knowledgeable persons among the angels. This fact caused him to be arrogant. Iblīs was from a genus called Jinn.*

Read the middle of that again. *One of the most active worshippers and knowledgeable persons.* The being who refused the command was not ignorant or lazy. He was outstanding.

*This fact caused him to be arrogant.* Not the refusal caused the arrogance. The excellence did.

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the same arc: *Due to the excellence of his worship, Allah had entered Iblīs into the company of the angels; but he then returned to his lowly nature, refusing to prostrate as Allah told him to, and becoming proud towards Ādam, leading to him becoming a disbeliever.*

Al-Jalālayn records what he said, quoting 7:12: *he refused to prostrate and disdained — became proud — and said, "I am better than he."*

**Maʿārif on who was actually commanded.**

He pushes the reading further than Ibn Kathīr:

*If we go by the words of the Holy Qurʾān, the command was given to the angels alone, but, in excepting Iblīs from those who obeyed, the text also suggests that the command was given to all the created beings that existed at that time and possessed understanding, including the jinns as well as the angels. But the Holy Qurʾān mentions the angels alone, because when superior beings like the angels were required to show their respect for Ādam, inferior creatures like the jinns must, it goes without saying, have been ordered to do the same.*

An argument from the greater to the lesser. If the angels were ordered, everybody was.

**Becoming unfaithful.**

*Kāna min al-kāfirīn.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And so became a disbeliever after this, because he refused to comply with Allah's command. It is also said that it was in Allah's foreknowledge that Satan was to become a disbeliever; as it is said that he was the first unbeliever ever.*

Al-Jalālayn takes the foreknowledge reading and makes it precise: *and so he became one of the disbelievers according to God's knowledge.*

That phrase matters. The verse is not saying Allah discovered something. Al-Jalālayn is saying the status was known, and the refusal made it manifest.

Ibn Kathīr's translation carries the same point in its gloss: *he refused and was proud and was one of the disbelievers (disobedient to Allah).*

**What Iblīs's name means.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān gives the etymology: *The word literally means one who was far from the truth, and from the mercy of God.*

Which is what the verse describes happening. Not punishment arriving. Distance.

**The verse's place in the story.**

Verse 30 announced the khalīfah. Verses 31–33 demonstrated why. Verse 34 enacts the honour — and immediately introduces the one who refused it.

The sūrah has now given the origin of the two lines it will follow for the rest of its length: those who submit when commanded, and those who think they know better. The angels are the first example of the one. Iblīs is the first of the other.

And verse 30's answer — *I know what you do not know* — turns out to have covered this too. Ibn Kathīr had recorded a reading of that phrase: *I know that Iblīs is not as you are, although he is among you.*

35.text:
*We cautioned, "O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers."*

**Was Ādam a prophet?**

Somebody asked. **Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr ibn Marduwyah** reported **Abū Dharr** saying: *I said, "O Messenger of Allah! Was Ādam a Prophet?" He said, "Yes. He was a Prophet and a Messenger to whom Allah spoke directly"* — and the proof given was this very verse.

*Kallamahu qibulā.* Spoken to directly, without an intermediary. That is what makes this verse the evidence: *We said, "O Ādam!"*

**Where Ḥawwāʾ came from.**

Ibn Kathīr notes the ordering the verse implies: *The verse indicates that Ḥawwāʾ was created before Ādam entered Paradise, as Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq stated.*

Then Ibn Isḥāq's account: *After Allah finished criticizing Iblīs, and after teaching Ādam the names of everything… Ādam fell asleep, as the People of the Book and other scholars such as Ibn ʿAbbās have stated. Allah took one of Ādam's left ribs and made flesh grow in its place, while Ādam was asleep and unaware. Allah then created Ādam's wife, Ḥawwāʾ, from his rib and made her a woman, so that she could be a comfort for him. When Ādam woke up and saw Ḥawwāʾ next to him, it was claimed, he said, "My flesh and blood, my wife."*

Al-Jalālayn confirms the detail in one clause: *and your wife, Eve — Ḥawwāʾ — who was created from his left rib.*

*So that she could be a comfort for him.* Sakān. The same word the verse uses for *live* — *uskun*. The dwelling and the comfort are the same idea.

**Eat freely.**

*Raghadan ḥaythu shiʾtumā.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *without restriction, thereof where ye will and whenever you will.*

Al-Jalālayn: *eat thereof, of its food, easefully, of anything without restrictions, where you desire.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *with nothing to ruin their bliss… to consume the delightful food from anywhere in the Garden.*

The permission is total. Every tree in the garden except one. Which is the shape of every prohibition in this sūrah — a wide allowance with a single boundary.

**The one word that carries the verse.**

Uskun. Live. Dwell. Settle.

It is the same root as the word used for Ḥawwāʾ in Ibn Isḥāq's account — *so that she could be a comfort for him* — and the same root as the earth's description in verse 22, *a place of settlement*, and again in verse 36, *you will find in the earth a residence*.

The sūrah uses this word for Paradise, for a wife, and for the earth. All three are described as places you settle in. Which means the expulsion in verse 36 is not a removal from the idea of dwelling. It is a transfer of it.

Al-Jalālayn also catches a small grammatical point in the address itself: *and We said, "Ādam, dwell" — anta, "you," of "dwell you," reiterates the concealed pronoun of the person of the verb uskun, so that wa-zawjuk — "and your wife" — may be made a supplement to it.*

The pronoun is stated twice so that Ḥawwāʾ can be added to it grammatically. She is included in the command, not merely present at it.

**Which tree.**

Nobody says. Al-Jalālayn records the candidates and refuses to choose: *but do not come near this tree to eat from it — and this was wheat, or a vine, or something else.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās offers a reading rather than a species: *but do not eat from this tree, the tree of knowledge, which includes all types and kinds.*

The sūrah's silence is deliberate, and the commentators honour it. What matters is that there was one.

**Do not come near.**

Not "do not eat." *Lā taqrabā.* Come not near.

Al-Jalālayn notes the verse then adds the eating anyway: *but do not come near this tree to eat from it.* The prohibition is on approach, and the eating is what approach leads to.

That is the same logic the sūrah uses throughout its rulings — the boundary is set before the act, not at it.

**Or you will be wrongdoers.**

*Fa-takūnā min aẓ-ẓālimīn.* Al-Jalālayn: *lest you become evildoers — that is, transgressors.* Al-Mukhtaṣar: *they would become wrongdoers for disobeying Him.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *lest you harm yourselves.*

Three glosses, and Tanwīr's is the one worth holding. Ẓulm is not only injustice to others. Its first meaning is putting a thing in the wrong place — and here the wrong done is to themselves.

**Why Iblīs was watching.**

Maʿārif sets up the next verse: *having been disgraced because of Ādam, Iblīs or Satan had an account to settle with him, and as soon as he got the opportunity, he tricked them into eating from this tree.*

And he notes what the command included, which the verse does not spell out: *they were at the same time warned that their existence on the earth would no longer be full of perpetual bliss as it had been in Paradise, but that there would be dissension and enmity among men, their progeny, which would spoil the joy of earthly life.*

Tazkīrul Qurʾān reads the whole episode as a demonstration set up in front of the angels:

*He was giving the first man on earth a practical demonstration of the two paths that would be open to his progeny. Either they would follow the example of the angels and bow to God's commandments, even if it meant bowing before someone they held inferior to themselves; or else they would be proud like Satan, and refuse to bow to others. This is the test that man faces throughout his entire life.*

36.text:
*But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the blissful state they were in, and We said, "Descend from the heavens to the earth as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay."*

**The verb, and a variant reading.**

*Fa-azallahumā.* Al-Jalālayn gives both readings and both meanings:

*Then Satan, Iblīs, caused them to slip — he caused them to be removed. Fa-azallahumā; a variant reading has fa-azālahumā, he caused them to be away from it, therefrom, that is, from the Garden.*

Slipped, or removed. One is a stumble; the other is an eviction. The two readings describe the same event from inside and outside.

**How he did it.**

Al-Jalālayn supplies the method, and it is the detail people usually miss:

*When he said to them, "Shall I point you to the tree of eternity?" (20:120), and swore to them by God that he was only giving good advice to them — and so they ate of it.*

He swore by Allah. That is what 7:21 records, and it is why they believed him.

Maʿārif raises the obvious problem and works through it:

*A question arises here as to how Satan got into Paradise for seducing Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ, when he had already been expelled from there for refusing to prostrate himself. There are many possible ways in which he can have played his trick. Possibly he never met them, but planted the suggestion in their minds from afar — a thing which Satan can always do, and of which we have a specimen in the work of the hypnotists. It is equally possible that Satan, being one of the jinns whom Allah has given certain unusual powers denied to man, assumed the shape of a snake or of something else, and thus succeeded in entering Paradise. Perhaps it was because of this disguise that Ādam did not remember Allah's warning that Satan was his enemy.
