According to the Holy Qurʾān, Satan assured them on oath that he was one of their well-wishers (7:21). It apparently suggests that he did actually meet them, and speak to them face to face.*

Three possibilities, and he keeps all three open.

**Who was sent down.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names four: *and We said to Ādam, Eve, the peacock and the serpent: "Fall down" — go down to the earth.*

Al-Jalālayn includes the whole line instead: *Go down to earth, both of you, and all those comprised by your seed.*

Which is why the verse speaks in the plural. Not two people. A species.

**As enemies to each other.**

Al-Jalālayn: *some of you, of your progeny, an enemy to the other, through your wronging one another.*

Maʿārif connects it to the warning already given in verse 35 — that earthly life would carry *dissension and enmity among men, their progeny, which would spoil the joy of earthly life.*

Enmity is not the punishment. It is a condition of the place they are going to.

**Who actually brought them out.**

Maʿārif makes a careful distinction about the Arabic:

*The Holy Qurʾān says that Satan fa-akhrajahumā — "brought them out" — of the state in which they had been living. In actual fact, they were "brought out" under a divine command, but since Satan served [as the means]…*

The verse attributes the expulsion to Satan because he was the instrument. The command was Allah's. Both are true and the verse holds both.

**A residence and provision for a time.**

*Ilaḥīn.* Al-Jalālayn: *a dwelling, a place of settlement, shall be yours, and enjoyment of whatever of its vegetation you may enjoy, for a while — until the time your terms of life are concluded.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *a habitation, a dwelling-place, and a provision, a benefit and livelihood, for a time — until the moment of death.*

Note what the earth is called. Not a punishment. A dwelling and a provision. Verse 22 had already described the earth as *a place of settlement* — the same word, given to everyone before this story was told.

**What the verse is really about.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān states the lesson:

*The practical lesson of the forbidden tree demonstrates how man goes astray by letting himself be deceived by Satan, and exceeding the bounds that God has laid down for him. As soon as he eats of the "forbidden fruit," he is deprived of God's grace or, in other words, Paradise. But this loss is not an irretrievable one. Man still has an opportunity to turn in repentance to his Lord, rectify his actions and seek forgiveness for his sins.*

Which is exactly what verse 37 does. The slip is not the end of the story, and the sūrah says so immediately.

37.text:
*Then Adam was inspired with words of prayer by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.*

**Which words.**

Ibn Kathīr opens with the majority position, and the list of authorities behind it is unusually long:

*It was reported that the above verse is explained by Allah's statement, "They said: 'Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You forgive us not, and bestow not upon us Your mercy, we shall certainly be of the losers'" (7:23), as Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, Khālid ibn Maʿdān, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam have stated.*

Ten named authorities. Al-Mukhtaṣar agrees and quotes the same verse.

Al-Jalālayn notes a variant that changes who receives them: *a variant reading of Ādamu has accusative Ādama and nominative kalimātu, meaning they — the words — came to him.*

Either Ādam received the words, or the words came to Ādam. Both readings put the initiative with Allah.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās adds why it matters beyond Ādam: *Ādam learnt from his Lord, and it is said that he was taught and inspired with words, so that they became a way for him and his progeny to repentance.*

The words were given so that everyone after him would have them.

**As-Suddī's version of the exchange.**

Ibn Kathīr records a second account, from **As-Suddī** reporting **Ibn ʿAbbās**:

*Ādam said, "O Lord! Did You not create me with Your Own Hands?" He said, "Yes." He said, "And blow life into me?" He said, "Yes." He said, "And when I sneezed, You said, 'May Allah grant you His mercy.' Does not Your mercy precede Your anger?" He was told, "Yes." Ādam said, "And You destined me to commit this evil act?" He was told, "Yes." He said, "If I repent, will You send me back to Paradise?" Allah said, "Yes."*

Then Ibn Kathīr gives the grading: *Similar is reported from al-ʿAwfī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Saʿīd ibn Maʿbad, and Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Ḥākim recorded this ḥadīth in his Mustadrak from Ibn Jubayr, who narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Ḥākim said, "Its chain is ṣaḥīḥ, and they (al-Bukhārī and Muslim) did not record it."*

Read the middle of that exchange. *Does not Your mercy precede Your anger?* That is the whole argument of repentance in one question, and it is answered yes.

**He accepted his repentance.**

*Fa-tāba ʿalayh.* Ibn Kathīr: *meaning that Allah forgives whoever regrets his error and returns to Him in repentance.*

Then he brings three verses to establish that this is general, not specific to Ādam:

9:104 — *Know they not that Allah accepts repentance from His servants?*
4:110 — *And whoever does evil or wrongs himself…*
25:71 — *And whosoever repents and does righteous good deeds…*

Al-Jalālayn: *truly He is the Relenting to His servants, the Merciful to them.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *the One Who overlooks misdeeds, the Merciful towards any that dies repentant.*

*Towards any that dies repentant.* The condition is attached to the mercy.

**Why this verse sits between the two descents.**

Verse 36 said *descend*. Verse 38 says *descend, all of you*. Between them, Ādam repented and was forgiven.

Maʿārif explains what that changes — and it is the most important observation in the six sources on this passage:

*The command for Ādam to go down to the earth was not withdrawn even when he had been pardoned: only the mode was now altered. Earlier the command had been given in the mode of authority, and the sending down to the earth intended as a punishment — hence the reference to the enmity among men. Now, it was in the mode of wisdom, and the sending down to the earth, an honour — the honour of vice regency. Hence the reference to things vice regency involves.*

The descent still happens. What changes is what it means. Punishment becomes office.

Tazkīrul Qurʾān describes the forgiveness itself: *When he turns to the Lord in repentance, God relents towards him, and cleanses him of his sins, as if he had never committed them.*

As if he had never committed them. Not reduced. Erased.

**And the two names.**

*At-tawwābu ar-raḥīm.* The Accepter of Repentance, the Most Merciful.

*Tawwāb* is intensive — not "one who accepts repentance" but one who does so repeatedly, who keeps accepting. Which is what a species descended from a man who slipped requires.

38.text:
*We said, "Descend all of you! Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve."*

**The command repeated.**

Al-Jalālayn explains why: *We said, "Go down from it, from the Garden, all together." He has repeated this phrase, qulnā ihbiṭū, in order to supplement it with [what follows].*

The repetition is grammatical, but it is also emphatic. The first descent in verse 36 carried enmity. This one carries guidance.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names the company again: *We said to Ādam, Eve, the serpent, the peacock and Satan: "Go down" from heaven, all of you. Then Allah mentioned Ādam's progeny.*

**What guidance is.**

Abū al-ʿĀliyah defined it, and Ibn Kathīr records the definition: *Al-hudā refers to the Prophets, Messengers, the clear signs and plain explanation.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās compresses it: *a scripture and an emissary.*

Al-Jalālayn: *there shall come to you from Me guidance — a Book and a prophet.*

Not an idea. A book and a person.

Maʿārif states what this means for the descent: *In commanding Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ and their progeny to live on the earth, Allah told them that He would be sending down to men His guidance — that is, the injunctions of the Sharīʿah — through revelation.*

**No fear, no grief.**

Ibn Kathīr assigns each to a direction in time:

*Whoever follows My guidance, meaning, whoever accepts what is contained in My Books and what I send the Messengers with — there shall be no fear on them regarding the Hereafter, nor shall they grieve regarding the life of this world.*

Fear is forward. Grief is backward. Neither one.

Maʿārif draws the practical consequence: *those who follow it faithfully shall be free from sorrow and anxiety — in other words, they shall not have to grieve about any loss in the past, nor to worry about some misfortune in the future.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives the same split and then an eschatological reading of it:

*There shall no fear come upon them regarding any torment in the future, neither shall they grieve about what they have left behind them. It is also said that this means that no fear will come upon them perpetually, nor will they grieve perpetually; no fear will come upon them when death is slain, and they will not grieve when Hell is closed.*

**The parallel verse, and Ibn ʿAbbās on it.**

Ibn Kathīr brings 20:123 alongside, which says the same thing in different words:

*"Get you down from the Paradise to the earth, both of you, together, some of you are an enemy to some others. Then if there comes to you guidance from Me, then whoever follows My guidance, he shall neither go astray, nor shall he be distressed."*

*Ibn ʿAbbās commented: "He will not be misguided in this life, or miserable in the Hereafter."*

Then he gives the counterpart, 20:124: *But whosoever turns away from My Reminder, verily, for him is a life of hardship, and We shall raise him up blind on the Day of Resurrection.*

**Why the descent was not a punishment.**

This is Maʿārif's argument from verse 37, and it explains why verse 38 sounds the way it does. A punishment does not come with a promise.

*Earlier the command had been given in the mode of authority, and the sending down to the earth intended as a punishment. Now, it was in the mode of wisdom, and the sending down to the earth, an honour — the honour of vice regency.*

Verse 38 is the terms of the office. You are going down. Guidance will follow you. If you follow it, you will not be afraid and you will not be sad.

Tazkīrul Qurʾān closes the story with what it was for:

*God does not become plainly visible in this world; He reveals Himself through His signs, thereby testing his creatures. It is only those who can interpret His signs who will discover God Himself.*

Which is what the earth is: a place where the signs are available and reading them is the test.

And the sūrah has now finished the whole of human history in nine verses. Verse 40 turns to one family within it.

39.text:
*But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.*

**The other half of verse 38.**

Verse 38 gave the promise to those who follow guidance. This verse gives the counterpart, and it is the same two-part structure: a description, then a permanence.

*Disbelieve* and *deny Our signs.* Two acts, and the second is what the first looks like from outside.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās identifies the signs with the same pair used for guidance: *But those who disbelieve, and deny our revelations — the scripture and the Emissary.*

So the rejection is of the same two things verse 38 promised. A Book and a prophet.

**Residents, not visitors.**

*Aṣḥābu an-nār.* The word *aṣḥāb* means companions, people who belong to a place. Not "inhabitants" but *those of* the Fire.

Al-Jalālayn: *those shall be the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein — enduring perpetually, neither perishing nor exiting therefrom.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *such are rightful owners of the Fire, the dwellers of Hell. They will abide therein forever: never to die, or be released from it.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *they are the people of the fire of Hell, who will live there eternally.*

**Neither perishing nor exiting.**

Al-Jalālayn's two negations cover both possible exits. You cannot die out of it, and you cannot leave it.

That is the same pair of words the sūrah used of Paradise at 2:25 — *they will be there forever*, *neither perishing nor departing therefrom.* The two verses are mirror images, and verse 25 was authored four verses before the story of Ādam even began.

Ibn Kathīr states it flatly: *meaning, they will remain in Hell for eternity and will not find a way out of it.*

**What the nine verses add up to.**

Verses 30–39 told one story: a khalīfah announced, a question asked, an answer demonstrated, an honour given, one refusal, one permission with one boundary, one deception, one repentance, and two destinations.

The sūrah has now set out the whole frame. Verse 40 begins *O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I have bestowed upon you* — and everything that follows, for two hundred verses, is that frame applied to one family and then to the community that receives the Book.

Tazkīrul Qurʾān's closing observation on the story is the one to carry forward:

*The preacher of truth is an "Ādam"; it is for people to bow before him. If, carried away by pride and prejudice, they refuse to acknowledge his position, they are following in Satan's footsteps. Such a denial amounts to having failed the test devised for man by God.*

The test at verse 34 was not a one-off event in the garden. It is the same test, running continuously, in every generation.

40.text:
*O children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you. Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine, and stand in awe of Me alone.*

**Why the sūrah turns here.**

Maʿārif's overview of what has come before is the clearest map of the sūrah's opening available:

*The Sūrah al-Baqarah begins by speaking of the Holy Qurʾān itself, and tells us that although it provides guidance to all men, yet only true Muslims will derive a full benefit from it. The Sūrah proceeds to warn the disbelievers against the grievous punishment which awaits them in the other world, and also to delineate the misdeeds of the two kinds of disbelievers — those who deny openly, and the hypocrites. Then, addressing all the three groups, it urges upon them to worship Allah alone, and, presenting the Holy Qurʾān as a miracle which cannot be imitated by man, invites them to have faith in it. Next, the Sūrah recounts how Ādam was created to be the vice regent of Allah, and thus shows the omnipotence and wisdom of Allah so that men may realize why they must obey and worship Him and never be disobedient to Him.*

And then he identifies who is actually in front of the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah — two kinds of people among the disbelievers and hypocrites, the idolaters on one side and the People of the Book on the other. Verse 40 turns to the second group.

**Children of Israel.**

*Banū Isrāʾīl.* Ibn Kathīr explains the form of address:

*He also reminded them with the example of their father Israel, Allah's Prophet Yaʿqūb, as if saying, "O children of the pious, righteous servant of Allah who obeyed Allah! Be like your father, following the truth." This statement is similar to one's saying, "O you son of that generous man! Do this or that," or "O son of the brave man, engage the strong fighters," or "O son of the scholar, seek the knowledge."*

The address is not neutral. It is an appeal to lineage used as an argument.

And he brings 17:3 as the parallel: *O offspring of those whom We carried in the ship with Nūḥ! Verily, he was a grateful servant.*

**Israel is Yaʿqūb — established on the record.**

Ibn Kathīr records the exchange that settles it:

*Israel is Prophet Yaʿqūb, for Abū Dāwūd aṭ-Ṭayālisī recorded that ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās said, "A group of Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and he said to them, 'Do you know that Israel is Yaʿqūb?' They said, 'Yes, by Allah.' He said, 'O Allah! Be witness.'"*

He asked them. They confirmed it. He called Allah as witness to the confirmation.

Then a second etymology: *Aṭ-Ṭabarī recorded that ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās said that "Israel" means "the servant of Allah."*

**Remember My favours.**

Mujāhid itemised them, and Ibn Kathīr records the list: *Allah's favor that He granted the Jews is that He made water gush from stones, sent down manna and quails for them, and saved them from being enslaved by Pharaoh.*

Abū al-ʿĀliyah read the favour differently — as the sending of prophets.

Al-Jalālayn gives the list with its purpose attached: *your forefathers, saving them from Pharaoh, parting the sea, sending clouds as shelter, and other instances, for which you should show gratitude by being obedient to Me.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās adds two: *I favoured you with the Scripture and the emissary, escape from Pharaoh and from drowning, as well as sending you honey and quails, and other blessings.*

Note that every one of these happened to *ancestors*. The verse addresses the living by what was done for the dead.

**The two covenants.**

*Awfū bi-ʿahdī ūfi bi-ʿahdikum.* Fulfil Mine and I will fulfil yours.

Al-Jalālayn states both sides: *and fulfil My covenant — that which I took from you, that you believe in Muhammad ﷺ — and I shall fulfil your covenant, that which I gave to you, that you shall be rewarded for this with Paradise.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās agrees on both: *fulfil my covenant regarding this Prophet ﷺ — I shall fulfil your covenant, by admitting you to Paradise.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar expands the second half: *He will fulfil His contract to you, as well as His promises to you of a good life on earth and a beautiful reward on the Day of Judgement.*

The condition comes first. That ordering matters — the fulfilment is promised, not given.

**Stand in awe of Me alone.**

*Iyyāya farhabūn.* Al-Jalālayn: *and be in awe of Me, fear Me and not anyone else, when you have abandoned belief in him, the Prophet.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās ties the fear to the covenant specifically: *and fear Me as regards the breaking of this covenant, and do not fear anyone save Me.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Fear Him alone and do not break His contract.*

That is the verse's real charge. Verse 41 will say plainly what they were afraid of losing — position and leadership. This verse names the fear and says who it should belong to.

**What went wrong, according to Tazkīrul Qurʾān.**

*Prior to the times of the Prophet Muhammad — the last of the prophets — this favour was the privilege of the Children of Israel. However, soon their religion ceased to be something that they accepted as a matter of conscious decision, and they let it deteriorate into a set of lifeless rituals passed on from one generation to the next. With the coming of the Prophet Muhammad the reality came to light. Those whose sensitivity to truth was still alive recognized the veracity of his prophethood and followed him. But those for whom religion had become a hereditary tradition found his message unfamiliar and failed to recognize the truth when they heard it.*

That is the diagnosis the whole address rests on. Not that they lacked evidence. That they had stopped looking.

And Tazkīrul adds the point that makes it harder: *In view of the clear prophecies in the Torah of the coming of an Arab Prophet, it would not have been difficult for the Israelites to recognize the truth of his [message].*

Which is what verse 41 is about.

41.text:
*Believe in My revelations which confirm your Scriptures. Do not be the first to deny them or trade them for a fleeting gain. And be mindful of Me.*

**Confirming, not replacing.**

*Muṣaddiqan limā maʿakum.* Al-Jalālayn states what the confirmation consists of: *confirming that which is with you, of the Torah, by its agreement with it in respect to affirmation of God's Oneness and prophethood.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās specifies three things: *confirming the Oneness of Allah, and the description and traits of Muhammad ﷺ, and some prescribed laws.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar adds a condition worth noticing: *confirming what came in the Torah, before its corruption, concerning the Oneness of Allah and the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.*

The Qurʾān confirms the Torah. It does not confirm every claim made about the Torah.

**Do not be the first to deny them.**

This is the verse's most consequential phrase, and Maʿārif's reading of it establishes a general principle:

*Verse 41 asks the Israelites not to be the first to deny the Holy Qurʾān, although being a disbeliever is in itself the ultimate sin, whether one be the first or the last. The verse, in fact, suggests that the man who is the first to deny and disbelieve will not only incur the sin of his own denial but also bear the additional burden of the sin of misleading all those who follow his example; and will thus have to undergo a multiple punishment.*

And then he generalises it beyond this verse:

*It follows from here that the man who is in any way responsible for others falling into any kind of sin will have to bear the burden of this sin along with the sinners; similarly, the man who in some way helps others to do a good deed will receive a reward for it along with them. Several verses of the Holy Qurʾān and the aḥādīth of the Holy Prophet ﷺ repeatedly stress this point.*

Al-Jalālayn gives the mechanism in the historical case: *and be not the first to disbelieve in it from among the People of the Scripture, for those who will come after you will depend on you, and so you will bear their sins.*

*Those who will come after you will depend on you.* They were the scholars. People took their word for it.

**Trade them for a fleeting gain.**

Maʿārif notes the word itself: *Verse 41 warns the Israelites against taking a paltry price for His signs or verses — the Arabic word āyāt has both meanings.*

Signs, and verses. The same word covers the miracle and the sentence.

Al-Jalālayn identifies both the price and the motive: *And do not sell, exchange, My signs — those that relate to the description of Muhammad ﷺ in your Book — for a small price, for a trivial and temporary affair of this world; that is to say, do not suppress this for fear of losing what you hope to earn from lowly individuals among you.*

That last clause is the sharpest thing said about them in this section. *Lowly individuals among you.* Their income came from ordinary people who paid them for religious standing. Telling the truth about the Prophet ﷺ would have ended that.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and part not with My revelations, by not revealing the description and traits of Muhammad, for a trifling price, in exchange for means of substance.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Do not exchange His signs — the verses which He has revealed — for the small price of position or leadership.*

Position or leadership. Not money exactly. Standing.

**The verse's structure.**

Three commands, and they escalate. Believe. Do not be first to deny. Do not sell.

The first is positive. The second is about timing — and it is an odd thing to prohibit, since being first is not obviously worse than being tenth. Maʿārif's explanation is why the prohibition exists at all: the first one creates the path the rest walk down.

The third is about motive, and it names the actual reason the first two were happening.

**And be mindful of Me.**

*Iyyāya fa-ttaqūn.* The same construction as verse 40's closing — Me alone, with the pronoun fronted for emphasis.

Al-Jalālayn: *and fear Me, and none other, in this matter.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *fear Me regarding this Prophet ﷺ.*

*In this matter.* Not fear in general. Fear about this specific decision — the one involving their income and their position.

Which is why verse 40's *stand in awe of Me alone* is repeated here. The two verses are one argument: remember what was done for your fathers, keep the promise, and be afraid of the right thing.

Al-Mukhtaṣar's summary of the verse's demand: *avoid His displeasure and punishment.*

And the verse has now named, in four clauses, everything the rest of this long address will work through — the confirmation, the precedence, the price, and the fear.

42.text:
*Do not mix truth with falsehood or hide the truth knowingly.*

**Two prohibitions, and Ibn Kathīr says so plainly.**

*So Allah forbade them from two things; He ordered them to make the truth known, as well as explaining it.*

Mixing, and concealing. They are different acts, and the verse treats them separately.

**Mixing.**

*Wa lā talbisū al-ḥaqqa bi-l-bāṭil.* Ad-Daḥḥāk said that **Ibn ʿAbbās** said: *Do not mix the truth with falsehood and the facts with lies.*

Qatādah gave it a specific historical referent: *Do not mix Judaism and Christianity with Islam, while you know that the religion of Allah is Islam, and that Judaism and Christianity are innovations that did not come from Allah.*

Ibn Kathīr adds: *It was reported that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said similarly.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads the mixture in a narrower and stranger way: *do not mix the Truth with falsehood, i.e. the description of the anti-Christ with the description of Muhammad ﷺ.*

Al-Jalālayn keeps it general and describes the effect: *And do not obscure, confuse, the truth that I have revealed to you with falsehood that you fabricate.*

*Confuse.* That is the harm. Not that falsehood replaces truth, but that the two become indistinguishable.

Maʿārif states the ruling the verse establishes:

*Verse 42 explicitly shows that it is not permissible to mix truth and falsehood together in such a way that the addressee falls into a confusion as to what the truth is, and that it is forbidden to conceal the truth because of fear or greed.*

Fear or greed. The two motives named in verse 41 — losing standing, and losing income.

**Concealing.**

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq narrated that **Ibn ʿAbbās** said: *Do not hide the knowledge that you have of My Messenger and what he was sent with. His description, which you know about, can be found written in the Books that you have.*

Al-Jalālayn agrees on what was concealed: *and do not conceal the truth — the description of Muhammad ﷺ — wittingly, that is, knowing it to be the truth.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *do not hide the truth of the description of Muhammad which came in His scripture, when you know what the truth is and are convinced of it.*

**While you know.**

*Wa antum taʿlamūn.* The phrase is doing heavy lifting, and Ibn Kathīr offers a second reading of it:

*It is possible that it means, "…although you know the tremendous harm that this evil will cause people, misguiding them and leading them to the Fire, because they will follow the falsehood that you mixed with the truth in your claims."*

So *knowing* covers two things: knowing the truth, and knowing what suppressing it does to other people.

That connects directly back to verse 41's principle — that the one who misleads bears the burden of everyone who follows.

**Al-Qurṭubī's story.**

Maʿārif records a story al-Qurṭubī brought under this verse, from Dārimī's Musnad, and it is about exactly this prohibition:

*During one of his visits to the Holy town of Madinah, the Umayyad Caliph Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik wanted to meet someone who had lived with a Companion of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, if such a man was still alive. On being informed that Abū Ḥāzim was the only man of this kind left in the town, he sent for him.*

*The Caliph said to him, "Abū Ḥāzim, why have you shown such discourtesy and disloyalty?"*

*"How have I been discourteous or disloyal to you?"*

*"Everybody who is anybody in Madinah has come to see me, but you haven't."*

Maʿārif introduces it as *a very illuminating story… which has come down to us through a chain of reliable reporters* — and it is placed under this verse because Abū Ḥāzim's answer concerned what a scholar owes the truth when power asks for something else.

**Why the two prohibitions are paired.**

Mixing produces confusion. Concealing produces absence. Between them they cover every way a truth can be removed from the world without ever being contradicted.

Tazkīrul Qurʾān describes how this worked in practice in Madinah:

*As the Israelites were considered representatives of revealed religion in the Arab world, people used to ask them about the Arab Prophet. Pretending innocence, they would put forward such points as would turn people away from the Prophet and his mission.*

Pretending innocence. Not denial. Mixture.

And Tazkīrul names the reason, which is the same one verse 41 gave: *When a positive response to the call of God means relinquishing positions of high honour and prestige, then those who have gained religious rank through worldly elevation find it extremely difficult to follow this course.*

Verse 42 is only nine words in English. It carries the whole charge.

43.text:
*Establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and bow down with those who bow down.*

**The turn from belief to practice.**

Maʿārif marks the shift: *The earlier three verses were concerned with the true faith and doctrines; the present verses speak of good deeds, mentioning only the most important of them.*

Verses 40–42 were about what to believe and what not to suppress. Verse 43 is about what to do. And it names the two acts the Qurʾān pairs more than any other.

**Establish prayer.**

*Aqīmū aṣ-ṣalāh.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *fulfil completely the five prescribed prayers.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar expands: *Establish the prayers properly, with its obligatory and recommended parts.*

The verb is *iqāmah* — to set up, to establish — not merely to perform. It implies something built and maintained.

**Pay alms-tax.**

*Wa ātū az-zakāh.* Al-Mukhtaṣar: *give Zakāt from your wealth, which Allah has put in your hands.*

That phrase — *which Allah has put in your hands* — is the whole theology of zakāt in six words. It is not your property being given away. It is property held on terms.

**Bow down with those who bow down.**

*Wa rkaʿū maʿa ar-rākiʿīn.* This is the verse's distinctive clause, and all the sources read it as congregation.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *pray the five prescribed prayers in congregation with Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *and be humble to Allah with those who are humble of Muhammad's nation ﷺ.*

Ibn Kathīr records Muqātil's reading: *Allah's statement to the People of the Book, "And perform aṣ-ṣalāh," commands them to perform the prayer behind [Muhammad ﷺ].*

The command is not to pray. It is to pray *with*.

**Why "with those who bow" matters here.**

Al-Jalālayn supplies the occasion, and it is the key to the verse:

*And bow with those that bow — that is, pray with those who pray, Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions. This was revealed concerning their religious scholars, who used to say to their kin from among the Muslims, "Stay firm upon the religion of Muhammad ﷺ, for it is the truth."*

Read that twice. Their scholars were telling their own Muslim relatives to stay Muslim.

That is exactly the contradiction verse 44 will name outright. And verse 43 is the command that would resolve it: if you believe it is the truth, pray with them.

The phrase *maʿa ar-rākiʿīn* — with those who bow — is doing something socially, not just ritually. It means joining a specific community, visibly. There is no way to do it privately.

**Why these two acts.**

Maʿārif explains the choice, and connects it forward to verse 45:

*It was usually the love of money and power that made it difficult for the Jews, especially for their scholars, to accept Islam. The verses prescribe the remedy for the twin diseases — they should fortify themselves with ṣabr (patience) and ṣalāh (prayer).*

Money and power. The two things verse 41 said they were protecting.

And the two remedies are named here and at 2:45 — prayer and patience. Prayer appears in this verse; patience comes two verses later.

Maʿārif then defines ṣabr properly, because the English word is too thin:

*"Patience" is a very weak translation of the Arabic word ṣabr, which has three connotations: (a) bearing pain and misfortune patiently, (b) restraining oneself from sin, (c) being steadfast in obeying Allah.*

And his argument for why that cures the love of money: *money cannot be an end in itself, but is sought only as a means of satisfying one's appetites; when a man has made a [decision to restrain himself]…*

**Why bowing is named rather than prostration.**

The prayer has two postures that could have stood for the whole of it — rukūʿ, the bow, and sujūd, the prostration. The verse names the bow.

Rukūʿ is the posture you hold while standing, in a line, in company. Sujūd is the posture of being alone on the ground. The verse asks for the one that is visible to the person next to you.

That reading is consistent with all three commentaries taking the clause as congregation rather than as prayer in general — Tanwīr al-Miqbās's *in congregation with Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions*, Al-Mukhtaṣar's *with those who are humble of Muhammad's nation*, and Muqātil's *commands them to perform the prayer behind [him]*.

And it answers the situation verse 43 was revealed into. Their scholars were telling their Muslim relatives the religion was true while staying out of the row.

**The verse's place in the sequence.**

Verse 40: remember, and keep the covenant. Verse 41: believe, and do not sell. Verse 42: do not mix, do not hide. Verse 43: pray, give, and join.

Three verses of prohibition, then one of command. And the command is the one act that cannot be done alone, cannot be done secretly, and cannot be done while telling other people to do it instead.

Which is why verse 44 follows immediately.

44.text:
*Do you preach righteousness and fail to practice it yourselves, although you read the Scripture? Do you not understand?*

**The question, and what it is doing.**

*Ataʾmurūna an-nāsa bi-l-birr wa tansawna anfusakum.* A question with no answer expected, because the answer is obvious and they have already given it.

Ibn Kathīr states it as Allah's own words: *How is it, O People of the Book, that you command people to perform al-birr, which encompasses all types of righteousness, yet forget yourselves and do not heed what you call others to? And you read Allah's Book (the Torah) and know what it promises to those who do not fulfill Allah's commandments.*

Then the closing question: *Have you then no sense? — of what you are doing to yourselves, so that you might become aware of your slumber and restore your sight from blindness.*

**Who the verse is about — and it is wider than the Jews.**

Ibn Jurayj said: *The verse "Enjoin you al-birr on the people" is about the People of the Book and the hypocrites. They used to command people to pray and fast. However, they did not practice what they commanded others. Allah reminded them of this behavior.*

And then he draws the general rule, which is the verse's lasting application:

*So whoever commands people to do righteousness, let him be among the first of them to implement that command.*

Maʿārif states the same widening explicitly:

*Though externally addressed to the Jewish scholars, the verse, in a larger sense, condemns all those who preach good deeds to others but do not act upon this principle, who ask others to have fear of Allah but show no such fear in their own behaviour.*

**What they actually did.**

Qatādah, via Maʿmar via ʿAbd ar-Razzāq: *The Children of Israel used to command people to obey Allah, fear Him and perform al-birr. Yet, they contradicted these orders, so Allah reminded them of this fact.* Ibn Kathīr adds: *As-Suddī said similarly.*

Al-Jalālayn gives the occasion, matching verse 43's: *Will you bid others to piety — to belief in Muhammad ﷺ — and forget yourselves, neglecting yourselves and not bidding them to the same, while you recite the Book, in which there is the threat of chastisement if what you do contradicts what you say?*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās identifies who they were preaching to: *do you enjoin the Oneness of Allah and the following of Muhammad ﷺ upon people of humble background, while you yourself refrain from following him?*

*People of humble background.* The same social line verse 41 drew — their income came from ordinary people, and their advice was sound.

Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the contradiction in one sentence: *What is more immoral than telling others to have faith and do good when you, upon reading the Torah, turn away from it and forget it yourselves, while knowing that it orders you to follow Allah's religion and have faith in His prophets?*

**"You forget yourselves."**

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq narrated that **Ibn ʿAbbās** said: *You forget to practice it yourselves, while you recite the Scripture — Have you then no sense? You forbid the people from rejecting the prophethood and the covenant that you have mentioned with you in the Torah, while you yourselves have [failed]…*

The verb is *tansawna* — you forget. Not "you refuse." Forgetting is stranger than refusing, and it is the word the verse chose.

Maʿārif explains what was actually going on, and it is not ignorance:

*They used to advise their friends and relatives to follow the Holy Prophet ﷺ and to be steadfast in their Islamic faith, which shows that they regarded Islam as the true faith, but, being enslaved to their desires, were not prepared to accept this faith themselves, although they were regular readers of the Torah and knew how emphatically it denounces the scholar who does not act upon his knowledge.*

*Which shows that they regarded Islam as the true faith.* That is the verse's most devastating point. Their own advice proves their own belief. They were not confused. They were unwilling.

**Do you not understand?**

*Afa-lā taʿqilūn.* Al-Jalālayn: *Do you not understand the evil nature of your actions, that you might then repent?*

He also gives a grammatical note on the verse's construction: *the sentence about "forgetting" constitutes the syntactical locus of the interrogative of disavowal.*

The whole verse is an interrogative of disavowal — the same form as 2:26's *"What does Allah mean by such a parable?"* A question that is not a question.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās makes the last line blunt: *Have ye then no sense? Do you not possess the common sense possessed by human beings?*

**What the verse warns about.**

Maʿārif records that the ḥadīth literature takes this seriously as a warning to preachers, and refers to the Companion **Anas** reporting, on the Night of the Ascension, what the Prophet ﷺ saw concerning *the dreadful punishments these men will have to bear in the other world.*

And Tazkīrul Qurʾān closes the section with the distinction the verse depends on:

*For the truly devout, however, these considerations are not a hindrance. The fulfillment that others find in worldly pleasures, true believers find in remembering God, in spending for His cause, in obeying His commandments and being steadfast in treading His path.*

Verse 44 is the hinge of this whole address. Verses 40–43 told them what to do. Verse 44 says that they already know, and that knowing is the problem.

45.text:
*And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble.*

**The remedy named at last.**

Maʿārif set this up at verse 43: *It was usually the love of money and power that made it difficult for the Jews, especially for their scholars, to accept Islam. The verses prescribe the remedy for the twin diseases — they should fortify themselves with ṣabr (patience) and ṣalāh (prayer).*

Verse 43 gave prayer. This verse gives both, and states plainly that they are hard.

**What patience means here.**

Ibn Kathīr collects the readings. Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said: *Utilize patience and the obligatory prayer in seeking the Hereafter. As for patience here, they say that it means fasting.*

*There are similar texts reported from Mujāhid. Al-Qurṭubī and other scholars commented, "This is why Ramaḍān is called the month of patience," as is mentioned in the ḥadīth literature.*

And a second, wider reading: *It was also said that "patience" in the verse means refraining from evil, and this is why "patience" was mentioned along with practicing acts of worship, especially and foremost, the prayer.*

Then **Ibn Abī Ḥātim** narrated that **ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb** said: *There are two types of patience: good patience when the disaster strikes, and a better patience while avoiding the prohibitions of Allah.* Ibn Abī Ḥātim adds that **al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī** said similarly.

The second kind is better. Enduring what happens to you is good. Holding yourself back from what you want is better.

**Why prayer.**

Ibn Kathīr brings 29:45: *Verily, aṣ-ṣalāh prevents from al-faḥshāʾ — great sins of every kind — and al-munkar.*

Al-Jalālayn supplies the practice behind it: *The singling out of this for mention is a way of emphasising its great importance; in one ḥadīth it is stated, "When something bothered the Prophet ﷺ, he would immediately resort to prayer."*

And he identifies the audience and the pairing: *it is said that the address here is to the Jews, when greed and desire for leadership became impediments to their faith, they were enjoined to forbearance — which constituted fasting and prayer — since the former stems from lust and the latter yields humility and negates pride.*

Fasting answers greed. Prayer answers the desire for leadership. Each remedy is matched to its disease.

**It is a burden.**

*Wa innahā la-kabīrah.* Ibn Kathīr settles what the pronoun refers to: *The personal pronoun in the verse refers to prayer, as Mujāhid is reported to have said, and it was also the choice of Ibn Jarīr. It is possible that the pronoun might be referring to the advice — to observe patience and the prayer — mentioned in the same verse.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās agrees: *for truly it — the prayer — is hard, heavy.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Prayer is a hardship except for those who are humble to their Lord.*

The verse does not pretend otherwise. Prayer is heavy. That is stated before the exception, not after.

**Except for the humble.**

*Illā ʿalā al-khāshiʿīn.* Al-Jalālayn: *except to the humble — those that are at peace in obedience.*

Maʿārif's treatment of khushūʿ is the fullest available, and it is careful about what the quality is not:

*The "humbleness of heart" (khushūʿ), which the Holy Qurʾān and the ḥadīth speak of, connotes a restfulness of heart and humility arising out of the awareness of Allah's majesty and of one's own insignificance in comparison to it. This quality, once acquired, shows its spiritual fruitfulness in making the obedience to Allah and submission to Him easy and pleasant for one.*

*Easy and pleasant.* That is the exception the verse names. The burden does not disappear; it stops being a burden.

Then the warning:

*If a man does not bear genuine humility and fear of Allah in his heart, he does not, with all his external modesty and downcast looks, really possess the quality of khushūʿ. In fact, it is not proper even to show the signs of khushūʿ in one's behavior deliberately. On seeing a young man sitting with his head bowed down, the rightly-guided Khalīfah Sayyidunā ʿUmar said: "Raise your head! Humbleness of heart is in the [heart]."*

Which connects this verse back to verse 44. Preaching righteousness without practising it, and performing humility without having it, are the same failure wearing different clothes.

**Why this verse sits here.**

Verses 40–44 made a demand. Verse 45 says how to carry it. Not by deciding harder. By fasting and praying until the decision becomes easy.

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the mechanism: *Ask for help in sacred and worldly affairs, with patience and prayer, which bring you close to Allah and allow you to reach Him, so that He will help you, protect you and take away your difficulties.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās ties it to the commands already given: *in performing the obligations prescribed by Allah and abstaining from transgression.*

And the verse ends by pointing at the next one. The humble are about to be defined.

46.text:
*Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and to Him they will return.*

**The definition of the humble.**

Verse 45 ended on *al-khāshiʿīn* — the humble. This verse says who they are, and it does not mention posture or appearance at all.

Two convictions. They will meet their Lord. They will return to Him.

**Certain.**

*Yazunnūna.* Al-Jalālayn glosses the word carefully, because in ordinary Arabic it can mean to suppose: *who reckon, who are certain that they shall meet their Lord at the Resurrection, and that to Him they are returning in the Hereafter, where He will reward them.*

Here it means certainty, not conjecture. The same word carries both senses in Arabic, and Al-Jalālayn fixes which one applies.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *who know that they will have to meet their Lord — see Him — and that unto Him they are returning after they die.*

*See Him.* That is a stronger claim than meeting, and Tanwīr makes it.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *The humble are convinced that they will meet their Lord on the Day of Judgement, that they are returning to Him and will be held accountable for their actions.*

**Why certainty makes prayer light.**

Verse 45 said prayer is heavy except for the humble. This verse explains the mechanism without stating it.

Someone who is certain they are going somewhere packs differently. The weight of the journey is not removed. It is re-weighed against the destination.

Maʿārif's description of khushūʿ at verse 45 said the same thing from the other direction: it *connotes a restfulness of heart and humility arising out of the awareness of Allah's majesty and of one's own insignificance in comparison to it.*

Majesty on one side, insignificance on the other. Both are convictions about what is real. This verse names them.

**Two clauses, two directions.**

*They will meet their Lord* — He comes into view. *To Him they will return* — they go back.

Al-Jalālayn assigns each to a time: meeting at the Resurrection, returning in the Hereafter.

The second clause uses the same verb the sūrah used at 2:28 — *then to Him you will all be returned* — where it described the fourth stage of every human life. Verse 46 takes that general fact and makes it the mark of the humble. Everyone returns. The humble are the ones who are certain of it beforehand.

**And it is a verse about the present.**

Not "they will believe." *Yazunnūna* is a present tense. They are certain now, and that present certainty is what makes the burden bearable now.

Which is the whole answer to verse 44. The scholars who told their relatives to stay firm while refusing to join them were not lacking information. They were lacking this.

47.text:
*O Children of Israel! Remember all the favours I granted you and how I honoured you above the others.*

**The same address, seven verses later.**

Verse 40 opened *O children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you.* This verse repeats it almost exactly, with one addition — *and how I honoured you above the others.*

The repetition is deliberate. Verses 40–46 made the demand. Verse 47 goes back to the beginning and restates the ground the demand stands on.

**What the preference was.**

Ibn Kathīr: *Allah reminds the Children of Israel of the favors that He granted their fathers and grandfathers, how He showed preference to them by sending them Messengers from among them and revealing Books to them, more so than any of the other previous nations.*

Then he brings two verses. 44:32 — *And We chose them over the nations with knowledge.* And 5:20, where Mūsā says to his people: *Remember the favor of Allah to you: when He made Prophets among you, made you kings, honored you above the nations.*

Prophets, kings, books.

Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī reported that ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said that **Abū al-ʿĀliyah** defined the preference precisely: *The kingship, Messengers and Books that were granted to them, instead of granting such to the other kingdoms that existed during their time, for every period there is a nation.*

Ibn Kathīr adds: *It was also reported that Mujāhid, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Qatādah and Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid said similarly.*

*For every period there is a nation.* That is the limit built into the definition, and Maʿārif states it plainly:

*As for Allah giving preference to the Israelites "over the worlds", the phrase means that they were given preference only in certain matters, or only over a large part of men — for example, over the contemporaries of the earlier Israelites.*

Al-Jalālayn agrees: *and that I have preferred you, your forefathers, above all the worlds of their time.*

**And the ummah of Muḥammad ﷺ is better.**

Ibn Kathīr heads a section on this and is direct about it:

*This is the only way the verse can be understood, because this ummah is better than theirs, as Allah said: "You are the best of people ever raised up for mankind; you enjoin good and forbid evil, and you believe in Allah. And had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them" (3:110).*

So the verse is not in dispute with 3:110. The preference was real, and it was for a time.

**Who actually received the favour.**

Maʿārif handles the obvious objection — that the people being addressed were not alive when any of it happened:

*The verse is addressed to the Jews contemporaneous with the Holy Prophet ﷺ while the blessing had been received by their forefathers. The point is that when a man receives a special favour, his children and grandchildren too usually partake of the benefits flowing from it; in this sense, the Jews who are being addressed may be said to have received the blessing themselves.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās lists the blessings: *with the scripture, the Messenger and Islam.*

**What went wrong with the idea of being chosen.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān gives the sharpest analysis in the six sources:

*The Israelites were chosen by God. He selected them for a special task: they were to receive God's scriptures and pass His commandments on to the rest of mankind. In relation to this office, they were granted many other blessings and facilities: victory over their enemies, forgiveness of their sins, special help in times of peril, divine provision for their physical needs, and so on. This misled later generations of Jews into thinking that they were God's chosen people, and were assured of salvation in the next world. But such matters as salvation are not a hereditary right of any group. Successive generations are to be judged on their own merits.*

Selection was for a task. It was read as a status. And the task — passing the commandments on — is exactly what verses 41 and 42 accused them of abandoning.

**Remember.**

Al-Jalālayn states the purpose of the command: *remember My favour wherewith I favoured you, by giving thanks through obedience to Me.*

Remembering is not recall. It is gratitude expressed as obedience.

And verse 48 follows immediately with the other reason to remember.

48.text:
*Guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another. No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given.*

**The turn in the argument.**

Verse 47 listed what was given. Verse 48 says none of it will be usable on the Day.

Ibn Kathīr marks the movement: *After Allah reminded the Children of Israel of the favors that He has granted them, He warned them about the duration of the torment which He will punish them with on the Day of Resurrection.*

**No soul will help another.**

*Lā tajzī nafsun ʿan nafsin shayʾan.* Ibn Kathīr brings three verses to establish it, and the third is the harshest:

35:18 — *And no bearer of burdens shall bear another's burden.*
80:37 — *Every man that Day will have enough to make him careless of others.*
31:33 — *O mankind! Have taqwā of your Lord, and fear a Day when no father can avail aught for his son, nor a son avail aught for his father.*

Then his comment: *This indeed should serve as a great warning that both the father and the son will not be of help to each other on that Day.*

Maʿārif explains what "availing" means in practice:

*As for no one being able to suffice another on that day, the phrase should be understood in the sense of one man paying the dues on behalf of another man. Let us, for example, suppose that a man is found wanting in the performance of obligatory acts of worship like ṣalāh and ṣawm (fasting), and another man should suggest [to make them up for him]…*

Not influence. Not pleading. The literal settling of an account. And it cannot be transferred.

**No intercession accepted.**

Ibn Kathīr is precise about the scope, and it matters: *meaning, from the disbelievers.*

Then two supporting verses. 74:48 — *So no intercession of intercessors will be of any use to them.* And the words of the people of the Fire at 26:100–101 — *Now we have no intercessors, nor a close friend.*

Al-Jalālayn adds a variant reading and its consequence: *read either tuqbal or yuqbal — from it, that is, it is not the case that it has power to intercede for it, then to be accepted from it or rejected, as God says, "So now we have no intercessors" (26:100).*

On one reading the intercession is not accepted. On the other it never had the power to be offered.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *nor will intercession be accepted from it, and no intercessor will be allowed to intercede.*

This is worth holding against verse 30, where Allah told the angels *I know what you do not know* and Ibn Kathīr explained that among those He would create were prophets and messengers. Intercession exists. It is not available here.

**No ransom taken.**

*Wa lā yuʾkhadhu minhā ʿadl.* Al-Mukhtaṣar states the scale: *no ransom will be taken, even if it were to be the earth filled with gold.*

Ibn Kathīr brings the verse that fixes that scale, 3:91: *Verily, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, the earth full of gold will not be accepted from any of them, even if they offered it as ransom.*

The whole earth, full of gold. Not accepted.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *nor will compensation be received from it, and no ransom accepted.*

**No help given.**

*Wa lā hum yunṣarūn.* The fourth clause, and the shortest.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *neither will they be helped to avoid Allah's chastisement.*

Al-Jalālayn: *nor any compensation — ransom — be taken, neither shall they be helped to avoid God's chastisement.*

**The pronouns, and who they belong to.**

The verse switches between singular and plural without warning. *No soul will be of help to another* is singular. *No intercession will be accepted* — *minhā*, from it — is singular again. Then *no help will be given* — *wa lā hum yunṣarūn* — is plural.

Ibn Kathīr's reading accounts for the shift: the singular clauses describe what any one soul can do for another, and the plural describes the group's final position. Individual help fails, and then the collective is left standing.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās makes the first clause explicitly about unbelief meeting unbelief: *when no soul will in anything avail another — no unbelieving soul will avail another unbelieving soul.*

Which narrows it in a way worth noticing. The verse is not saying nobody helps anybody on that Day. It is saying that this company cannot help itself.

**Why four negatives.**

Help from another soul. Intercession. Ransom. Assistance. These are the four things people actually rely on — family, advocates, money, allies.

The verse removes them in that order. And Al-Mukhtaṣar's closing question is the verse's whole force in one line:

*Without appeal, ransom or helper, to where will they turn?*

**Guard yourselves.**

*Ittaqū yawman.* The same root as verse 21's *so that you may become mindful* and verse 24's *then fear the Fire*. This sūrah has used it at every hinge.

Al-Mukhtaṣar states what guarding means: *Protect yourselves against the Day of Judgement by following Allah's instructions and staying away from what He has prohibited.*

Not by preparing an argument for the Day. By living differently before it.

**And the answer to verse 47.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān closes the pair:

*On the Day of Judgement people will be judged individually, according to their actions. To think that anything other than good deeds will avail one, is to underestimate the rigours of that Day.*

Verse 47 said they were preferred above the nations of their time. Verse 48 says the preference will not be counted. Verse 2:25 promised gardens to *those who believe and do good* — and the two conditions are the only currency left on the Day this verse describes.

49.text:
*Remember how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord.*

**The list begins.**

Verse 47 said *remember My favours*. Verse 48 warned that none of them will count on the Day. Now the favours are itemised, and this is the first.

Maʿārif marks the turn: *Verse 47 had spoken of the special favours shown to the Israelites by Allah. Now, with verse 49 begins the account of these favours.*

**Why Pharaoh killed the boys.**

There are two accounts, and Ibn Kathīr gives both.

The first is a dream: *This favor came after the cursed Pharaoh had a dream in which he saw a fire emerge from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and then the fire entered the houses of the Copts in Egypt, with the exception of the Children of Israel. Its purport was that his kingship would be toppled by a man among the Children of Israel.*

The second is intelligence: *It was also said that some of Pharaoh's entourage said that the Children of Israel were expecting a man among them to arise who would establish a state for them.*

Maʿārif has the same prediction without the dream: *Someone had made a prediction to the Pharaoh that a child was going to be born among the Israelites who would destroy his kingship.*

Ibn Kathīr notes where the fuller account comes: *We will mention the ḥadīth on this subject when we explain Sūrat Ṭā Hā (20).*

**And what he did about it.**

*After the dream, Pharaoh ordered that every newborn male among the Children of Israel be killed, and that the girls be left alone. He also commanded that the Children of Israel be given tasks of hard labour and assigned the most humiliating jobs.*

Al-Jalālayn supplies the reasoning the Egyptians gave themselves, and it is worth reading because of who gave it: *and retaining your women — doing so because of the saying of some of their priests, that a child born among the Israelites shall bring about the end of your rule, Pharaoh.*

Their own priests told them. The policy was not paranoia invented on the spot; it was a response to a prophecy from inside their own religious establishment.

Maʿārif notes the self-interest running through the leniency: *he would spare the females, as there was nothing to fear from them, and, moreover, they could, on growing up, serve as maid-servants. So, even this leniency was motivated by self-interest.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar states it flatly: *slaughtering your sons so you would not survive, and letting your women live so they could serve them, taking great pains to humiliate and insult you.*

**Which torment the verse means.**

Ibn Kathīr settles it: *The torment here refers to killing the male infants. In Sūrat Ibrāhīm (14) this meaning is clearly mentioned* — and he quotes 14:6, which spells out in one sentence what 2:49 splits across two: *Who were afflicting you with horrible torment, and were slaughtering your sons and letting your women live.*

**A severe test — and the word means two opposite things.**

*Wa fī dhālikum balāʾun min rabbikum ʿaẓīm.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives both readings in one line: *That was a tremendous trial from your Lord — a tremendous calamity from your Lord; and it is also said this means: a tremendous blessing.*

Maʿārif explains why the word carries both, and it is the verse's real content:

*What the verse refers to as "a great trial" is either the slaughter of the sons — which was a calamity, and it is the quality of patience that is tested in a calamity — or the deliverance from the people of the Pharaoh — which was a blessing, and it is the quality of thankfulness which is tested when one receives a blessing.*

Balāʾ is a test either way. Suffering tests patience. Rescue tests gratitude. And both are in this one verse.

Al-Jalālayn keeps the same ambiguity open: *and for you therein — chastisement or deliverance — was a tremendous trial, a test or a grace, from your Lord.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar takes the second reading and states its purpose: *When you were saved from the oppression of Pharaoh and his people, it was a great test for you from your Lord, to see if you would be thankful.*

**Who is being addressed.**

Al-Jalālayn makes a point that governs every verse from here on: *the address here, and henceforth, directed to those living at the time of our Prophet, is about how God blessed their forefathers, and is intended to remind them of God's grace so that they might believe.*

The people hearing this in Madinah were not in Egypt. The verse speaks to them as though they were, because the favour ran down the family.

And that is exactly the assumption Tazkīrul Qurʾān challenges, in the passage that spans 2:47–52:

*This misled later generations of Jews into thinking that they were God's chosen people, and were assured of salvation in the next world. But such matters as salvation are not a hereditary right of any group. Successive generations are to be judged on their own merits.*

**Why this verse is first in the list.**

It is the oldest. Everything the sūrah will recount — the sea, the forty nights, the manna, the water from the rock — happened after this. And it is the one where they did nothing. They were being slaughtered, and Allah intervened.

Which is the right beginning for a list of favours. The first one was not earned.

50.text:
*And remember when We parted the sea, rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh's people before your very eyes.*

**The narrative, compressed into one verse.**

Maʿārif gives the sequence the verse assumes:

*He, in his capacity as a messenger of Allah, continued efforts for a long time to make the Pharaoh and his people see Truth, but when they persisted in their denial, Allah commanded him to take the Israelites along with him and leave Egypt surreptitiously. On their way, they came across a sea while the Pharaoh was behind him with his army in hot pursuit. Allah commanded the sea to split, and make way for Sayyidunā Mūsā and his people. So, they went over smoothly. But when the Pharaoh and his army followed them into the sea, it gathered the water back so that the Pharaoh and his men were drowned then and there.*

Ten years of preaching, a night departure, an army behind them, water in front. The verse gives it three clauses.

**Three verbs.**

Parted. Rescued. Drowned. Two for them, one against their enemies — and the order matters, because the rescue is stated before the destruction.

Al-Jalālayn: *And remember when We divided, split in two, for you, on account of you, the sea, such that you were able to cross it and escape from your enemy; and We delivered you from drowning, and drowned Pharaoh's folk — his people — with him, while you were beholding the sea crashing down on top of them.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps the dryness of the crossing: *He parted the sea and made it a dry path for you to go through, while drowning your enemies, Pharaoh and his followers, before your very eyes, as you looked on.*

**Before your very eyes.**

*Wa antum tanẓurūn.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās adds a detail none of the others give: *while you were looking at them, three days later.*

The verse's emphasis is on witnessing. They did not hear about it afterwards. They watched.

Which is why the verse is phrased as a command to remember rather than as a story. Something you watched is not a report.

**Maʿārif's doctrinal point.**

He draws an inference from the verse and names the people he is arguing against:

*Verse 50 speaks of the splitting of the sea, and clearly proves that miracles do occur at the hands of prophets, which some Westernized Muslims have been trying to deny.*

His argument is not that the sea parted because the sūrah says so. It is that the sūrah is unintelligible if the sea did not part — the verse has no metaphorical reading available to it. It states a physical event with witnesses.

**Why this verse follows verse 49 immediately.**

Verse 49 ended on *a severe test*. This verse is the rescue half of that test. The slaughter tested patience; the sea tested whether they would be grateful.

And the verse has already set up the failure. Verse 51 begins with the forty nights — and the calf.

Ibn Kathīr's summary of the favour is the plainest available: *I — Allah — saved you from them and delivered you from their hands in the company of Mūsā, after they subjected you to horrible torture.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar's version puts the whole thing in one clause: *Remember Allah's favour in saving you.*

51.text:
*And remember when We appointed forty nights for Moses, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully.*

**The forty nights — and why forty.**

Ibn Kathīr gives the cross-reference that explains the number:

*These forty days were mentioned in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, when Allah said, "And We appointed for Mūsā thirty nights and added to the period ten more" (7:142).*

Then the timing: *It was said that these days were during the month of Dhū al-Qaʿdah plus the first ten days in Dhū al-Ḥijjah, after the Children of Israel were delivered from Pharaoh and they safely crossed the sea.*

Maʿārif gives the reason for the extra ten, and it is the strangest detail in the whole story:

*Allah answered the prayer of Sayyidunā Mūsā and promised that if he came to the Mount Ṭūr (Sinai) and devoted himself to worship for a month, he would receive a Divine Book. He gladly obeyed the Commandment, and was granted the Torah. But he was ordered to continue to worship for ten days more, because he had broken his fast after a month and thus lost the special odour which rises from the mouth of a fasting person and which is very pleasant to Allah; so Allah commanded him to fast for ten additional days and regain that odour. Thus, Sayyidunā Mūsā completed forty days of total fasting and devotion.*

Al-Jalālayn notes the variant in the verb: *wāʿadnā or waʿadnā Mūsā — forty nights, at the end of which We shall give him the Torah for you to implement.*

*For you to implement.* The appointment was not for Mūsā's benefit. The Book was for them.

Al-Mukhtaṣar states what the forty nights produced: *the revelation of the Torah, with its light and guidance, was completed.*

**Then you took the calf.**

Al-Jalālayn names who made it: *then you took to yourselves the calf — the one which the Samaritan fashioned for you — as a god, after him, that is, after he departed for Our appointment.*

Maʿārif sets the scene: *While he was on Mt. Sinai, something very odious happened to the Israelites.*

And he explains how they got there, which the verse does not: *When the Pharaoh had been drowned, the Israelites, according to one report, went back to Egypt, or, according to another, began to live somewhere else. Having at last found a peaceful existence, they now wished they could receive a Sharīʿah, or a religious code of laws, from Allah, which they should follow.*

They asked for a law. Mūsā went to get it. And while he was getting it, they built a god.

**Acting wrongfully.**

*Wa antum ẓālimūn.* Al-Jalālayn explains the word with unusual precision: *and you were evildoers, for taking it in worship, because you directed your worship to the wrong place.*

Not that they worshipped wrongly. That they aimed worship at the wrong object. The act was right; the direction was not.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and you were wrong-doers — harmful both to yourselves and others.*

That is the same word the sūrah used at 2:35 — *or else you will be wrongdoers* — where Tanwīr glossed it *lest you harm yourselves.* Ẓulm as putting something where it does not belong, starting with yourself.

**Why the verse says "nights" and not "days".**

*Laylah*, not *yawm*. The appointment is counted in nights.

7:142 says the same — thirty nights, plus ten. The night is the time of fasting and withdrawal, which is what the forty were for. The days were not the point.

**The verse's place in the list.**

Verses 49 and 50 were favours with no failure attached. This one has the favour and the failure in a single sentence: *We appointed forty nights for Moses* — and — *you worshipped the calf.*

The sūrah does not wait for a separate verse of accusation. It puts them side by side in one breath, which is how the rest of this address will run.

And verse 52 answers it before the reader has finished.

52.text:
*Even then We still forgave you, so perhaps you would be grateful.*

**The shortest verse in this section, and the fastest turn in it.**

Verse 51 ended with them worshipping a calf. This verse says they were forgiven. There is no verse in between.

Ibn Kathīr states it as the favour it is: *Remember My favor on you when I forgave you for worshipping the calf.*

**"Even then."**

*Min baʿdi dhālik.* After that. Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Then, even after that — after you worshipped the calf — We pardoned you, left you alone and did not exterminate you.*

Al-Jalālayn: *Then We pardoned you, erasing your sins, after that act of worship, so that you might be thankful for Our favour upon you.*

*Erasing.* Not reduced, not deferred.

Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the condition and the consequence: *Then Allah forgave you when you asked for forgiveness, and did not take you to account for it, so that you might be thankful to Him, worshipping Him in the best way and doing as He instructed.*

*When you asked.* The forgiveness was not automatic. Maʿārif confirms it and points forward: *The Israelites were forgiven only when they had offered tawbah (repentance), as recounted in verse 54.*

Verse 54 is where the actual repentance is described. This verse gives the result.

**"So perhaps you would be grateful."**

*Laʿallakum tashkurūn.* Maʿārif handles the particle carefully, because it is the same one Al-Jalālayn discussed at 2:21:

*In saying that they were pardoned so that they might learn gratefulness, the present verse employs the Arabic word laʿalla, which indicates expectation. In the present context it does not mean that Allah had or could have any doubt or misgiving about this or any other matter; what the word implies here is just that when a man receives a pardon, the onlookers may expect him to feel grateful.*

At 2:21 Al-Jalālayn said the opposite — that *laʿalla* is affirmative when Allah speaks. The two are not in conflict. The particle expresses expectation; who holds the expectation is what differs.

**Grateful for what.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās specifies: *so that you might give thanks to Us for pardoning you.*

Not gratitude for the rescue at the sea, which was verse 50's gift. Gratitude for the pardon. The second favour is the forgiveness itself.

**Why this verse is so short.**

Four clauses of narrative behind it and three words of response. The brevity is the point — the sūrah does not linger on the calf. It names it, forgives it, and moves on.

Which is also the pattern of the whole address. The favours keep coming. The failures keep being named. Neither stops the other.

Al-Jalālayn's closing phrase is the verse's whole theology in five words: *so that you might be thankful for Our favour upon you.*

And verse 53 gives them the thing to be grateful for.

53.text:
*And remember when We gave Moses the Scripture—the standard to distinguish between right and wrong—that perhaps you would be rightly guided.*

**The favour the forty nights were for.**

Verses 51 and 52 covered the appointment and the failure during it. This verse gives what came out of it.

Ibn Kathīr: *"And remember when We gave Mūsā the Scripture" means the Torah.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar places it in the list: *Allah's giving Mūsā the Torah as a criterion between truth and falsehood, discriminating between guidance and misguidance, so that you might be guided to the truth through it, were from the blessings of Allah.*

**The Criterion.**

*Al-furqān.* Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar and the meaning together: *and the Criterion — waʾl-furqān is an explicative supplement of Torah, that is, the one that discriminates (faraqa) between truth and falsehood, and between what is licit and illicit.*

So on his reading it is not a second book. It is a description of the first.

Ibn Kathīr agrees: *"And the criterion" — that is, that which differentiates between truth and falsehood, guidance and deviation.*

Maʿārif sets out the three readings, and they are genuinely different:

*In the language of the Holy Qurʾān, al-furqān is a term signifying something which separates truth from falsehood or distinguishes the one from the other. In the present verse, it refers either to (a) the injunctions of the Sharīʿah which are to be found in the Torah, for the Sharīʿah resolves all the differences that may arise with regard to the doctrines or the practice of good deeds; or to (b) miracles, which decide between a true or a false claim in a palpable manner; or even to (c) the Torah itself, which has the twin qualities of being a Book of Allah and of being an instrument for separating truth from falsehood.*

Law. Miracle. Book. All three are called furqān in the Qurʾān.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās holds the first and fourth together and adds a fifth: *and the Criterion — i.e. We showed in it the lawful and the unlawful, the commands and the prohibitions, as well as other things; it is also said that this means: triumph over Pharaoh.*

Triumph as furqān. The crossing of the sea decided a claim the way a miracle does — visibly, in front of witnesses. That reading connects this verse straight back to verse 50.

**So that you would be guided.**

*Laʿallakum tahtadūn.* Ibn Kathīr ties it to the sequence: *so that you may be guided aright, after escaping the sea.*

Then he brings the parallel, 28:43: *And indeed We gave Mūsā — after We had destroyed the generations of old — the Scripture (the Torah) as an enlightenment for mankind, and a guidance and a mercy, that they might remember.*

*After We had destroyed the generations of old.* The Book comes after the rescue, not before. Which is the order this sūrah has kept: sea at verse 50, Scripture at verse 53.

Al-Jalālayn: *so that you might be guided by it away from error.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *that you might be led rightfully — guided to avoid error.*

**Why the verse is a favour and not a demand.**

It is phrased as *We gave*, not *We commanded*. The Torah is listed among the blessings, alongside the rescue from Pharaoh and the parting of the sea.

That is the sūrah's argument against the people it is addressing. Verses 41 and 42 accused them of concealing the description of Muḥammad ﷺ found in their own Book. This verse reminds them that the Book was a gift — and that a gift can be misused by its recipients.

**What Tazkīrul Qurʾān draws from it.**

Its run covering 2:53–57 states what the Scripture was for in practical terms:

*True piety is to worship God alone, to believe in Him though one has not seen Him, to live in fear of Judgement Day, to subsist on the pure things of the earth, to prevent whomsoever one can from falling into sin. It is those who adopt this way of life who will be successful in the next world.*

Five things. None of them is lineage.

Which is the answer to verse 47's *I honoured you above the others* — the honour was real, it was for a task, and the task is this.

54.text:
*And remember when Moses said to his people, "O my people! Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf, so turn in repentance to your Creator and execute the calf-worshippers among yourselves. That is best for you in the sight of your Creator." Then He accepted your repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.*

**The verse verse 52 pointed to.**

Verse 52 said they were forgiven. Maʿārif confirmed the condition: *The Israelites were forgiven only when they had offered tawbah (repentance), as recounted in verse 54.*

This is that verse. The pardon came first in the narration because the pardon is the favour; the repentance comes now because the repentance is what it cost.

**You have wronged yourselves.**

*Innakum ẓalamtum anfusakum.* Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī located the moment precisely, and Ibn Kathīr records it:

*"When their hearts thought of worshipping the calf — and when they regretted and saw that they had gone astray, they said: 'If our Lord does not have mercy upon us and forgive us' (7:149). This is when Mūsā said to them, 'O my people! Verily, you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf.'"*

The regret came first. The verse is spoken to people already sorry.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *O my people! Ye have wronged yourselves — harmed yourselves — by your choosing of the calf, by worshipping the calf.*

That is the third time the sūrah has used ẓulm of them — 2:35, 2:51, and here. And each time the wrong is done to themselves.

**To your Creator.**

*Fa-tūbū ilā bāriʾikum.* Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said it means *to your Creator.*

Then Ibn Kathīr explains why that particular name was chosen, and it is the sharpest observation on the verse:

*Allah's statement "to your Bāriʾ (Creator)" alerts the Children of Israel to the enormity of their error and means, "Repent to He Who created you after you associated others with Him in worship."*

Not "your Lord." Not "your God." *The One who made you.* The name itself is the argument against a calf somebody built.

**Execute the calf-worshippers among yourselves.**

This is the hardest command in the sūrah so far, and the sources explain it rather than soften it.

Al-Jalālayn states who killed whom: *and slay one another — that is, let the innocent of you slay the guilty.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās records how the instruction was arrived at: *and when Mūsā was then asked what to do, he said to them: "so turn in penitence to your Creator." Again they asked him how to turn in penitence to Allah, and he said: "and kill the guilty among yourselves" — let those who did not worship the calf kill those who worshipped it.*

Twice they asked how. The command was not obvious to them either.

Ibn Kathīr brings the report that makes it concrete. **An-Nasāʾī**, **Ibn Jarīr** and **Ibn Abī Ḥātim** recorded **Ibn ʿAbbās** saying:

*Allah told the Children of Israel that their repentance would be to slay by the sword every person they meet, be he father or son. They should not care whom they kill. Those were guilty whom Mūsā and Hārūn were not aware of their guilt; they admitted their sin and did as they were ordered. So Allah forgave both the killer and [the killed].*

Father or son. And both parties forgiven.

Al-Jalālayn adds a detail that makes the scene bearable to picture:

*Who made it easier for you to accomplish this, and sent down a dark cloud over you so that none of you was able to see the other and show him mercy — such that almost seventy thousand of you were killed.*

The cloud was mercy. It removed the faces.

**Maʿārif on why this is not unique to them.**

He draws the ruling forward into Islamic law:

*This verse describes the special mode of offering their tawbah (repentance) which was prescribed for the Israelites in this situation — that is to say, those who had not indulged in the worship of the golden calf should execute those who had.
