*People who are good to those who wield no worldly power and possess scant resources, do so for God's sake alone, for they have no other incentive.*

Then the failure mode, described with uncomfortable accuracy:

*Benefactors frequently regard themselves as "superior" persons and, when they are not shown what they consider to be due deference, they tend to treat people less fortunate than themselves with disdain. Then the thought of a permanent liability is often so irksome to them that they resort to ill-mannered behaviour to rid themselves of a burdensome obligation. This attitude leaves no room for the notion that the weak also have their self-respect.*

**Speak kindly to people.**

*Wa qūlū li-n-nāsi ḥusnā.* Al-Jalālayn: *and speak well — good words — to men, commanding good and forbidding evil, being truthful with regard to the status of Muhammad, and being kind to them. A variant reading for ḥasanan has ḥusnan, the verbal noun used as a hyperbolic description.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās narrows it: *and speak kindly to mankind — say the Truth regarding Muhammad.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the manner: *to say good words to people, telling them to do what is right and not what is wrong, without harshness or severity.*

**Maʿārif on the tone the verse requires.**

He draws a general rule from it, and it is the most practically useful comment in his commentary on this passage:

*The verse asks us to adopt a gentle tone and an open-hearted manner in speaking to others, whether they are good or evil, pious or impious, orthodox or aberrant, followers of the Sunnah or adherents to partitive innovations in it. In religious matters, however, one should not try to hide the truth for the sake of pleasing people or of winning their approval.*

*The Holy Qurʾān tells us that when Allah sent Sayyidunā Mūsā and Sayyidunā Hārūn to the Pharaoh, He instructed them to use gentle and soft words (20:42). None of us who addresses another today can be superior to Sayyidunā Mūsā, nor can the man addressed be viler than the Pharaoh.*

*Nor can the man addressed be viler than the Pharaoh.* The argument from the extreme case, and it closes the matter.

Gentle in manner, unhidden in content. That is the distinction Maʿārif draws, and the verse supports both halves.

**Prayer and alms.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and establish prayer — perfect the five daily prayers — and pay the poor-due, and give from your wealth what is due to the poor.*

Al-Jalālayn: *and observe prayer and pay the alms.*

The list ends where the sūrah's own command to the believers ends — 2:43, *establish prayer and pay alms*. Same two, same order.

**But you turned away.**

*Thumma tawallaytum.* Al-Jalālayn: *which you actually accepted, but then you turned away, refusing to fulfil these obligations. Here the second person address is used, but their forefathers are still meant; all but a few of you, rejecting it like your forefathers.*

*Their forefathers are still meant.* The address is to Madinah, the covenant was at Sinai. Verse 75's principle — counted as counterparts — is operating again.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Then, after that, ye slid back — you turned back on this covenant, save a few of you from amongst your forefathers; as it is said that this refers to ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his Companions, being averse — denying and leaving it aside.*

*ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām.* A named exception — the Jewish scholar of Madinah who accepted Islam.

**Except for a few.**

Maʿārif identifies them: *the few people it refers to as having been true to the pledge were those who acted upon the Sharīʿah of Sayyidunā Mūsā as long as it was in force, and when it was abrogated, followed the Sharīʿah of Sayyidunā Muhammad.*

Kept the covenant while it stood, then followed what replaced it. Not a minority that never broke it — a minority that kept following.

**And were indifferent.**

*Wa antum muʿriḍūn.* Al-Mukhtaṣar: *But all they did after making this promise was to turn away, rejecting the promise they had made.*

Ibn Kathīr's summary is the harshest: *how they intentionally and knowingly turned away from all of that.*

*Intentionally and knowingly.* The same two words verse 75 used — *after they understood it, knowingly*.

**Why this verse sits here.**

Verse 82 gave the standard: believe and do good. Verse 83 gives the content — what "do good" meant when it was revealed at Sinai. Six duties, and not one of them is obscure.

The sūrah has been describing failures for forty-three verses. This one lists what they walked away from.

84.text:
*And remember when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other's blood nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge and bore witness.*

**The second covenant, and it is a different kind.**

Verse 83's covenant was between the Israelites and Allah. Verse 84's is between them and each other.

Al-Jalālayn: *And when We made a covenant with you, and We said, "You shall not shed your own blood" — spilling it by slaying one another — "neither expel your own from your habitations" — let no one of you expel the other from his house; then you confirmed it, that is, you accepted this covenant, and you bore witness upon your own souls.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And when We made with you a covenant in the Book: shed not the blood of your people — do not kill one another — nor turn your people, i.e. one another, out of your dwellings — from your homes, meaning: the Banū Qurayẓah and Banū an-Naḍīr.*

*Meaning: the Banū Qurayẓah and Banū an-Naḍīr.* Tanwīr names the tribes in the verse itself. The covenant is not ancient history here — it is a description of Madinah.

**Your own blood.**

*Dimāʾakum.* Your blood, plural. Al-Jalālayn's gloss — *spilling it by slaying one another* — makes the point: the blood is shared. Killing one of them is spilling your own.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Remember the contract Allah made with you in the Torah: forbidding you from killing each other and forcing people to leave their homes.*

**Nor expel each other from their homes.**

Ibn Kathīr gives the sense: *"Shed not the blood of your people, nor turn out your own people from their dwellings" — meaning, "Do not kill each other..."*

Maʿārif explains the second prohibition precisely, and the explanation matters:

*They had agreed not to kill one another by engaging themselves in an internecine war, and also not to send their men into exile — that is to say, not to harass a man so as to force him to migrate.*

*Not to harass a man so as to force him to migrate.* Expulsion here is not a formal decree. It is making a place unliveable until the person leaves.

**You gave your pledge.**

*Thumma aqrartum.* Maʿārif makes a careful point about the quality of the agreement, and it is the verse's real emphasis:

*They had willingly taken this pledge. Now, it may sometimes happen that one does not express one's willingness in so many words, but the manner of his speech suggests it. The agreement of the Israelites was not of this order, but as clear and explicit as the statement of a witness usually is.*

*As clear and explicit as the statement of a witness.* Not reluctant consent. Testimony.

Al-Jalālayn: *then you confirmed it — that is, you accepted this covenant — and you bore witness upon your own souls.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Then ye ratified Our covenant — you agreed to it — and ye were witnesses thereto, while knowing what you were doing.*

*While knowing what you were doing.* The same phrase the sūrah has used since verse 59 — *bi-ghayri al-ḥaqq*, knowingly, with full awareness.

**Two prohibitions, and the third that follows.**

Maʿārif sets out all three injunctions of the covenant, and verse 85 will be about the arithmetic between them:

*Allah had laid down three special injunctions for the Israelites: (1) They should not kill one another in an internecine war. (2) They should not force their own people into exile. (3) If they found a man from amongst them a prisoner of war, they should pay a ransom, and get him released.*

Three. Verse 84 states the first two. Verse 85 introduces the third and says which ones they kept.

**Why this verse is so short.**

It is twenty-four words. A covenant, two prohibitions, a pledge, a witness.

The sūrah is not explaining. It is establishing that the agreement was made, that it was made willingly, and that they testified to it themselves.

Verse 85 then describes Madinah, and the description is exact enough to name the tribes.

**And what "each other" means.**

The verse says *your* blood and *your* homes four times. Not "the blood of others." The prohibition is internal — it is about what members of one community do to each other.

Ibn Kathīr's commentary on verse 85 will show what that meant in practice: three Jewish tribes, allied to two Arab tribes, killing each other in someone else's war.

Verse 84 says they promised not to. Verse 84 also says they witnessed it.

85.text:
*But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression; and when those expelled come to you as captives, you still ransom them—though expelling them was unlawful for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest? Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment? For Allah is never unaware of what you do.*

**The longest verse in the address, and the most specific.**

Verses 40 to 84 have moved between Sinai, the wilderness and Madinah. This one stays in Madinah and names the tribes.

**The situation.**

Ibn Kathīr sets it out completely, and it is the clearest account in the six sources:

*Allah criticized the Jews who lived in al-Madīnah during the time of the Messenger of Allah. They used to suffer, because of the armed conflicts between the tribes of al-Madīnah, Aws and Khazraj. Before Islam, the Aws and Khazraj worshipped idols, and many battles took place between them. There were three Jewish tribes in al-Madīnah at that time: Banū Qaynuqāʿ and Banū an-Naḍīr, the allies of the Khazraj, and Banū Qurayẓah, who used to be the allies of the Aws.*

*When war erupted between Aws and Khazraj, their Jewish allies would assist them. The Jew would kill his Arab enemy, and sometimes they also killed Jews who were the allies of the other Arab tribe, although the Jews were prohibited from killing each other according to clear religious texts in their Books.*

*They would also drive each other from their homes and loot whatever furniture and money they could. When the war ended, the victorious Jews would release the prisoners from the defeated party, according to the rulings of the Tawrāh.*

Read that last sentence again. The same people, in the same war, on the same day: killing, expelling, looting — and then ransoming, because the Torah required it.

**Maʿārif's account, with the arithmetic.**

He gives the same history and then states the pattern exactly:

*There lived in Madinah two tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj, who were hostile to each other, and would often go to war. In the environs of Madinah, there also lived two tribes of the Jews, the Banū Qurayẓah and the Banū Naḍīr. The former had friendly relations with the Aws, and the latter with the Khazraj.*

*When the Aws and the Khazraj went to war against each other, the two tribes of the Jews also took part in the battle, each on the side of its own friends. In these battles, many Jews lost their lives or were rendered homeless as much as the non-Jews. In other words, the Jews of the Banū Qurayẓah tribe had a share in the slaughter and exile of the Jews of the Banū Naḍīr tribe, and vice versa.*

*However, when some of the Jews became prisoners of war, each of the two Jewish groups would persuade their respective friends among the non-Jews to accept a ransom and to release the prisoners.*

Then the three injunctions from verse 84's commentary: *(1) They should not kill one another in an internecine war. (2) They should not force their own people into exile. (3) If they found a man from amongst them a prisoner of war, they should pay a ransom, and get him released.*

*The Israelites disregarded the first two injunctions, and acted upon the third alone, which they supposed easier to be carried out.*

*Which they supposed easier.* That is the verse's whole diagnosis. Not hypocrisy exactly — selection. They kept the one that cost least.

**The question they were asked.**

Maʿārif records it: *When they were asked why they showed such a solicitude for the prisoners, they would say that it was obligatory for them to get [them released].*

They had a religious reason. It was correct. And it was the only one of the three they obeyed.

**Tazkīrul's version, with the third tribe.**

It adds a detail and then makes the general point:

*Before the advent of Islam, three Jewish tribes inhabited the area around Madinah: the Banū Naḍīr, the Banū Qurayẓah, and the Banū Qaynuqāʿ. Despite the fact that all of them adhered to Mosaic law, ignorant prejudices had divided them into two groups. They had become enmeshed, along with the polytheist tribes of Madinah — al-Aws and the Khazraj — in political manoeuvring.*

Then the diagnosis, which applies well beyond Madinah:

*The basic teachings of Islamic law demand the total renunciation of pagan ways, the suppressing of one's selfish desires and the controlling of one's worldly needs — that is why the commands of Islamic law are ignored in politics. Obedience to them would bring about true piety, but people do not like to involve themselves in such arduous practices. They prefer to put on a pretence of piety by conducting certain superficial rituals.*

*This is tantamount to issuing a self-made edition of divine religion.*

*A self-made edition.* That is verse 79's writing with their own hands, in political form.

**Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest?**

*Afa-tuʾminūna bi-baʿḍi al-kitābi wa takfurūna bi-baʿḍ.* The sūrah's most quoted line.

Al-Jalālayn gives the text and a grammatical note on the verse that precedes it: *conspiring — taẓẓāharūna, the original tāʾ has been assimilated with the zāʾ; a variant reading has it without the assimilation, that is tazāharūna — assisting one another against them, in sin, in disobedience, and enmity, injustice; and if they come to you as captives — a variant reading for usārā has asrā — you ransom them — a variant reading for tafdūhum has tufādūhum — that is to say, you deliver them from captivity with money, etc., and this ransoming was one of the things to which they were pledged; yet their expulsion was forbidden you.*

Then the grammar of the parenthetical: *muḥarramun ʿalaykum ikhrājuhum is semantically connected to wa-tukhrijūna, "and expelling," and the statement that comes in between is parenthetical — that is, expulsion was forbidden you in the same way that non-ransoming was forbidden you.*

Both were commanded. Both were in the same covenant.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives the two readings of the question, and the second is the one that travels:

*Believe ye in part of the Scripture — the part that stipulates freeing your captives from the enemy — and disbelieve ye in part thereof? — and leave the captives of your friends without ransoming them. It is also said that this verse means: do you believe in those parts of the scripture that suit your whim, and disbelieve in those parts that do not?*

*Those parts that suit your whim.* Al-Mukhtaṣar phrases it the same way: *How is it that you believe in some of what is in the Torah about the ransom of captives, and reject some of it — about not killing each other and driving people from where they live?*

**The two punishments.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *For those of you who do that, there is only humiliation in this life and the most severe torment in the Afterlife.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names the worldly one concretely: *and what is the reward of those who do so save ignominy in the life of the world — by being killed or captured as slaves.*

*By being killed or captured as slaves.* Not an abstraction. The Aws and Khazraj wars, and what came after.

**Allah is never unaware.**

The same closing as verse 74. Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Allah knows what you do; in fact, He is fully aware, and He will hold you to account.*

**Why this verse is the centre of the address.**

It is the only place in the whole passage where the sūrah describes a specific, datable, political situation in its audience's own city — three tribes, two alliances, a war, and a ransom practice.

And the charge is not that they ignored their Book. It is that they kept the part that was cheap.

Tazkīrul's line covers the rest of the sūrah: *they prefer to put on a pretence of piety by conducting certain superficial rituals.*

Verse 86 says what that trade costs.

86.text:
*These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped.*

**The trade, named.**

Verse 85 described the behaviour. Verse 86 says what it was: a transaction.

Al-Jalālayn: *Those are the ones who have purchased the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter, by preferring the former to the latter.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Such are those who buy the life of the world at the price of the Hereafter — they choose this lower world instead of the Hereafter, and disbelief instead of belief.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *They are the people who exchange the Afterlife for this life, preferring what is temporary to what is eternal.*

**The sūrah's word.**

*Ishataraw* — to buy, to exchange. This is the vocabulary the sūrah has used from the beginning: 2:16 *their trade brought no profit*, 2:41 *do not exchange My signs for a small price*, 2:79 *seeking a fleeting gain*, 2:86 *trade the Hereafter for the life of this world*.

Four verses, one metaphor. And in every case the buyer loses.

**Why the punishment is not reduced.**

Al-Jalālayn: *for them the punishment shall not be lightened, neither shall they be helped, neither shall they be protected against it.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Their punishment will not be lightened — will not be reduced; as it is said: it will not be lifted — neither will they have support, be precluded from Allah's chastisement.*

Two things closed: relief, and rescue.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Their suffering will not be lightened, and they will have no one to help them.*

**Maʿārif on why.**

He explains the connection between the trade and the sentence, and it is the verse's argument:

*This verse explains why the Jews will have to undergo such a severe punishment. They have been disobeying Allah in order to satisfy their desires and to enjoy worldly pleasures; they have also sacrificed for these things their salvation in the other world. Their sin being so great, Allah will not reduce or mollify their punishment, nor will He allow anyone to intercede on their behalf.*

*They have sacrificed their salvation for these things.* Not merely sinned. Traded it away, knowingly, for something temporary.

**Tazkīrul's closing.**

Its comment on verses 84 to 86 ends the sequence, and it names what the trade actually was:

*It is to disregard the Hereafter and attach importance to the worldly aspect of religion, in the hope that zeal in performing actions which promise worldly fame and honour will qualify them for the reward reserved for true piety.*

*But such brazen distortion of religion can only earn one God's wrath; it does not merit any reward from God.*

The ransoming was not fake. It was a real religious act, correctly performed. And it earned nothing, because it was the cheap one.

**Why the verse is short.**

Nineteen words. After the longest verse in the address, the sūrah closes with the shortest possible statement of consequence.

They bought. They lost. Nothing will reduce it. Nobody will help.

**What the sequence 84–86 establishes.**

Verse 84: a covenant, willingly given, witnessed. Verse 85: three commands, one kept — the cheapest. Verse 86: the trade named, and the sentence fixed.

The charge is not irreligion. It is selective religion, priced by cost.

And that is why the verse uses commerce. The sūrah has been describing a market all along — signs sold for a small price, a Book rewritten for a fee, a paradise that did not have to be earned, and now the Hereafter exchanged for Madinah.

Verse 87 turns to Mūsā again, and to what happened to the messengers who came after him.

87.text:
*Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you, Israelites, with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others?*

**The verse that closes the historical section and opens the Madinah one.**

Verses 40 to 86 moved between Sinai, the wilderness and Madinah. Verse 87 steps back and gives the whole pattern in one sentence — and then asks the question the rest of the sūrah answers.

**We gave Moses the Book.**

Ibn Kathīr's commentary is blunt about what happened to it:

*Allah mentioned that He gave Mūsā the Book, the Tawrāh, and that the Jews changed, distorted, and defied its commands, as well as altered its meanings.*

Then the verse he uses to explain "successive messengers":

*"Verily, We did reveal the Tawrāh, therein was guidance and light, by which the Prophets, who submitted themselves to Allah's will, judged for the Jews. And the rabbis and the priests too judged for the Jews by the Tawrāh after those Prophets, for to them was entrusted the protection of Allah's Book, and they were witnesses thereto" (5:44).*

*By which the Prophets judged.* The Torah was not a monument. It was a working legal text, and the prophets after Mūsā were its judges.

**Successive messengers — and what the word means.**

*Qaffaynā.* Ibn Kathīr records the glosses:

*As-Suddī said that Abū Mālik said that qaffaynā means, "Succeeded," while others said, "Followed." Both meanings are plausible, since Allah said, "Then We sent Our Messengers in succession" (23:44).*

*Tazkīrul Qurʾān names the line: After Moses, several prophets arose among the Jewish people — Joshua, David, Zachariah, John the Baptist and finally Jesus, to name but a few.*

**Why ʿĪsā needed signs.**

Ibn Kathīr explains, and the reason is a legal one:

*Thereafter, Allah sent the last Prophet among the Children of Israel, ʿĪsā the son of Mary, who was sent with some laws that differed with some in the Tawrāh. This is why Allah also sent miracles to support ʿĪsā.*

He changed rulings. Changing rulings requires evidence, and the evidence was the miracles.

*These included bringing the dead back to life, forming the shape of birds from clay and blowing into them, after which they became living birds by Allah's leave, healing the sick and foretelling the Unseen, as Ibn ʿAbbās stated.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar lists the same: *clear signs of the truth of what he came with, such as bringing the dead back to life and healing the blind and the lepers.*

Al-Jalālayn: *the clear proofs — that is, the miracles of bringing the dead back to life and healing the blind and the leper.*

And the Qurʾān's own words, which Ibn Kathīr quotes: *"And to make lawful to you part of what was forbidden to you, and I have come to you with a sign from your Lord."*

*To make lawful part of what was forbidden.* That was the change. The signs were its warrant.

**The holy spirit.**

*Rūḥ al-qudus.* Every source identifies it, and Maʿārif gives the fullest treatment.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *He strengthened him with the angel Gabriel, the Holy Spirit.*

Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar: *the expression rūḥ al-qudus is an example of annexing, in a genitive construction, the noun described to the adjective qualifying it — in other words al-rūḥ al-muqaddasa — that is, Gabriel, so described on account of his, Jesus's, sanctity; he would accompany him wherever he went.*

*On account of Jesus's sanctity.* Not Gabriel's. The title reflects on the one supported.

Maʿārif establishes the identification from scripture and poetry:

*The Archangel Jibrāʾīl has often been called "Rūḥ al-Qudus" (the Holy Spirit) in the Noble Qurʾān and the ḥadīth. For example, in verse 16:102 — "Say: the Holy Spirit has brought it down" — or in a couplet of the poet and blessed Companion Ḥassān ibn Thābit, reported in the ḥadīth: "Jibrāʾīl, the messenger of Allah, comes to us; he is the Holy Spirit, the incomparable."*

**The four ways Gabriel supported ʿĪsā.**

Maʿārif lists them, and the list is the most complete account in the six sources:

*Allah helped and supported Sayyidunā ʿĪsā through Jibrāʾīl in several ways. (1) He was conceived through the breath of the Archangel. (2) Jibrāʾīl protected him against being touched by Satan at the time of his birth. (3) The Archangel always accompanied him in order to defend him against the hostility of the Jews. (4) It was through him that Sayyidunā ʿĪsā was raised to the heavens.*

Four points of contact: conception, birth, life, ascension. The support was not occasional. It was structural.

**The question.**

*Afa-kullamā jāʾakum rasūl.* Al-Jalālayn parses it and names the tone:

*Still you refuse to be upright, and whenever there came to you a messenger with what your souls did not desire — did not like, in the way of truth — you became arrogant, you disdained to follow him. Istakbartum, "you became arrogant," is the response to the particle kullamā, "whenever," and constitutes the interrogative, and is meant as a rebuke.*

An interrogative of rebuke again — the same form as 2:44, 2:61 and 2:75.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Is it ever so, that, when there cometh unto you, O group of Jews, a messenger with that which ye yourselves desire not — which does not agree with your hearts and religion — ye grow arrogant, you disdain believing in him?*

*What your souls did not desire.* The criterion was never truth. It was appetite.

**Rejecting some and killing others.**

The verse's two verbs, and both sources name the people.

Al-Jalālayn: *and some of them you called liars — such as Jesus — and some you slay — such as Zachariah and John. The present tenses of these verbs are used to narrate the past events, as though they were events in the present.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And some ye disbelieve — you disbelieve in a group of them, namely Muhammad and Jesus — and some ye slay, and some you killed, namely, John the Baptist and Zachariah.*

Tanwīr adds Muhammad to the list of those they called liars. Al-Jalālayn does not.

**Tazkīrul on what went wrong before any of this.**

Its diagnosis is the most searching in the six sources, and it explains the Torah itself:

*The Torah was the Book of God revealed to the Jews. Gradually, however, they ceased to treat it as a source of divine guidance and came to regard it as a sacred relic of their national heritage, a symbol of ethnic superiority; it became more a guarantee of salvation than a guide as to how salvation could be earned.*

*A guarantee of salvation rather than a guide.* That is verse 80's forty days, and verse 78's paradise that did not have to be earned, in one sentence.

Then: *It is futile to believe in the sacredness of the holy scriptures if one does not implement their message in one's everyday life. But the Jews, the very people who held the Torah in such high esteem, were extremely intolerant of the Prophet's exhortations. The reason for such a reaction on their part was that they had allowed self-interest and worldly ambitions to rule their lives, while passing themselves off as bearers and upholders of the true faith.*

*As long as religion served to consolidate their worldly status, they welcomed it, but were loath to accept the message of truth — presented to them in all its purity — which they saw as a threat to the hegemony they had secured for themselves on the basis of religion.*

**Ibn Kathīr's summary.**

*Yet, the Children of Israel became more defiant and envious of him, and did not want to differ with even one part of the Tawrāh.*

*More defiant and envious.* The miracles were the answer to the legal change, and the response was envy.

Verse 88 gives their own explanation. Verse 88 also says why it is wrong.

88.text:
*They say, "Our hearts are unreceptive!" In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief. They have but little faith.*

**Their own words, quoted against them.**

Four verses of indictment, and then the sūrah lets them speak.

**Ghulf — and the five readings.**

Ibn Kathīr collects them, and the disagreement is the verse:

*Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said that "And they say, 'Our hearts are ghulf,'" means, "Our hearts are screened." Mujāhid also said that it means, "They are covered." ʿIkrimah said, "There is a stamp on them." Abū al-ʿĀliyah said, "They do not comprehend."*

*Muḥammad and Qatādah said that Ibn ʿAbbās read the verse in a way that means, "Our hearts contain every type of knowledge and do not need the knowledge that you have, O Muhammad." This is the opinion of ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn ʿAbbās.*

Two opposite readings from the same phrase. Either *our hearts are sealed against you*, or *our hearts are full and need nothing more*.

Al-Jalālayn takes the first: *And they say to the Prophet mockingly, "Our hearts are encased" — ghulf is the plural of aghlaf — that is to say, wrapped up in covers, and cannot comprehend what you say.*

*Mockingly.* On this reading it is not an excuse. It is a boast.

**Maʿārif on what they thought they were saying.**

He reads it the same way and explains the pride in it:

*The Jews used to say sarcastically that their hearts were "veiled", by which they meant that their hearts were so well protected against Islam that it could never touch them. This was their way of congratulating themselves on being staunch in their belief.*

*Congratulating themselves.* They thought it was strength.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives the version that combines both readings: *Our hearts are hardened vis-à-vis what you say, O Muhammad — i.e. our hearts are capable of absorbing any knowledge, but they prove incapable of comprehending your knowledge or what you say.*

*Capable of absorbing any knowledge, but incapable of comprehending yours.* That is the boast and the excuse in one.

**The reply.**

*Bal laʿanahumu Llāhu bi-kufrihim.* Ibn Kathīr: *"Nay, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief" — meaning, "Allah expelled them and deprived them of every type of righteousness."*

Al-Jalālayn: *God says, "Nay" — bal introduces the rebuttal — "but God has cursed them," removed them far from His mercy and degraded them, when they rejected the messengers, for their unbelief, which is not the result of anything defective in their hearts.*

*Which is not the result of anything defective in their hearts.* This is the verse's whole point. They described a condition. The Qurʾān describes a verdict.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *On the contrary, Allah deprived them of His mercy due to their disbelief, so that they will not have faith.*

**Maʿārif's reframing.**

He states the reversal precisely:

*The Holy Qurʾān points out that this is not the firmness of faith, but a damnation, for they deny Islam which now is the true religion, and stick to a religion which has been abrogated.*

Not firmness. Damnation that feels like firmness.

**They have but little faith.**

*Fa-qalīlan mā yuʾminūn.* There are two readings, and Ibn Kathīr sets out the disagreement:

*Qatādah said that the verse, "So little is that which they believe," means, "Only a few of them believe."*

*There is a difference of opinion regarding the meaning of Allah's statement, "So little is that which they believe," and His statement, "So they believe not except a few." Some scholars said that the verses indicate that a few of them would believe, or that their faith is minute, because they believe in Resurrection and in Allah's reward and punishment that Mūsā foretold.*

Few people, or little faith. Both readings stand.

Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar: *and little will they believe — fa-qalīlan mā yuʾminūn; the mā here is extra, emphasising the "littleness" involved — that is, their belief is minimal.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās takes it further: *Little is that which they believe — they believe neither much nor a little; it is also said that this means: they do not believe in what you say at all.*

**Maʿārif on what the "little" is.**

He identifies it, and it is the most illuminating comment on the verse:

*The little "faith" which they possessed pertained to the doctrines which are common to Islam and Judaism — for example, belief in Allah, or belief in the Day of Judgment. But they did not accept Sayyidunā Muhammad as a prophet, and the Holy Qurʾān as the Word of Allah. So, their faith was not complete.*

They believed in God and the Last Day — the two conditions verse 62 named. And it was not enough.

Then he makes a technical point about the word itself:

*If the verse describes "the little faith" as īmān, it does so only in the lexical sense, for īmān signifies total certitude, even if it pertains to certain things, and not to others. But from the point of view of the Sharīʿah, such a partial faith cannot be described as īmān. The Sharīʿah would accept as valid only that īmān which affirms with certitude each and everything that the Sharīʿah requires one to affirm.*

The verse uses the word. Maʿārif explains that it is being used loosely, and says what the term properly requires.

**The parallel verses.**

Ibn Kathīr supplies both, and they show this is a settled charge:

*"And they say: 'Our hearts are under coverings, screened, from that to which you invite us' (41:5)."*

*"And of their saying: 'Our hearts are wrapped with coverings — nay, Allah has set a seal upon their hearts because of their disbelief, so they believe not but a little' (4:155)."*

*It is not as they claim. Rather, their hearts are cursed and stamped.*

**Why this verse is so short.**

It is a claim, a rebuttal, and a diagnosis in twenty words.

They said their hearts were wrapped. The verse says: no, they were cursed — and the difference is that a wrapped heart is a fact about the heart, while a cursed heart is a fact about what the person did.

Verse 89 shows what they did.

89.text:
*Although they used to pray for victory by means of the Prophet over the polytheists, when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had in their hands, they rejected it. So may Allah's condemnation be upon the disbelievers.*

**The verse that turns their own prayers into evidence.**

They had been asking for this prophet. The verse says so, and quotes what they said.

**They prayed for victory through him.**

*Yastaftiḥūn.* Ibn Kathīr explains the practice:

*Before this Messenger came to them, they used to ask Allah to aid them by his arrival, against their polytheistic enemies in war. They used to say to the polytheists, "A Prophet shall be sent just before the end of this world, and we, along with him, shall exterminate you, just as the nations of ʿĀd and Iram were exterminated."*

Not a private hope. A threat delivered to their neighbours, with the prophet as the instrument.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names the neighbours: *though before that — before Muhammad — they were asking for a signal triumph, through Muhammad and the Qurʾān, over those who disbelieved, of their enemies: the tribes of Asad, Ghaṭafān, Muzaynah and Juhaynah.*

Al-Jalālayn: *they formerly, before it came, prayed for victory, for assistance over the disbelievers, saying, "God, give us assistance against them through the Prophet that shall be sent at the end of time."*

Maʿārif: *the Jews themselves used to tell the Arabs that a new prophet and a new Divine Book was soon to come.*

**The exchange that triggered the verse.**

Ibn Kathīr records it from Ibn ʿAbbās, via Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, and it is the most specific narrative in the passage:

*"The Jews used to invoke Allah for the coming of Muhammad in order to gain victory over the Aws and Khazraj, before the Prophet was sent. When Allah sent him to the Arabs, they rejected him and denied what they used to say about him."*

*"Hence, Muʿādh ibn Jabal and Bishr ibn al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr, from Banū Salamah, said to them, 'O Jews! Fear Allah and embrace Islam. You used to invoke Allah for the coming of Muhammad when we were still disbelievers, and you used to tell us that he would come and describe him to us.'"*

*"Salām ibn Mushkim from Banū an-Naḍīr replied, 'He did not bring anything that we recognize. He is not the Prophet we told you about.'"*

*"Allah then revealed this verse about their statement."*

Named people on both sides. Two men from Banū Salamah quoting the Jews' own earlier words back at them, and one man from Banū an-Naḍīr retracting.

*He is not the Prophet we told you about.* The admission is complete: there was a prophet they told them about.

Abū al-ʿĀliyah, also recorded by Ibn Kathīr: *"The Jews used to ask Allah to send Muhammad so that they would gain victory over the [polytheists]."*

**A Book confirming what is with them.**

*Muṣaddiqun limā maʿahum.* Ibn Kathīr: *"a Book from Allah" — meaning, the Qurʾān that Allah sent down to Muhammad — "confirming what is with them" — meaning, the Tawrāh.*

Maʿārif explains what "confirming" does here, and it is the verse's argument:

*The verse says that the Holy Qurʾān confirms the Torah. It means that the Holy Qurʾān is a concrete evidence of the truth of the prophecies made in the Torah with regard to the coming of the Holy Prophet and of the Holy Qurʾān. One who believes in the Torah cannot justifiably deny the Holy Qurʾān and the Holy Prophet, for such a denial would involve a denial of the Torah itself.*

*Such a denial would involve a denial of the Torah itself.* The Qurʾān arriving as predicted is the proof that the Torah is true. Rejecting it is not loyalty to the Torah — it is disproof of it.

**They recognized it.**

Al-Jalālayn: *but when there came to them what they recognised as the truth — that is, the mission of the Prophet — they disbelieved in it, out of envy and for fear of losing leadership.*

*Out of envy and for fear of losing leadership.* Two motives, both worldly.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and when there cometh unto them that which they knew — of his traits and description in their Book — they disbelieved therein, they denied it was him.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *But when the Qurʾān and Muhammad came to them, according to the description they recognised and the truth they knew, they disbelieved him.*

**Maʿārif's heading: knowledge is not enough for faith.**

He raises the obvious objection and answers it, and the answer is the most consequential comment in the six sources:

*One may want to know why the Holy Qurʾān calls the Jews kāfirūn (infidels), when they did recognize the truth as truth, which should qualify them to be called "believers." Let us explain that īmān (faith) does not merely mean "knowing the truth", but really signifies "accepting the truth and affirming it deed-wise."*

*Otherwise, Satan too will have to be called a believer, for he knows fully well what the truth is. In fact, this knowledge of the truth on the part of Satan intensifies the gravity of his kufr (infidelity) all the more.*

Satan knows. Knowing is not believing. And knowing while refusing makes it worse.

**Tazkīrul on what the prayer really was.**

Its reading is the least charitable and the most precise:

*The Jews of Arabia behaved similarly with the Prophet Muhammad. They had seen prophecies of the coming of a final prophet in their scriptures, and had eagerly anticipated his arrival. When he comes, they used to say, we will join with him in a grand alliance against the pagans and idolators.*

*But these proved to be empty words on their part, a pretence aimed at consolidating their status as undisputed guardians of divine faith. When the Prophet came, the truth of their position was exposed. They were shown to be steeped in bigotry, reluctant to believe in a prophet who did not come from the Jewish race.*

*Reluctant to believe in a prophet who did not come from the Jewish race.* The objection was never about the evidence.

Then: *They could not dispute the authentic indications presented by the Quran in support of his prophethood; all they could say was, "It all sounds very impressive, but our ancestral religion is good enough for us. Our hearts are sealed and we will not accept anything besides the faith we have inherited from our forefathers."*

That is verse 88's boast, quoted back.

**So may Allah's condemnation be upon the disbelievers.**

Al-Jalālayn: *and the curse of God is on the disbelievers.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *The curse of Allah — His wrath and torment — is on disbelievers, the Jews.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Allah curses those who disbelieve Him and His Prophet.*

The verse ends not with an argument but with a prayer against them — the first in the address.

**Why this verse lands where it does.**

Verse 87 asked why they reject every messenger. Verse 88 gave their answer: our hearts are wrapped. Verse 89 answers that with a fact about their own history.

They had been asking for this one. Out loud. To their neighbours' faces. And when he came they said he was not the one they meant.

The condemnation is not for ignorance. It is for the distance between the prayer and the refusal.

90.text:
*Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for—denying Allah's revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants! They have earned wrath upon wrath. And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment.*

**The trade, again — and this time what motivated it.**

Verse 86 said they traded the Hereafter for this world. Verse 90 says what they traded for, and it is not a thing. It is a feeling.

**Miserable is the price.**

*Biʾsa mā ishtaraw bihi anfusahum.* Mujāhid, recorded by Ibn Kathīr: *"The Jews sold the truth for falsehood, and hid the truth about Muhammad."*

As-Suddī, also via Ibn Kathīr: *the verse means, "The Jews sold themselves" — meaning, what is worse is what they chose for themselves by disbelieving in what Allah revealed to Muhammad instead of believing, aiding and supporting him.*

*The Jews sold themselves.* Not sold something. Sold themselves.

Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar: *Evil is that for which they sell their souls — that is, their share of the reward in the Hereafter. Biʾsamā, "evil is that for which" — mā here is an indefinite particle representing "a thing" and constitutes a specification qualifying the subject of the verb biʾsa, "evil is," the very thing being singled out for criticism.*

**Resenting Allah.**

*Baghyan an yunazzila Llāhu min faḍlih.* This is the verse's centre, and it is not about the Prophet.

Ibn Kathīr: *This behavior of theirs is the result of their injustice, envy and hatred — "grudging that Allah should reveal of His grace unto whom He wills of His servants." There is no envy worse than this.*

*There is no envy worse than this.* Envy directed at God's choice rather than at a person.

Al-Jalālayn: *that they disbelieve in that Qurʾān which God has revealed, grudging — baghyan here is an object denoting reason for yakfurū, "they disbelieve," that is, out of envy that God should reveal — read either yunzil or yunazzil — of His bounty, the Inspiration, to whomever He will of His servants, to deliver the Message.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *grudging — resentfully envious — that Allah should reveal of His bounty — that out of His bounty, Allah sent Gabriel with the Book and prophethood — unto whom He will of His bondmen, meaning Muhammad.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *They disbelieved what Allah revealed, and unjustly and enviously rejected His prophets, because He gave prophethood and the Qurʾān to Muhammad.*

**Maʿārif on why this is the root.**

He states the principle the verse assumes:

*Prophethood cannot be earned through one's own efforts or one's own merit; it is a special grace which Allah bestows on whomsoever He likes. But the Jews were so envious and malicious that they denied the Holy Prophet and the Holy Qurʾān out of sheer spite. In doing so, they were questioning the will of Allah Himself.*

*Questioning the will of Allah Himself.* Not disagreeing with a claim. Objecting to a distribution.

**Wrath upon wrath.**

*Fa-bāʾū bi-ghaḍabin ʿalā ghaḍab.* Three readings, and Ibn Kathīr gives all of them.

Ibn ʿAbbās: *"Allah became angry with them because they ignored some of the Tawrāh and disbelieved in the Prophet that He sent to them."*

Abū al-ʿĀliyah: *"Allah became angry with them because of their disbelief in the Injīl and ʿĪsā, and He became angry with them again because they disbelieved in Muhammad and the Qurʾān."* Similar was said by ʿIkrimah and Qatādah.

Ibn Kathīr's own gloss on the verb: *the meaning of bāʾū, "and they drew on themselves," is that they deserved and acquired multiplied anger.*

*Multiplied anger.* Not one offence but a running account.

Al-Jalālayn connects the two wraths to the two rejections: *and they were laden — they returned with anger from God for their disbelief in what He has revealed. The indefinite form bi-ghaḍabin, "with anger," is used to emphasise the awesomeness of the "anger" — upon anger, which they deserved formerly when they neglected the Torah and disbelieved in Jesus.*

Two wraths: one for ʿĪsā, one for Muhammad. Verse 87 named both rejections; verse 90 prices them.

**A humiliating punishment.**

*ʿAdhābun muhīn.* Ibn Kathīr explains why this punishment has this quality, and the reasoning is exact:

*Since their disbelief was a result of their transgression and envy, which was caused by arrogance, they were punished with disgrace and humiliation in this world and the Hereafter.*

Then the verse he uses: *"Verily, those who scorn My worship — they will surely enter Hell in humiliation" (40:60) — meaning, "Disgraced, degraded and humiliated."*

Arrogance produced the envy. The punishment matches the arrogance. The same logic as the ape punishment at verse 65 — *their punishment was compatible with their crime.*

**Maʿārif on the distinction this draws.**

He makes a point that separates this from ordinary sin, and it is the most pastorally significant comment in his commentary here:

*The Holy Qurʾān says that the Jews will have to undergo a punishment which would involve not only pain, but also disgrace and abasement. The latter condition has been added to suggest that this kind of punishment is peculiar to the infidels, and is not meant for a true Muslim at all, for a Muslim, no matter how great his sins are, will be punished for the purpose of being purified, not for being disgraced.*

*Purified, not disgraced.* Two kinds of punishment, distinguished by purpose. The humiliating one is for those who were arrogant about God's choice.

**Tanwīr and al-Jalālayn on the same phrase.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *For disbelievers is a shameful doom, through which they shall be humiliated; and it is said: theirs is a severe punishment.*

Al-Jalālayn: *and for the disbelievers there shall be a humiliating chastisement.*

**Why this verse follows verse 89.**

Verse 89 said they recognised him and rejected him. Verse 90 says why: not doubt, but resentment that Allah chose someone else.

That is why the price is called miserable. They did not buy anything. They paid their share of the Hereafter to avoid acknowledging a grace they could not claim.

And verse 91 gives the argument they used instead.

91.text:
*When it is said to them: "Believe in what Allah has revealed," they reply, "We only believe in what was sent down to us," and they deny what came afterwards, though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures! Ask them, O Prophet, "Why then did you kill Allah's prophets before, if you are truly believers?"*

**The argument, and the question that ends it.**

This verse states their position fairly, states why it fails, and then asks one question.

**Their position.**

Al-Jalālayn: *And when it was said to them, "Believe in what God has revealed" — that is, the Qurʾān and other Books — they said, "We believe in what was revealed to us," that is, the Torah.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And when it is said unto them, i.e. the Jews: "Believe in that which Allah hath revealed," meaning: the Qurʾān — they say: "We believe in that which was revealed unto us," i.e. the Torah.*

Ibn Kathīr gives the sense: *"We believe in what was sent down to us" — meaning, it is enough for us to believe in what was revealed to us in the Tawrāh and the Injīl, and this is the path that we choose.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *they said that they believed in what had been revealed to their prophets, and denied anything besides this.*

**Maʿārif on what the argument reveals.**

He reads the phrase *"sent down to us"* closely, and the reading is devastating:

*The Jews flatly refused to believe in any Book of Allah — like the Evangel or the Holy Qurʾān — except in the Torah. This denial is a clear evidence of their infidelity. Moreover, they also used to add that they believe in the Torah, for it had been sent down to them. This comes to mean that they denied the other Books just because they had not been sent down to them. Such an argument betrays their envy and malice.*

*Just because they had not been sent down to them.* The criterion was not truth. It was ownership. That is verse 90's resentment stated as a doctrine.

**And they deny what came afterwards.**

Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar: *and wā here indicates a circumstantial qualifier — they disbelieve in what is beyond that, what is other than that, or what came afterwards, such as the Qurʾān; yet it is the truth — wa-huwa al-ḥaqq is a circumstantial qualifier — confirming — muṣaddiqan, a second circumstantial qualifier for emphasis — what is with them.*

Two circumstantial qualifiers stacked. The verse says the same thing twice: it is the truth, and it confirms what you have.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And they disbelieve in that which cometh after it — other than the Torah — though it is the Truth, i.e. the Qurʾān is the Truth, confirming — affirming the Oneness of Allah — that which they possess of the Book.*

**Ibn Kathīr on why this is a proof against them.**

*This means that since what was sent to Muhammad conforms to what was revealed to the People of the Book, then this fact constitutes a proof against them.*

Then the verse that says how completely they recognised it: *"Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize him as they recognize their sons" (2:146).*

*As they recognize their sons.* Not approximately. With the certainty of a parent.

**The question.**

*Fa-lima taqtulūna anbiyāʾa Llāhi min qablu in kuntum muʾminīn.*

Ibn Kathīr gives the full force of it:

*This means, "If your claim that you believe in what was revealed to you is true, then why did you kill the Prophets who came to you affirming the Tawrāh's Law, although you knew they were true Prophets? You killed them simply out of transgression, stubbornness and injustice with Allah's Messengers. Therefore, you only follow your lusts, opinions and desires."*

*The Prophets who came to you affirming the Torah's Law.* This is what makes the question unanswerable. The ones they killed were not outsiders bringing something new. They were Torah-observant prophets, sent to Torah-observant people, teaching the Torah.

Al-Jalālayn notes the address: *Say to them, "Why then were you slaying the prophets of God formerly, if you were believers?" — in the Torah, and in it you were forbidden to kill them. This address, concerning what their forefathers did, is directed towards those present at the time of our Prophet, on account of their approval of it — that is, of what the forefathers had done.*

*On account of their approval of it.* The Madinah Jews did not kill anyone. They approved of those who did. That is the standard verse 75 set — counted as counterparts because they did not abhor their forefathers' deeds.

**Maʿārif's three refutations.**

He sets out the argument systematically, and it is the most complete treatment in the six sources:

*The Holy Qurʾān refutes their argument in three ways:*

*(1) When the truth and authenticity of the other Books has been established on the basis of irrefutable arguments, what does, then, this denial mean? If they had any doubts as to the arguments on the basis of which authenticity was being claimed for these Books, they could very well have voiced this doubt, and satisfied themselves on this point. But why this flat refusal to believe?*

*(2) The other Books, like the Holy Qurʾān, confirm the Torah. If one denies them, one at the same time denies the Torah itself.*

*(3) To slay a prophet is tantamount to infidelity, according to all the Divine Books. Moreover, the prophets whom the Jews had killed were themselves Israelites, and their teachings were based on the injunctions of the Torah. But the Jews not only killed these prophets, but also accepted the killers as their chiefs. This is a direct denial of the Torah, and falsifies their claim that they believe in the Torah.*

*They accepted the killers as their chiefs.* That is the third refutation's edge. Not merely that the killings happened — that the community honoured the killers afterwards.

*In short, nothing that the Jews say or do is acceptable and valid from any possible point of view.*

**Al-Jalālayn's addition.**

He adds the internal contradiction: *and in it you were forbidden to kill them.*

The Torah prohibits killing prophets. They claim to believe only in the Torah. They killed prophets.

**Tazkīrul on what lay underneath.**

Its reading names the feeling, and connects verse 91 to the ethnic claim:

*The Jews were not ready to accept the Quran, because they thought they were already rightly guided. They were sure that the very fact that they belonged to the largest group of the followers of truth, that is, the Israelites, would be enough to earn them salvation. But, in fact, this was a feeling of ethnic superiority which they mistook for love of truth.*

*Ethnic superiority mistaken for love of truth.* That is what *"what was sent down to us"* means.

**And the verse after.**

Verse 92 answers the question before they can. Mūsā came with clear proofs, and they worshipped the calf after he left.

So the sequence is: they claim to believe only in what was sent to them. The sūrah asks why they killed the prophets who came affirming it. And then reminds them what they did with the first one.

The question is rhetorical because the answer is already in the sūrah — forty-three verses of it.

92.text:
*Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully.*

**The answer to verse 91's question.**

Verse 91 asked why they killed the prophets if they believed. Verse 92 does not wait for an answer. It gives the first example, and it is the worst one.

**The clear proofs.**

Maʿārif lists them and dates them:

*The "clear signs" mentioned in the verse refers to the miracles which had manifested themselves even before the Torah was given to Sayyidunā Mūsā — for example, his staff that turned into a snake, the palm of his hand which shone brightly, the splitting of the sea to make a path for the Israelites, etc.*

*Before the Torah was given.* The evidence preceded the law. They were not asked to obey on trust.

*These miracles were meant to affirm the Oneness of Allah and His omnipotence, and to provide an evidence for the prophethood of Sayyidunā Mūsā.*

Al-Jalālayn: *And Mūsā came to you with clear proofs — miracles, such as the staff, his hand, and the parting of the sea.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And Moses came unto you with clear proofs — with commands, prohibitions and signs.*

**Then you worshipped the calf.**

*Thumma ttakhadhtumu al-ʿijl.* Al-Jalālayn: *then you took to yourselves the calf as a god, after him — after he had gone to the appointment — and you were evildoers, for taking it in worship.*

*After him.* Baʿdah — after Mūsā, meaning after his departure. Not after his death. He left for forty nights and came back to this.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *yet while he was away ye chose the calf — you worshipped the calf — and ye were wrong-doers, unbelievers.*

*Tanwīr translates ẓālimūn as unbelievers*, not merely wrongdoers. Al-Mukhtaṣar agrees: *You were wrongdoers for worshipping others alongside Allah, since only He is worthy of worship.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar sets the timing: *after that you made the calf into a god and worshipped it, when Moses had gone to meet his Lord.*

**Maʿārif on what the verse is really arguing.**

He states the charge, and it is more severe than idolatry:

*In refutation of the Jews, the verse points out that although they lay a claim to īmān (faith), yet they have been falling into the sin of shirk (association), which involves a denial not only of Sayyidunā Mūsā but even of Allah Himself.*

*A denial not only of Mūsā but of Allah Himself.* The claim to faith and the act of shirk in the same sentence.

**Why the Madinah Jews are addressed about it.**

Maʿārif gives the reason, and it is the same principle as verse 75:

*Although the Jews who were the contemporaries of the Holy Prophet did not themselves take part in the worship of the golden calf, yet they respected such of their forefathers as had done so, and took their side. So, for all practical purposes, they too were guilty of the same sin.*

*They respected such of their forefathers as had done so, and took their side.* Not for doing it. For approving of it.

Then the inference the verse draws: *The verse also suggests that no wonder if these people, whose forefathers denied Sayyidunā Mūsā, should now be denying the Holy Prophet.*

**Tazkīrul on what the calf revealed.**

Its comment is the sharpest observation on the verse, because it identifies what the forty days actually tested:

*They had seen Moses perform undeniable miracles, but when he was not with them in person, having left them to spend forty days on Mount Sinai, they started worshipping the golden calf; it had only been his personal authority which had kept them under control.*

*It had only been his personal authority.* The miracles had convinced them of Mūsā. They had not convinced them of Allah.

That is why the absence mattered. The proof they had accepted was a person, and the person left.

**Why this verse is short.**

Fifteen words. Miracles, a calf, an absence, a charge.

The sūrah has told this story twice already — at verse 51 and verse 54. This is the third time, and it is the shortest telling, because by now the reader knows it.

Verse 93 goes back to the mountain, and adds the sentence they have not yet heard: *we hear and disobey.*

93.text:
*And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you, saying, "Hold firmly to that Scripture which We have given you and obey," they answered, "We hear and disobey." The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, O Prophet, "How evil is what your so-called belief prompts you to do, if you actually believe in the Torah!"*

**The mountain, again — and this time what they said under it.**

Verse 63 told the same event. Verse 93 tells it again, and adds two things verse 63 did not have: their answer, and the calf.

**The covenant and the mountain.**

Al-Jalālayn: *And when We made a covenant with you to act according to what is in the Torah, and raised over you the Mount to drop it on you, when you had refused to accept it; We said, "Take forcefully — seriously and with effort — what We have given you, and listen," to what you have been commanded, and be prepared to accept it.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And when We made with you a covenant — when we took your consent — and caused the Mount to tower above you: extracted it, elevated it and fixed it above your heads: "Hold fast by that which We have given you — be diligent and earnest with what We have given you of the Book — and hear," obey what you have been commanded.*

Ibn Kathīr: *Allah reminded the Jews of their errors, breaking His covenant, transgression and defiance, when He raised Mount Ṭūr above them so that they would believe and agree to the terms of the covenant. Yet, they broke it soon afterwards.*

*Soon afterwards.* Not eventually. Soon.

**"We hear and disobey."**

*Samiʿnā wa ʿaṣaynā.* The sūrah's most quoted phrase, and it appears only here.

Al-Jalālayn: *They said, "We hear your words, and disobey your command."*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās supplies the thought behind it, and it is the most revealing gloss available:

*They said: We hear and rebel — it is as if they were saying: if it were not for the mountain we would have heard your saying and disobeyed your command.*

*If it were not for the mountain.* They said "we hear" because of the mountain. The mountain produced the hearing. It did not produce the obedience.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *you said that you heard with your ears and rebelled in your actions.*

*With your ears.* Hearing located in the ear, and rebellion located in the act. The two halves of the phrase are in different parts of the person.

**Maʿārif on what they actually said.**

He reads it as a statement made under duress, and the reading matters:

*This verse reports the Jews as having replied that they had heard the Command of Allah, but they would not obey, or would not be able to obey. It means that out of sheer fright they said — only with their tongues — that they had heard.*

*Only with their tongues.* The mountain produced a verbal compliance and nothing else.

**The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts.**

*Wa ushribū fī qulūbihimu al-ʿijla bi-kufrihim.* The verb is the verse's strangest feature, and Ibn Kathīr collects its glosses:

*ʿAbd ar-Razzāq said that Maʿmar narrated that Qatādah said that "and their hearts absorbed the worship of the calf" means, "They absorbed its love, until its love resided in their hearts." This is also the opinion of Abū al-ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas.*

Al-Jalālayn gives the image in full: *and they were made to drink the calf in their hearts — that is to say, the love of it; the golden calf intoxicated their hearts in the way that wine does, on account of their unbelief.*

*In the way that wine does.* Ushribū — they were made to drink. The love entered them as a drink enters.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And worship of the calf was made to sink into their hearts — their love of worshipping the calf sank into their hearts — because of their rejection, as a punishment for their disbelief.*

*As a punishment.* On this reading the drinking is not merely descriptive. It is a consequence.

**Maʿārif on how the calf got into their hearts in the first place.**

He traces it back before Sinai, and the account is the most complete in the six sources:

*When the Israelites succeeded, with the help of Allah, in escaping from Egypt and crossing the sea, they came upon a people who used to worship idols. They found this cult so attractive that they requested Sayyidunā Mūsā to fabricate a visible and concrete god for them too. When he reprimanded them, they realized their error, and offered repentance.*

This is verse 7:138 — the request for a god on the way out of Egypt.

*But repentance has many degrees. Since their repentance was not of a very high order, the darkness of their error did not altogether leave their hearts, but continued to grow, and finally manifested itself in the worship of the golden calf.*

*Repentance has many degrees.* The calf was not a sudden fall. It was an incomplete repentance completing itself.

Then the division inside the camp:

*As an act of penance, some of them had to be slain, and others, as some commentators report, were forgiven and not slain. Possibly the repentance of these latter was again of a low order. As for those who had not indulged in the worship of the calf, they did not hate the action of the worshippers of the calf as much as they should have. So, their hearts too carried a trace of the sin of association.*

*They did not hate the action as much as they should have.* The bystanders carried a trace too. That is verse 75's standard again — counted as counterparts for not abhorring.

*So, either through the feebleness of their repentance or through a want of proper hatred for infidelity, their hearts became indolent in religious matters, so much so that when Allah asked them to take a pledge to follow the injunctions of the Torah steadfastly, Mount Ṭūr was suspended over their heads to threaten them.*

The mountain was needed because the hearts had already gone soft. The sequence runs backwards from the mountain to the calf to Egypt.

**How evil is what your belief prompts you to do.**

*Biʾsamā yaʾmurukum bihi īmānukum.* The rebuke, and it takes their own claim as its premise.

Al-Jalālayn: *Say to them, "Evil is that thing which your belief in the Torah enjoins on you, in the way of the worship of the golden calf, if you are believers" in it as you claim; meaning, you are not believers, for faith does not command that you worship the calf — their forefathers are meant here.*

Then he extends it to the present: *Likewise, you do not believe in the Torah, because you have denied the prophethood of Muhammad, whereas faith in it does not command you to reject him.*

Two applications, one argument. Faith in the Torah does not command calf-worship, and it does not command rejecting Muhammad.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Say unto them, O Muhammad! If love of worshipping the calf is equal in your eyes to love of your Creator, then: "Evil is that which your belief enjoineth on you" — the worship of the calf enjoins on you — "if ye are believers," if you are truthful that your forefathers were believers.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *what their faith commands them to do is evil: disbelieving and turning away from what Allah instructs them to do — if they have any faith at all — because if they truly had faith they would not disbelieve and turn away from it.*

**Ibn Kathīr's expansion.**

He takes the rebuke further than any other source:

*"Worst indeed is that which your faith enjoins on you if you are believers" means, "Worse yet is the manner in which you behaved in the past and even now, disbelieving in Allah's āyāt and defying the Prophets. You also disbelieved in Muhammad, which is the worst of your deeds and the harshest sin that you committed."*

*"You disbelieved in the Final Messenger and the master of all Prophets and Messengers, the one who was sent to all mankind. How can you then claim that you believe, while committing the evil of breaking Allah's covenant, disbelieving in Allah's āyāt and worshipping the calf instead of Allah?"*

**Tazkīrul on the pattern.**

Its account of verses 91 to 93 gives the sequence in one breath:

*When the Mount was raised threateningly above their heads, they temporarily agreed to do "all that the Lord hath spoken" (Exodus 19:5, 8, 16, 18), but, after that, most of them returned to their disobedient ways.*

It cites Exodus for the words they said under the mountain. Then:

*If they had really been seeking God, their attention would have been entirely focused on the life after death; but, in fact, they, more than all the others, were obsessed with the love of the present world.*

That is the bridge to verses 94 to 96, and Tazkīrul is the only source to make it.

**Why the mountain appears twice.**

Verse 63 gave the mountain as a favour. Verse 93 gives it as evidence — because now the reader knows what they said under it.

The same event, two readings. And the second one includes the answer.

94.text:
*Say, O Prophet, "If the eternal Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you, Israelites, out of all humanity, then wish for death if what you say is true!"*

**The challenge.**

After fifty-four verses of argument, the sūrah proposes a test that can be settled in a moment.

**The claim it answers.**

Maʿārif sets out the claim and collects the verses where it appears:

*The Jews used to claim that the blessings of the other world were specially reserved for them, and were not meant for any other people. Certain other verses of the Holy Qurʾān too refer to such a claim on the part of the Jews, and also of the Christians:*

*"They say: The fire will not touch us but for a few days" (2:80), "And they say: No one will enter Paradise except he who is a Jew or Christian" (2:111), "And the Jews and the Christians said: We are the sons of Allah and His close friends" (5:18).*

Three claims, in three verses, two of them still ahead in this sūrah.

Then his summary of what the three add up to:

*What they meant in making such a claim was that since their own faith was the true one, they must certainly attain salvation in the other world — the repentant and the forgiven being admitted to Paradise from the very beginning, the sinners finding release from the fires of Hell after undergoing a punishment for a few days, and the obedient receiving a welcome like sons and beloved friends.*

Three categories, all saved. Nobody left outside.

**And Maʿārif's concession.**

He does something unusual here — he grants the claim's logic before refuting its premise:

*The use of certain improper expressions like "sons of Allah" notwithstanding, these claims are in themselves quite correct, provided that they pertain to people who follow a true and valid faith. But the Jews, and the Christians as well, were still following a faith which had been abrogated, and was thus no longer valid — a fact which nullified their claim.*

*Correct, provided that…* The principle is sound. The premise fails.

**The test proposed.**

Al-Jalālayn explains the logic of the challenge, and the explanation is the clearest available:

*Say to them, "If the Abode of the Hereafter — that is, Paradise — with God is purely yours, that is, exclusively and not for other people, as you allege, then long for death — if you speak truly." Here both conditionals are connected to the verb tamannū, "long for," so that the first is dependent upon the second — in other words, "If you speak truly when you claim that it is yours, then you will naturally incline to what is yours, and since the path to it is death, long for it — death."*

*Since the path to it is death.* The argument in one clause. If Paradise is yours, the only thing standing between you and it is dying.

Ibn Kathīr records what the challenge actually was, from Ibn ʿAbbās via Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq:

*"Allah said to His Prophet, 'Say to them: If the home of the Hereafter with Allah is indeed for you especially and not for others of mankind, then long for death if you are truthful' — meaning, 'Invoke Allah to bring death to the lying camp among the two, Muslims and Jews.' The Jews declined this offer by the Messenger of Allah."*

*To the lying camp among the two.* Not suicide. A prayer that God settle it.

Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbās: *"Then long for death" means, "Invoke Allah for death."*

**What would have happened.**

Three reports, all from Ibn ʿAbbās, all recorded by Ibn Kathīr, and all with the same conclusion:

*ʿIkrimah said that Ibn ʿAbbās commented, "Had the Jews invoked Allah for death, they would have perished."*

*Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded Saʿīd ibn Jubayr saying that Ibn ʿAbbās said, "Had the Jews asked for death, one of them would have choked on his own saliva." These statements have authentic chains of narration up to Ibn ʿAbbās.*

And Ibn Kathīr's own note: *Had they wished death that day, no Jew would have remained alive on the face of the earth.*

*One of them would have choked on his own saliva.* The most vivid of the three.

Ibn Jarīr adds a prophetic ḥadīth to the same effect, which Ibn Kathīr quotes: *"We were told that the Prophet said, 'Had the Jews wished for death, they would have died and seen their seats in the Fire.'"*

**The refusal.**

Ibn Kathīr: *The Jews declined this offer by the Messenger of Allah.*

That is the whole outcome. The challenge was made. It was declined. Verse 95 explains why.

**Tanwīr and al-Mukhtaṣar on the claim.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Say unto them: "If the abode of the Hereafter — i.e. Paradise — in the providence of Allah is indeed for you alone, specifically for you alone, and not for others of mankind, and not for the believers in Muhammad and his Companions, as you pretend, then long for death — for ye must long for death — ask for death, if ye are truthful in your claim."*

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the practical form of the invitation: *Jews, if Paradise in the Afterlife is just for you, and no other people will enter it, then wish for death, and ask for it, so that you reach this place quickly, and can rest from the burdens and worries of the life of this world, if you are truthful about what you claim.*

*So that you reach this place quickly.* On their own claim, death is not a loss. It is an early arrival.

**Why the challenge works.**

It requires nothing. No miracle, no argument, no evidence. One wish.

And the wish would only be rational if the claim were true. If Paradise is exclusively theirs, wanting it costs nothing and gains everything.

The fact that they could not make it is the evidence. That is what verse 95 states, and verse 96 explains.

95.text:
*But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done. And Allah has perfect knowledge of the wrongdoers.*

**The verse that explains the refusal.**

Nineteen words. The sūrah proposes a test, records the answer, and gives the reason.

**They will never wish for it.**

*Wa lan yatamannawhu abadan.* Al-Jalālayn: *But they will never long for it, because of that which their own hands have sent before them, as a result of their rejection of the Prophet — the consequence of their mendacity.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *But they will never long for it — they will never ask for death — because of that which their own hands have sent before them, because of what they themselves have done in the religion of Judaism.*

*Never.* Abadan. Not "they did not." They will not, at any time.

**Because of what their hands have done.**

*Bimā qaddamat aydīhim.* Al-Mukhtaṣar names the three things:

*They will never wish for death, because of what they have done in their lives: disbelieving in Allah, rejecting His prophets and distorting His scriptures.*

Three charges, and all three have appeared in the last fifty verses — verse 87 for the prophets, verse 79 for the distortion, verse 92 for the calf.

**Ibn Kathīr on the specific reason.**

His gloss is the most precise, and it points at verse 89:

*"But they will never long for it because of what their hands have sent before them" — meaning, "Since they know that they recognize you, and yet disbelieve in you."*

*They recognize you.* Not uncertainty. Knowledge, and refusal — which is what Maʿārif said at verse 89 about Satan knowing the truth.

**And Allah has perfect knowledge of the wrongdoers.**

*Wa Llāhu ʿalīmun bi-ẓ-ẓālimīn.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And Allah is Aware of evil-doers, i.e. the Jews.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar widens it: *Allah knows the wrongdoers among them and other people: each person will be given what they have earned.*

*And other people.* The verse names the Jews and then states a rule that covers everyone.

**Why the verse is so short.**

Verse 94 was a challenge with a full logical structure. Verse 95 is the answer, and it needs no elaboration.

They will not make the wish. Allah knows why.

**What the two verses establish together.**

The claim was that the Hereafter is exclusively theirs. The test was: then want it. The result was: they will never want it.

The conclusion is not stated, and it does not need to be. A person who believes a place is exclusively his does not avoid the door.

Maʿārif's framing from verse 94 covers it: *the habitual method of settling a dispute is to have a discussion and let both the parties [present their case]* — but this verse does not settle it by discussion. It settles it by observing what they will not do.

**And the word ẓālimūn.**

Wrongdoers. The sūrah has used it since verse 51 — *you were wrongdoers* — and at 2:92, *acting wrongfully*.

Here it closes the exchange. Not disbelievers. Wrongdoers — which is the charge the whole address has been building.

Verse 96 goes further, and says something no one expects: they love life more than the polytheists do.

96.text:
*You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years. But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do.*

**The comparison nobody expects.**

Verse 95 said they would not wish for death. Verse 96 says how strongly they feel the opposite, and then makes a comparison that indicts them more than any charge so far.

**More than the polytheists.**

Al-Jalālayn explains why the comparison is devastating:

*And you shall find them — the lām of la-tajidannahum is for oaths — the people most covetous of life, and more covetous of it than the idolaters, who reject the idea of the Resurrection. For the former know that their journey's end will be the Fire, while the idolaters do not believe even in this.*

*The former know that their journey's end will be the Fire.* The polytheists do not believe in an afterlife, so their attachment to this life is coherent. The Jews do believe — and are more attached anyway.

Al-Mukhtaṣar makes the same point at greater length:

*You will find, O Prophet, that the Jews are the most desirous for life, even if it is miserable and lowly. They are even greedier for it than the idolaters, who worship others alongside Allah, who do not believe in being brought back to life after death or in being held to account for what they have done. Despite being People of the Scripture, and believing in the resurrection and the reckoning, they would love to live a thousand years.*

*Even if it is miserable and lowly.* Not a good life. Life.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And thou, O Muhammad, wilt find them, the Jews, greediest of mankind for any life, to remain in this world, and greedier than the idolaters, even greedier than the Arab idolaters.*

**A thousand years.**

Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar, which shows how the wish is constructed:

*Any one of them would love — wishes that he might be given life for a thousand years. Law yuʿammar, "if only he might be given life" — the particle law, "if only," relates to the verbal noun and functions with the sense of "an," that is, "that," and together with its relative clause explains the implicit verbal noun in the object of the verb yawaddu, "he would love."*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Each one of them would like, would hope, to be allowed to live a thousand years.*

Not a figure of speech for a long life. A number, and a specific one.

**Maʿārif on what the wish reveals.**

He draws the conclusion, and it is the verse's real argument:

*This verse shows the basic weakness of the Jews, which did not allow them to accept the challenge proposed in verse 94, and thus exposes the hollowness of their claim to the blessings of the other world being reserved for them.*

Then the reasoning, which is the sharpest in the six sources:

*The Holy Qurʾān puts a special emphasis on the fact that the Jews loved physical life much more than did the Arab polytheists. Such an inclination should not have been surprising on the part of the latter, for, after all, they did not believe in the other world, and physical life was the be-all and end-all for them.*

*But the Jews acknowledged the existence of the other world, and even had the illusion that they alone deserved its joys, and yet it was they who, above all others, wished to live in this world as long as possible.*
