*This very desire shows how baseless their pretention was, and how they themselves knew that they would have to face the fires of Hell in the other world, and that physical life was, as long as it lasted, a kind of protection against their final fate.*

*A kind of protection against their final fate.* The wish for a thousand years is not a love of life. It is a postponement.

That is the verse's diagnosis, and it explains verse 95's "never" completely.

**It would not save them.**

Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar and the meaning:

*Yet any one of them — his being given life, an yuʿammarā, "that he should be given life," constitutes the subject of the verb muzahzihihi, "that it should budge him"; this verb comes later, as though it were taʿmīruhu, "the giving of life to him" — shall not budge, remove him, from the chastisement of the Fire.*

*Shall not budge him.* The verb is about moving something heavy a small distance. A thousand years would not shift him an inch.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And to live that long would by no means remove him, save him, from the doom, if he were to live a thousand years.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Yet however long a life they might be given, it would not distance them from Allah's punishment.*

*Would not distance them.* Not delay the punishment — fail to change the distance to it.

**Allah is All-Seeing of what they do.**

*Baṣīrun bimā yaʿmalūn.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās specifies what is seen:

*And Allah is Seer of what they do, of contraventions, rebellion, and what they conceal about the description and traits of Muhammad.*

*What they conceal about the description and traits of Muhammad.* The verse closes on the concealment of verse 76 — the thing the leaders were afraid of leaking.

Al-Jalālayn notes a variant: *God sees what they do — yaʿmalūna may be alternatively read taʿmalūna.*

*Taʿmalūna* — what you do. The same shift from third person to second that appeared at verses 59 and 74.

**Why the sequence 94–96 works as one argument.**

Verse 94: if the Hereafter is exclusively yours, wish for death. Verse 95: they never will. Verse 96: because they want a thousand years, more than people who do not believe in an afterlife at all.

The claim was about the next world. The evidence is about this one.

Tazkīrul Qurʾān states the conclusion in a single line: *If they had really been seeking God, their attention would have been entirely focused on the life after death; but, in fact, they, more than all the others, were obsessed with the love of the present world.*

**And the sūrah's commerce metaphor, once more.**

Verse 90 said they sold their souls for a miserable price. Verse 96 says what they were buying: a thousand years.

The longest life imaginable, purchased with the Hereafter — and the verse says it would not move them any closer to safety.

That is the sūrah's fourth use of the metaphor, and the starkest. Every buyer in this passage has paid everything and received nothing.

97.text:
*Say, O Prophet, "Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this Quran to your heart by Allah's Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers."*

**The verse that answers an objection to a messenger, not to a message.**

Every argument so far has been about the Book or the claim. This one is about the angel who delivered it.

**What they said.**

Maʿārif gives the objection in full, and it is stranger than anything so far:

*When they learnt that it was Archangel Jibrāʾīl (Gabriel) who brought the Glorious Qurʾān to the Holy Prophet, they said that the Archangel was their enemy, as it was through him that rigorous commandments or catastrophic punishments had always descended on them, and that for this reason they would not accept a Book which had been revealed through his agency.*

*They also added that they could have accepted the Holy Qurʾān, if the Archangel Mīkāʾīl (Michael) had brought it down, for he is connected with rain and with divine mercy.*

They would have accepted the same Book from a different courier. The content was not the problem.

Ibn Kathīr records the scholarly consensus on the occasion: *Imām Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr said, "The scholars of tafsīr agree that this verse was revealed in response to the Jews who claimed that Jibrīl is an enemy of the Jews and that Mīkāʾīl is their friend."*

**Tazkīrul on why they felt that way.**

Its account explains the resentment rather than merely reporting it:

*Owing to their own rebelliousness, the Israelites had severe punishments meted out to them in ancient times. It was God's way to warn them of these impending punishments beforehand, and such warnings came to them through the prophets, who were acting on the words of the Archangel Gabriel.*

*But, instead of heeding these admonitions, the Israelites came to regard Gabriel as their enemy, because it had always been he who gave prior warning through the prophets about impending doom.*

They hated the messenger who brought warnings. Then they blamed him for the warnings.

Then Tazkīrul quotes what they actually said, and it is the clearest statement of the objection anywhere in the six sources:

*Consequently, when the Prophet Muhammad proclaimed that he was receiving his revelation through Gabriel, they said, "So, it is our old enemy Gabriel, who always brings commands from heaven against us! That explains why the scriptures, the birthright of the Israelites, are being conveyed to one who belongs to another tribe."*

*The birthright of the Israelites.* The objection was never about Gabriel. It was about who received the Book.

**And what angels actually are.**

Tazkīrul answers it directly:

*Now angels, being the rarefied creatures that they are, do not hold grudges against ordinary mortals; they descend to earth only by divine command in order to carry out the tasks assigned to them by their Creator — in this case, the revelation of the Scriptures to the prophet whom God Himself had chosen.*

*Do not hold grudges.* Gabriel is not a party to the quarrel. He is not capable of being one.

**The answer.**

The verse does not defend Gabriel. It describes what he did.

Al-Jalālayn: *Say to them, "Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, let him die in exasperation — he it was that brought it, the Qurʾān, down upon your heart, by the leave, by the command, of God, confirming what was before it of scriptures, a guidance from error, and good tidings of Paradise for the believers."*

*Let him die in exasperation.* The verse does not argue with the hostility. It dismisses it.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *whoever is against Gabriel — who revealed the Qurʾān to your heart, with Allah's permission, affirming the sacred scripture that came before it, such as the Torah and the Gospel, showing the way to what is good, and bringing the good news to the believers of the bliss Allah has prepared for them — then he is misguided.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Who is an enemy to Gabriel! — is automatically an enemy to Allah. For he it is who hath revealed to your heart — sent Gabriel to you with the Qurʾān — by Allah's leave, by Allah's command, confirming, affirming the Oneness of Allah, that which was before it of the Book, and a guidance from error, and glad tiding, good news, to believers, that Paradise will be theirs.*

**Maʿārif on the shape of the answer.**

He sets out the logic, and it is the verse's whole method:

*In refuting this argument, the Holy Qurʾān points out that Jibrāʾīl is only a messenger, and has, acting only as a messenger, brought down the Holy Qurʾān under a divine command to the Holy Prophet. So, why should the Jews be so particular about the messenger, and not look at the Book itself?*

*As for the Book, it confirms the earlier Books of Allah, provides guidance to men, and gives good tidings to the believers. This being what the Divine Books are meant for, the Holy Qurʾān is evidently enough a Divine Book, and must, as such, be obeyed.*

*To deny it on account of one's hostility to Jibrāʾīl is sheer stupidity or outright perversity.*

Three tests for a divine book — confirming, guiding, giving good news — and the Qurʾān meets all three. The courier is irrelevant to all three.

**The occasion, in Ibn Kathīr's account.**

He records the ḥadīth from Anas ibn Mālik, and it is where the verse comes from:

*"When ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām heard of the arrival of the Prophet in al-Madīnah, he was working on his land. He came to the Prophet and said, 'I am going to ask you about three things which nobody knows except a Prophet. What will be the first portent of the Hour? What will be the first meal taken by the people of Paradise? Why does a child resemble its father, and why does it resemble its maternal uncle?'"*

*"Allah's Messenger said, 'Jibrīl has just told me the answers.' ʿAbdullāh said, 'He — i.e. Jibrīl — among all the angels, is the enemy of the Jews.'"*

*"Allah's Messenger then recited the verse, 'Whoever is an enemy to Jibrīl, for indeed he has brought it down to your heart.'"*

*"On that ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām said, 'I testify that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and you are the Messenger of Allah.'"*

The verse was recited at the moment of a conversion, in answer to a warning about who the Jews hate.

**The etymology al-Bukhārī records.**

Ibn Kathīr adds a linguistic note: *Al-Bukhārī said, "Allah said, 'Whoever is an enemy of Jibrīl.' ʿIkrimah said, 'Jibr, Mik and Israf all mean worshipper, while īl means Allah.'"*

Gabriel — worshipper of God. Michael — worshipper of God. Isrāfīl — worshipper of God. The three names share a structure, and the structure is the same confession.

**Why this verse is here.**

Verses 87 to 96 ended with the challenge to wish for death and the refusal. Verses 97 and 98 answer the last remaining objection — not about the Book, not about the Prophet, but about the angel.

And the answer is that the angel is beside the point.

98.text:
*Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael, then let them know that Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers.*

**The verse that widens the objection into a verdict.**

Verse 97 answered a specific complaint. Verse 98 states what the complaint amounts to.

**The list.**

Allah. His angels. His messengers. Gabriel. Michael.

Al-Jalālayn notes why the last two are named separately, and the grammar is the point:

*Whoever is an enemy to God, and His angels, and His messengers, and Gabriel — read Jibrīl or Jabrīl, Jibraʾīl or Jabraʾīl, Jibrāʾīl or Jabraʾīl — and Michael, Mīkāl, also read Mīkāʾīl or Mīkāʾīl; a supplement to malāʾikatihi, "His angels" — an example of the specific being supplemented to the collective — then surely God is an enemy to the disbelievers.*

*The specific being supplemented to the collective.* Gabriel and Michael are already inside "His angels." They are named anyway, because they are the two the objection was about.

Six readings of Gabriel's name and three of Michael's, all recorded in one clause. Al-Jalālayn keeps every variant.

**Why naming them matters.**

Maʿārif explains what the verse establishes:

*As for the attitude of the Jews towards Jibrāʾīl, the Holy Qurʾān declares that to be hostile to the angels — including Jibrāʾīl and Mīkāʾīl — or to the prophets is tantamount to being hostile to Allah Himself.*

*Tantamount to being hostile to Allah Himself.* Not a lesser offence. The same one.

Then: *Verse 98 puts down the enemies of angels and prophets as infidels, in saying that Allah [is their enemy].*

**Allah is the enemy of the disbelievers.**

Al-Jalālayn notes the shift, and it is the verse's final move:

*He says, "to the disbelievers," instead of "to them," in order to point out their status.*

*Instead of "to them."* The verse could have said "Allah is their enemy." It says "the enemy of the disbelievers" — which places them in a category and names the category.

The same technique as verse 59, where the verse stepped back from addressing them directly.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās goes further: *Then, lo! Allah Himself is an enemy to disbelievers — to the Jews, just as Gabriel, Michael and all the believers are enemies of the Jews.*

*And all the believers.* Tanwīr adds a third party to the enmity.

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the consequence: *then certainly Allah is a rival to the disbelievers from among you, and from other than you. Certain defeat faces whoever has Allah as his rival.*

*From among you, and from other than you.* The rule is not specific to them.

**Tazkīrul's closing on the whole exchange.**

Its summary of verses 97 and 98 states why the objection fails:

*Given the clear proofs that the Arab Prophet had had the same revelation communicated to him as had been received by Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and that it tallied with the previous divine scriptures, there were no grounds for the Israelites to reject the divine message.*

*The same revelation… as had been received by Abraham, Moses and Jesus.* The test is the message's continuity, not its courier.

Then its diagnosis: *Their negative reaction was the result of their having led insincere, unrestricted lives, which had become dominated by self-interest, empty convention and racial prejudice.*

*Racial prejudice.* The same word verse 91's *"what was sent down to us"* implied, and Tazkīrul is the only source to name it directly.

**Why Gabriel and Michael are paired.**

Maʿārif gives the reason the two names appear together, and it is in the objection itself: Gabriel brings commandments and warnings, Michael brings rain and mercy.

The Jews said they preferred the merciful one. The verse names both, and says hostility to either is hostility to Allah.

There is no version of the message with only mercy in it. The verse will not allow the selection.

**And the verse's place.**

Verses 97 and 98 close the objections. Verse 99 turns to the evidence, and verse 100 to the covenants.

The sequence is: they objected to the messenger. The sūrah says the messenger is irrelevant. Then it says the message is clear. Then it says they have broken every promise about it.

99.text:
*Indeed, We have sent down to you, O Prophet, clear revelations. But none will deny them except the rebellious.*

**The shortest verse in the sequence, and the harshest.**

Two clauses. Clear signs were sent. Only the rebellious deny them.

**Clear revelations.**

*Āyātin bayyināt.* Ibn Kathīr explains what makes them clear, and the explanation is unusual:

*Imām Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr said that Allah's statement, "And indeed We have sent down to you manifest āyāt," means, "We have sent to you, O Muhammad, clear signs that testify to your prophethood."*

*These āyāt are contained in the Book of Allah, the Qurʾān, which narrates the secrets of the knowledge that the Jews possess, which they hid, and the stories of their earlier generations. The Book of Allah also mentions the texts in the Books of the Jews that are known to only the rabbis and scholars, and the sections where they altered and distorted the rulings of the Tawrāh.*

*The secrets of the knowledge that the Jews possess, which they hid.* The evidence is not miracles. It is that an unlettered man in Arabia knows what the rabbis concealed.

*Since Allah mentioned all of this in His Book revealed to His Prophet Muhammad, then this fact alone should be enough evidence for those who are truthful with themselves.*

Al-Jalālayn: *And We have revealed to you, O Muhammad, clear proofs — lucid ones; bayyinātin, "clear proofs," is a circumstantial qualifier.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Verily We have revealed unto thee, sent you Gabriel with clear tokens, with manifest signs expounding commands and prohibitions.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *I have revealed to you, O Prophet, clear signs proving the truth of your prophethood and revelation.*

**The occasion.**

Al-Jalālayn names who the verse answers:

*This was in response to Ibn Sūryā saying to the Prophet, "You have not brought us anything."*

*"You have not brought us anything."* Not "we disagree." A flat denial that anything was brought.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās records the same person at verse 97: *the saying of one of the Jews, ʿAbdullāh ibn Suriyyah, that Gabriel was the enemy of the Jews.*

One man, two objections, two verses.

**None will deny them except the rebellious.**

*Wa mā yakfuru bihā illa al-fāsiqūn.* Al-Jalālayn: *and none disbelieves in them except the wicked — these have disbelieved in them.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and only miscreants, the unbelievers and the Jews, will disbelieve in them, will deny the signs.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *The only people who reject these signs, despite their clarity, are those who have abandoned Allah's path.*

*Fāsiq* — one who exits, who breaks out of a boundary. The word the sūrah used at 2:26 and at 57:16 in verse 74's cross-reference.

**Maʿārif on what the verse establishes.**

He draws the inference, and it is the verse's argument:

*In denying the Holy Prophet, the Jews used to say that no clear evidence or sign of his prophethood had been revealed to him such as they could recognize and accept. In reply to this the Holy Qurʾān says that Allah has revealed a number of very clear signs and evidences of his prophethood which even they know and understand very well.*

*Which even they know and understand very well.* Not disputed evidence. Acknowledged evidence.

*So, their denial is not based on a lack of recognition or knowledge, but on their habitual disobedience, for, as a general rule, no one denies such evidence except those who are willful and stubborn in their disobedience.*

*No one denies such evidence except…* The verse states a general rule, and Maʿārif applies it.

**Tazkīrul on the general pattern.**

Its comment on verses 99 to 101 explains why clear evidence gets refused, and it is the most searching account in the six sources:

*Perversion sets in in the People of the Book for just one reason. They come to believe that by uttering mere words, or by performing lifeless rituals, they will be able to earn salvation, but salvation can be earned only by performing righteous actions. During this stage of decline, superstition comes to be more highly regarded than actual good deeds.*

*This thinking, initially centring on salvation, later comes to dominate the entire national policy of the group. A realistic approach is thus replaced by a superstitious approach.*

Then the political consequence:

*Now those who merely make an outward show of following their religion are inevitably averse to responding in earnest to the proclamation of true, unadulterated religion. For such people, the call is seen as a threat to the worldly honour and status that they enjoy owing to their worldly interpretation of religion.*

*A threat to the worldly honour and status.* The clear signs are not unclear. They are inconvenient.

*Due to their negativism, they begin to make such representations as are outwardly correct but which, in terms of the inner reality, are totally meaningless.*

**And its conclusion.**

*All arguments point to the fact that the Arab Prophet received the same message as was sent down to Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and that the revelation received by the Arab Prophet tallied exactly with the predictions made in previous divine scriptures. This proves beyond all doubt that it was sent by God Himself.*

*People make many protestations of their faith, but all these mouthings being hollow and meaningless, they bear no relation to true faith and piety.*

**Why this verse is so short.**

Verse 97 answered the objection about Gabriel at length. Verse 99 does not answer Ibn Sūryā's denial at all. It states that the signs are clear and that only the rebellious deny them.

There is nothing to argue with. The claim was *"you have not brought us anything."* The answer is that what was brought is clear, and the denial is a fact about the denier.

Verse 100 moves to the covenants — and to the specific promise in their own Book.

100.text:
*Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside? In fact, most of them do not believe.*

**The verse that generalises.**

Verses 40 to 99 have listed specific failures. Verse 100 states the pattern, and it is a question rather than an assertion.

**Every time.**

*Awa-kullamā.* Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar and the tone:

*Why, whenever they make a covenant with God that they will believe in the Prophet when he appears, or that they will not give assistance to the idolaters against the Prophet, does a party of them reject it? — cast it away, repudiating it. This is the response to the clause beginning with kullamā, the interrogative of rebuke.*

*Kullamā* — every time. Not once. The verse is about a repeated event, and the interrogative is a rebuke rather than a question.

Two covenants named: to believe in the Prophet when he appears, and not to assist the idolaters against him. Both are political, and both were live in Madinah.

**A group of them.**

*Farīqun minhum.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās identifies the group: *Is it ever so that when they make a covenant — i.e. the Jewish leaders with Muhammad — a party of them set it aside? — reject and break it.*

*The Jewish leaders with Muhammad.* Specific treaties, in Madinah, with named parties.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Due to their corrupt state, a group of the Jews would always break any commitment that they made, including the duty to have faith in what the Torah revealed about the prophethood of Muhammad.*

**Maʿārif on the covenant in their own Book.**

He states what the covenant was and what happened when it was raised:

*Allah had, as the Torah itself reports, made the Jews take the pledge that they would have faith in the Holy Prophet when he appeared. On being reminded of it, the Jews flatly denied even having taken such a pledge.*

*Denied even having taken such a pledge.* Not that they broke it. That it never existed.

Then the Qurʾān's answer:

*Commenting on this effrontery, the Holy Qurʾān says that this is not the only instance of such a conduct on their part, for the Jews have, in fact, never fulfilled even those pledges which they acknowledge, and one group or another from among them has always been breaking the compacts they have entered into, especially with regard to religious matters.*

*Never fulfilled even those pledges which they acknowledge.* The argument does not depend on the disputed covenant. It uses the ones they admit to.

**Breaking a pledge versus not believing in it.**

Maʿārif then makes a distinction that explains the verse's second half:

*It can even be said that most of those who have been guilty of such gross violations did not at all believe in the compacts which they made with Allah. Going against a pledge is only a sin and transgression, but having no faith in the pledge which one gives to Allah is outright infidelity.*

*A sin* versus *outright infidelity.* Breaking a promise is one thing. Making it without believing in it is another.

That is why the verse ends where it does.

**In fact, most of them do not believe.**

*Bal aktharuhum lā yuʾminūn.* Al-Jalālayn: *Nay — bal indicates a transition — but most of them are disbelievers.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās goes further than the text: *The truth is, most of them, all of them in fact, believe not.*

*All of them in fact.* Tanwīr's gloss exceeds "most," and the verse says "most."

**Maʿārif on why the verse says "most" and not "all".**

He notices the precision and explains it, and it is the most careful comment on the verse:

*The Holy Qurʾān specifically speaks of one group or another breaking the pledge, and not of all the Jews. For there were some among them who did fulfil the pledges, so much so that many Jews finally accepted Sayyidunā Muhammad as a true prophet, and joined the ranks of the Muslims.*

*Many Jews finally accepted.* The exceptions are kept in view throughout the sūrah — the "few of you" at verse 83, and the "few of them" at verse 88.

The verse is precise because the facts are precise. Not all of them. Most.

**Al-Mukhtaṣar on why faith and keeping promises are the same issue.**

*Most of them do not really have faith in what Allah revealed, because faith leads to keeping to and honouring commitments and promises.*

*Because faith leads to keeping commitments.* The verse treats promise-keeping as evidence of belief rather than as a separate virtue. Break the pattern and the belief is in question.

**Tazkīrul on the general law.**

Its comment covers verses 99 to 101 and states the principle:

*People make many protestations of their faith, but all these mouthings being hollow and meaningless, they bear no relation to true faith and piety.*

*Protestations of faith.* The covenant is the protestation. Verse 100 asks why it keeps getting cast aside, and answers that the people making it did not believe in it.

**Why this verse sits between 99 and 101.**

Verse 99: the signs are clear. Verse 100: and they keep breaking their promises anyway. Verse 101: and here is the latest instance, in their own Book.

The sequence moves from evidence, to character, to a specific case. And the specific case is the Torah's own prophecy.

101.text:
*Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming their own Scriptures—some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know.*

**The latest instance.**

Verse 100 said they cast covenants aside as a habit. Verse 101 gives the example that matters, and it is not a treaty. It is their Book.

**Confirming their own Scriptures.**

*Muṣaddiqun limā maʿahum.* The same phrase as verse 89, and it does the same work.

Al-Jalālayn: *When there came to them a messenger from God — namely Muhammad — confirming what was with them.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And when there cometh unto them a messenger from Allah, confirming, conforming in traits and description, that which they possess of the Book.*

*Conforming in traits and description.* The confirmation is not abstract. He matched the description they held.

**Cast the Book of Allah behind their backs.**

*Nabadhū Kitāba Llāhi warāʾa ẓuhūrihim.* The image is physical, and the commentators take it literally.

Al-Jalālayn: *a party of them who were given the Scripture have cast away the Scripture of God — that is, the Torah — behind their backs, that is to say, they have not acted according to what it said about belief in the Messenger and otherwise.*

*They have not acted according to what it said.* Not that they destroyed it. They did not use it.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *a party of those who have received the Scripture fling the Scripture of Allah, i.e. the Torah, behind their backs, disbelieving in what it contains of the traits and description of Muhammad, nor did they exposit this.*

*Nor did they exposit this.* They did not teach it either. The concealment of verse 76 again.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *a group of them turned away from the scripture that showed this, throwing it behind their backs, unmindful of it, not benefitting from its truth or guidance, like fools.*

**As if they did not know.**

*Ka-annahum lā yaʿlamūn.* Al-Jalālayn gives the two things they are pretending not to know:

*As though they did not know what is contained in it, to the effect that he is a true Prophet, or that it is the Book of God.*

Two levels. Not knowing that Muhammad is a prophet, and not knowing that their own Book is from God. The second is the deeper denial.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *as if they knew not, as if they were ignorant people who knew nothing.*

*Ignorant people.* The ummiyyūn of verse 78 — except these are the scholars.

**Maʿārif on what the act amounts to.**

He states the logic, and it is the verse's argument:

*The Torah had already given the Jews the good tidings of the coming of the Holy Prophet. When he actually came with all signs which the Torah had indicated, thus confirming the Sacred Book of the Jews, a large number of them refused to accept him as a prophet.*

*In doing this, they were, in fact, denying the Torah itself, and behaving as if they know nothing of the prophecy, or even the Torah being a Book of Allah. Thus, they were being guilty of infidelity even in terms of the Torah itself.*

*Guilty of infidelity even in terms of the Torah itself.* Not by the Qurʾān's standard. By their own.

That is the same argument Maʿārif made at verse 89 — that denying the Qurʾān involves denying the Torah — and here he states it as a charge rather than an inference.

**And why the verse says "some".**

Maʿārif is consistent about the precision: *a large number of them refused to accept him as a prophet.*

Not all. Verse 100 said "most," verse 101 says "a party." The sūrah keeps the exceptions in view, as it did at verses 83 and 88.

**Tazkīrul on the confirmation.**

Its account of verses 99 to 101 makes the evidential point:

*All arguments point to the fact that the Arab Prophet received the same message as was sent down to Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and that the revelation received by the Arab Prophet tallied exactly with the predictions made in previous divine scriptures. This proves beyond all doubt that it was sent by God Himself.*

*Tallied exactly with the predictions.* The confirmation is checkable, and they had the text to check it with.

**Why the image is "behind their backs".**

Not thrown away. Not burned. Placed behind, where it cannot be seen and cannot be consulted.

The Book remained in their possession. They kept it. They simply stopped looking at the part that mattered — which is what verse 85 described with the three injunctions, keeping the cheap one.

Ibn Kathīr's framing of the whole passage covers it: the āyāt sent to the Prophet contain *the texts in the Books of the Jews that are known to only the rabbis and scholars, and the sections where they altered and distorted the rulings of the Tawrāh.*

They had the Book. They knew what it said. Verse 101 says they put it behind them and acted as though they did not.

**And what follows.**

Verse 102 turns to what they followed instead — the magic taught at Babylon in the time of Sulaymān.

The sequence is complete: they were given a Book that confirmed itself, and they put it behind their backs. What they picked up in its place is the subject of the next verse.

102.text:
*They instead followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon. Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved. They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, "We are only a test for you, so do not abandon your faith." Yet people learned magic that caused a rift even between husband and wife; although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah's Will. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew.*

**The longest verse in the sūrah so far, and its strangest.**

Verse 101 said they cast the Book behind their backs. Verse 102 says what they picked up instead — and clears a prophet's name in the middle of doing it.

**What they followed.**

*Wa ttabaʿū mā tatlū ash-shayāṭīnu ʿalā mulki Sulaymān.* Al-Jalālayn connects the verse to the one before it:

*And they follow — wa-ttabaʿū is a supplement to nabadha, "it cast away" — what the devils used to relate during the time of Solomon's kingdom, in the way of sorcery.*

What they cast the Book aside for. That is the grammar.

**Where the magic came from — and the account varies.**

Al-Jalālayn gives two versions:

*It is said that they — the devils — buried these books of sorcery underneath his throne when his kingdom was taken from him; it is also said that they used to listen stealthily and add fabrications to what they heard, and then pass it on to the priests, who would compile it in books; this would be disseminated, and rumours spread that the jinn had knowledge of the Unseen.*

*Solomon gathered these books and buried them. When he died the devils showed people where these books were, and the latter brought them out and found that they contained sorcery and said, "Your kingdom was only thanks to what is in here"; they then took to learning them and rejected the Scriptures of their prophets.*

The second version is the more complete one: Solomon buried the books. After his death the devils told people where they were. The people dug them up, concluded his power had been magic, and started practising.

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the charge directly: *lying about the kingdom of the Prophet Solomon by claiming that it was established through black magic.*

**Why the verse clears Solomon.**

Al-Jalālayn gives the occasion, and it is a specific accusation:

*In order to demonstrate Solomon's innocence, and in repudiation of the Jews when they said, "Look at this Muhammad — he mentions Solomon as one of the prophets when he was only a sorcerer," God says, "Solomon disbelieved not" — that is, he did not work magic, because he disbelieved — "but the devils disbelieved, teaching the people sorcery."*

*"Look at this Muhammad."* The accusation was not against Solomon. It was against the Prophet for counting him among the prophets.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Solomon did not disbelieve by practicing black magic, as the Jews claimed; but the satans were disbelievers when they taught people the black magic.*

Maʿārif explains why the denial is a parenthesis:

*The Jews were impertinent and senseless enough to attribute magic and sorcery to a prophet — namely, Sayyidunā Sulaymān. So, in saying that they used to learn the black arts of the devils, the Holy Qurʾān takes care to deny, as a parenthesis, such a vile allegation against Sayyidunā Sulaymān.*

The verse interrupts its own argument to defend a prophet's name.

**Tazkīrul on why the story spread.**

Its account explains the economics, and it is the sharpest observation in the six sources:

*When superstition and apathy set in in the declining Jewish race, certain individuals exploited this tendency in order to make commercial gains, by providing success-seekers with magical prescriptions. To make their business flourish, these unscrupulous profiteers attributed their art to Solomon, saying that the extraordinary powers he exercised over the spirits and winds were, in fact, based on his knowledge of magic, and claimed that this knowledge had been passed on to them by the spirits.*

*To make their business flourish.* The attribution to Solomon was marketing. It gave the art an authoritative founder.

*This claim to authority accounted in great measure for the rapid spread of sorcery, which soon developed into a highly popular art among the Jews.*

That is verse 79's business model again — a paradise sold for a fee — in a different product.

**Hārūt and Mārūt at Babylon.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *the black magic revealed to the two angels, Hārūt and Mārūt, in the city of Babel in Iraq.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās is careful about what the angels were and were not taught: *and it is said that this means: they also taught what the angels were inspired with, in Babel, Hārūt and Mārūt.*

*The angels were not taught sorcery.* Tanwīr states the qualification first.

**Tazkīrul's parallel.**

It explains the two angels by comparison, and the comparison is the clearest available:

*When angels came to Lot's people, who were practising homosexuals, they came in the garb of handsome boys in order to test them. Similarly, angels were sent to the Jews in Babylon in the garb of holymen to teach them magic, at the same time making it quite clear that they were only putting the Jews to the test, this being a form of knowledge that should not be practised.*

*In the garb of holymen.* Angels appearing as teachers, as they appeared as guests at Sodom. The test is in the appearance.

**"We are only a test, so do not abandon your faith."**

*Innamā naḥnu fitnatun fa-lā takfur.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives the angels' own words at their strangest:

*Nor did they teach it to anyone — nor did the angels describe anything to anyone — till they had said, at the outset: "We are only a temptation — we have been tried with calling people to this in order that we reduce the intensity of the torment inflicted on ourselves — therefore disbelieve not," do not learn or act upon it.*

*We have been tried.* On this reading the angels are themselves under trial by having to teach it.

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the plain version: *These two angels would only teach black magic to someone after explaining that they were simply a trial and a test for people, warning them not to be ungrateful to Allah by learning it.*

The warning came first, every time. The teaching was conditional on it.

**What the magic did.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And from these two angels people learn — without being taught by them — that by which they cause division between man and wife, that by which a man finds excuse to leave his wife.*

*Without being taught by them.* The learning happened despite the warning, not because of the instruction.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Those who learned black magic from them but did not listen to their advice would, through it, separate a man and his wife by sowing hatred between them.*

**Except by Allah's Will.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the limit: *These sorcerers are not able to harm anyone except with Allah's permission and by His will.*

The verse does not deny that magic does something. It denies that it does anything on its own.

**They knew.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *This group of Jews knew that whoever exchanges the scripture of Allah for black magic will have no portion in the Afterlife.*

*Exchanges the scripture of Allah for black magic.* That is verse 101's casting the Book behind their backs, and the commerce metaphor again — verse 16, 41, 79, 86, 90, 96.

**Maʿārif on the Zuhrah story.**

He raises the famous narrative and handles it carefully, and the handling is the most instructive thing in his commentary here:

*These verses condemn the Jews for indulging in black magic. In connection with the verses, some commentators have reported a long and well-known story about a woman called Zuhrah, which is not based on any authentic Islamic tradition. Those scholars who have found the story to be infringing the regulations of the Sharīʿah have rejected it as mere fiction; but those who believe that it can be interpreted so as to come in line with the Sharīʿah have not dismissed it totally.*

*For the moment we are not concerned with the question whether the story is true or false. But what we would like to insist upon is the fact that a proper understanding does in no way depend on this story.*

He names the story, records the disagreement, declines to resolve it, and then says the verse does not need it. That is a rare move in classical commentary, and it is the right one.

**Maʿārif on the three things they knew.**

*The Jews knew very well that their indulgence in black magic was not only a sin, but also involved infidelity. They could also see that such activities would do them no good even in this world, for their sorcery could not harm anyone except when Allah willed it so.*

Three pieces of knowledge, and they proceeded anyway. The verse's closing — *if only they knew* — is not saying they were ignorant. It is saying they knew and it made no difference.

**Tazkīrul's closing.**

*But the Jews took no heed of this warning: they practised magic with great fervour and even used it for illicit ends.*

The warning was delivered every time. It was ignored every time.

**Miserable was the price.**

*Biʾsa mā ishtaraw bihi anfusahum.* The sūrah's commerce metaphor for the fifth time, and it closes the verse the way verse 90 closed its argument.

They sold their souls. They bought magic. And the verse says they already knew what the transaction would cost them.

103.text:
*If only they were faithful and mindful of Allah, there would have been a better reward from Allah, if only they knew.*

**The verse that ends the passage in eleven words.**

After the longest verse in the sūrah, the shortest possible conclusion.

**If only they were faithful and mindful.**

*Law annahum āmanū wa ttaqaw.* Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar and the omitted half:

*Yet if only they — the Jews — had believed in the Prophet and the Qurʾān, and been fearful of God's chastisement by abandoning acts of disobedience towards Him, such as sorcery — the response to the conditional clause beginning with law, "if," has been omitted, but it is intimated to be "they would have been rewarded," and this is indicated by His following words.*

The answer to the "if" is not stated. The verse leaves it for the reader to supply, and then supplies it in the next clause.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And if they, i.e. the Jews, had believed, in Muhammad and the Qurʾān, and kept from evil, repented from Judaism and sorcery.*

*Repented from Judaism and sorcery.* Tanwīr joins the two, as the verse does.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *If the Jews had really had faith in Allah, and been mindful to obey His sacred law and not rebel, His reward would have been far better for them, if they only knew.*

**A better reward.**

*La-mathūbatun min ʿindi Llāhi khayr.* Al-Jalālayn parses it:

*Verily a reward from God would have been better than that for which they sold themselves — if they had but known that this is better, they would not have preferred that over this. La-mathūbatun, "verily the reward," is the subject; the lām is that of oaths; and min ʿindi Llāhi khayrun, "from God would have been better," is the predicate.*

*Than that for which they sold themselves.* The comparison is explicit. On one side, the reward from Allah. On the other, the magic.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *a recompense from Allah, a reward from Allah, would be better, than Judaism and sorcery.*

**If only they knew.**

*Law kānū yaʿlamūn.* The verse ends where verse 102 ended, and the repetition is the point.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives both readings, and the second is the harder one:

*If they only knew, if they believed in Allah's reward, but they do not know nor do they believe; and it is said that they knew all this from their Book.*

*It is said that they knew all this from their Book.* On that reading, "if only they knew" is not a statement about their ignorance. It is a rebuke about their knowledge.

Al-Jalālayn's gloss points the same way: *if they had but known that this is better, they would not have preferred that over this.*

They would not have preferred it. Which implies the preference was not made in ignorance.

**Why this verse is so short.**

Verse 102 took four hundred words to describe the trade. Verse 103 states the alternative in eleven.

Two options were on the table. The verse does not argue for the better one. It says it was better, and that they knew.

Maʿārif's summary of the passage covers both verses: the Jews *could also see that such activities would do them no good even in this world.*

**And the transition.**

Verse 104 turns away from the Children of Israel and addresses the believers directly — *O believers* — for the first time since verse 104's opening words.

The sūrah has spent sixty-five verses on what the Children of Israel did. Now it tells the believers what to say.

That shift is what verse 104 is about, and it begins with a single word.

104.text:
*O believers! Do not say, "Râ'ina." [Herd us!] But say, "Unẓurna," [Tend to us!] and listen attentively. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment.*

**A verse about one word.**

After magic, abrogation and covenant-breaking, the sūrah pauses over a single term of address — and it turns out to matter enough to legislate.

**The word.**

*Rāʿinā.* Al-Jalālayn gives both its Arabic sense and its Hebrew one, and the verse depends on the difference:

*O you who believe, do not say to the Prophet, "Observe us" — rāʿinā is an imperative form from murāʿāt, which they used to say to him, and this was a derogatory term in Hebrew, derived from the noun al-ruʿūna, "thoughtlessness." They found this very amusing and used to address the Prophet in this way, and so the believers were forbidden to use it.*

Maʿārif tells the story behind it:

*When they presented themselves before the Holy Prophet they would address him with the word rāʿinā, which, in Arabic, means "be mindful of us", but is, in Hebrew, a curse. The latter is what they intended, but the Arabs, not knowing Hebrew, could not see the point, and some Muslims too, with the Arabic sense of the word in mind, began to address the Holy Prophet in the same manner, to the great glee of the Jews, who had thus found a way of insulting him openly, and had even tricked the Muslims into joining them.*

*Tricked the Muslims into joining them.* The believers were repeating an insult without knowing it. That is why the verse addresses them and not the Jews.

**Tazkīrul on the phonetics.**

Its account is the most precise on how the trick worked:

*Some people would sit in the Prophet's company and, by playing on words, make a mockery of his teachings. For instance, instead of using the unambiguous Arabic word for "May we have your attention" — "unẓurnā" — they would say "rāʿinā." "Rāʿinā," when pronounced properly, has much the same meaning as "unẓurnā," but with the protraction of the second vowel, it becomes "rāʿīnā," meaning "our shepherd," and with the protraction of the first it becomes "rāʿīnā," which means idiot.*

Two vowel lengths, two different words. The insult lived in the pronunciation, not the spelling.

**Say unẓurnā.**

Al-Jalālayn: *but say instead, "Regard us," that is, look at us, and give ear to what you are commanded, and be prepared to accept it.*

Maʿārif explains why this word instead: *In order to frustrate the design of the Jews, the Holy Qurʾān commands the Muslims to use the word unẓurnā instead of rāʿinā, for the meanings of the two words are the same in Arabic.*

*The meanings of the two words are the same in Arabic.* The believers lost nothing. The Jews lost their joke.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *say not to Muhammad: "Listen to us" — lend us your ear — but say, "Look upon us," look at us and hear us, and it is for this reason that Allah forbade the believers to use the Jews' vocabulary, and be ye listeners, to what you have been commanded to do and obey.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *He instructed them to say "unẓurnā" instead, meaning "watch over us," because the use of this word has no negative implications.*

*No negative implications.* The criterion for choosing a word.

**And listen.**

*Wa smaʿū.* The third command in the verse, and the only one not about vocabulary.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and be ye listeners, to what you have been commanded to do and obey.*

Al-Jalālayn: *and give ear to what you are commanded, and be prepared to accept it.*

This is the answer to verse 93's *"we hear and disobey."* The believers are told to hear — and the hearing is defined as readiness to accept.

**Ibn Kathīr on the wider rule.**

He sets the verse in a general principle, and quotes the parallel:

*Allah forbade His believing servants from imitating the behavior and deeds of the disbelievers. The Jews used to use devious words that hide what they really meant. When they wanted to say, "hear us," they would use the word rāʿinā, which is an insult in Hebrew, but means "hear us" in Arabic.*

Then the verse from sūrah 4: *"Among those who are Jews, there are some who displace words from their right places and say: 'We hear your word and disobey,' and 'Hear, and let you hear nothing.' And rāʿinā, with a twist of their tongues and as a mockery of the religion. And if only they had said: 'We hear and obey,' and 'Do make us understand,' it would have been better for them, and more proper; but Allah cursed them for their disbelief, so they believe not except a few" (4:46).*

*A twist of their tongues.* Liyyan bi-alsinatihim. The phrase names the technique.

Ibn Kathīr adds the second instance, and it is the one still in use:

*Also, the ḥadīths stated that when they would greet Muslims, they would say, "as-sāmu ʿalaykum," meaning, "death be to you." This is why we were commanded to answer them by saying, "wa ʿalaykum," meaning, "and to you too" — then our supplication against them shall be answered, rather than theirs against us.*

The same trick with a greeting, and the same solution: change the reply.

**Maʿārif's ruling drawn from the verse.**

He draws a legal principle, and it is the most consequential comment on the verse:

*The verse shows that if a perfectly legitimate action on one's part provides room for others to commit illegitimate actions, even the legitimate action no longer remains lawful for one. For example, if a permissible action on the part of a scholar is likely to lead the ignorant into error and to induce them to do impermissible things, that permissible action will then become forbidden for him, provided that the action concerned is not essential according to the Sharīʿah and is not included among its objects.*

*Rāʿinā* was permissible. It became forbidden because of what others did with it. That is a general rule about speech, drawn from one word.

**And the charge against the Jews.**

Maʿārif states it plainly:

*The verse describes the insolent Jews as kāfirūn (infidels), which means that being intentionally disrespectful towards a prophet, even in an indirect manner, constitutes infidelity.*

*Even in an indirect manner.* The insult was deniable. The verse does not allow the denial.

**For disbelievers there is a painful punishment.**

Al-Jalālayn: *and for disbelievers awaits a painful chastisement, that is, the Fire.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās specifies: *For disbelievers, for the Jews, is a painful doom, which will extend to their hearts.*

*Will extend to their hearts.* The hearts of verse 74 and 88 — the wrapped hearts, the hearts that drank the calf.

**Tazkīrul's general lesson.**

*The Muslims were told therefore to avoid ambiguous words, and to be quite clear in their speech; words with a derisive shade of meaning should be especially avoided. Furthermore, they were enjoined to pay close attention to what the Prophet said and to try to understand it on their own, without resorting to excessive questioning; receptiveness rather than obstinacy was to mark their attitude to his instructions.*

*Receptiveness rather than obstinacy.* And the contrast is with verses 68 to 71 — the three questions about the cow.

That is the verse's real subject. The believers are being told how to receive a command, by people who watched another community fail at exactly that.

105.text:
*The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord, but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty.*

**The verse that turns to the believers' situation.**

Verses 97 to 104 have been about what the People of the Book say. Verse 105 states what they want — and the two groups are named together.

**Two groups, one attitude.**

Al-Jalālayn: *Those disbelievers of the People of the Scripture, and the idolaters from among the Arabs — al-mushrikīna, "idolaters," is a supplement to ahl al-kitābi, "People of the Scripture," and the min, "of," is explicative — do not wish that any good, any Inspiration, should be revealed to you from your Lord, out of envy of you.*

*Out of envy of you.* The motive is named, and it is the same one verse 90 identified — *baghyan*, resentment at Allah's choice.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names the people on both sides: *Neither those who disbelieve among the people of the Scripture — Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his companions — nor the idolaters, the idolaters of Arabia: Abū Jahl and his companions — love that there should be sent down unto you, that Allah should send Gabriel unto your Prophet, any good thing, the good of prophethood, Islam and the Book.*

Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and Abū Jahl. One Jewish leader in Madinah, one Qurayshī leader in Makkah. Named together, on the same side.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *The disbelievers, whether they are from the People of the Scripture or from among the idolaters, do not like that Allah should send down any good thing, big or small, to you.*

*Big or small.* Not opposition to a particular revelation. To any.

**Maʿārif on the claim they made.**

He describes a specific social performance, and it is the most detailed account in the six sources:

*Some of the Jews used to assure the Muslims of their sincerity towards them, and to pretend that they would very much have liked the Muslims to have received from Allah religious doctrines and commandments superior to what they themselves had received, so that they too could accept them, but unfortunately Islam did not seem to be a better religion.*

*Pretend that they would very much have liked…* The posture of the reasonable sceptic — we would follow it if it were better.

*The Holy Qurʾān refutes their claim to be the well-wishers of the Muslims, and declares that the infidels, whether they be the Jews or the associators, are so jealous of Muslims that they can never like the idea of their receiving from Allah any kind of blessing whatsoever.*

**And Maʿārif's observation about the two claims.**

He notices which one the verse answers, and why:

*These Jews used to make two claims — firstly, that Judaism was a better religion than Islam; secondly, that they were the well-wishers of the Muslims. They could not establish the first of these claims on the basis of any valid argument, and it remained an empty assertion.*

*Moreover, the difference between Islam and Judaism does not primarily depend on the question of one being better than the other. For, when something new comes to abrogate something older, the latter is automatically given up — and Allah has sent Islam to abrogate all the earlier religions. The fact being so obvious, the Holy Qurʾān says nothing in refutation of the first claim, and takes up only the second.*

The verse ignores the comparative claim and answers the claim of goodwill. Because the first is settled by abrogation — which verse 106 is about.

**Allah selects whoever He wills.**

Al-Jalālayn: *but God singles out for His mercy — for the office of His Prophet — whom He will.*

*For the office of His Prophet.* The mercy here is specific: prophethood.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *But Allah chooseth for His mercy — chooses for His religion, prophethood, Islam and the Book — whom He will, whoever deserves to be chosen, i.e. Muhammad.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Through His mercy Allah favours whom He wills of His servants with prophethood, revelation and faith.*

**The connection to verse 90.**

Verse 90 said they resented *that Allah should reveal of His grace unto whom He wills of His servants*. Verse 105 says *Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy*.

The same phrase. Verse 90 named the resentment. Verse 105 states the fact they resented, without apology.

Maʿārif makes the point about why it cannot harm: *Of course, this jealousy can do no harm to the Muslims, for Allah is Beneficent and All-Powerful, and can shower his special blessings on whomsoever He chooses.*

**Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty.**

*Dhū al-faḍli al-ʿaẓīm.* Al-Jalālayn: *God is of bounty abounding.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and Allah is of infinite mercy, His favour in giving Muhammad prophethood and Islam is great indeed.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar draws the general conclusion: *Allah's bounty is vast. No one in creation gets any good except that it is from Him, and it is from His bounty that He sent His Prophet and revealed His scripture to us.*

*No one in creation gets any good except that it is from Him.* The bounty is not a limited supply that someone else's receipt diminishes.

**Tazkīrul's instruction to the believers.**

Its comment on verses 104 and 105 turns the verse into guidance:

*The believers were also told not to be jealous of another person's valuable possessions, for it was God Himself who had bestowed that particular blessing on His servant. God Himself decreed that the Prophet be the recipient of divine revelation. If one were earnest in seeking to learn from him, one could share in the blessing he received.*

*One could share in the blessing.* The alternative to envying a gift is learning from the person who received it.

**Why this verse sits before the one on abrogation.**

Verse 105 says Allah gives His bounty to whom He chooses. Verse 106 says He also replaces what He has given when He chooses.

Both are about the same thing: the giving is Allah's to arrange. And verse 106 answers the specific objection that arrangement produced.

106.text:
*If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything?*

**The sūrah's statement on abrogation, and the objection that produced it.**

This is the verse that established naskh as a principle in Islamic jurisprudence, and it arrives as a reply to a taunt.

**The objection.**

Al-Jalālayn gives it directly:

*When the disbelievers began to deride the matter of abrogation, saying that one day Muhammad enjoins his Companions to one thing and then the next day he forbids it, God revealed…*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names who said it: *as a direct reference to the claim of the Quraysh, who said to the Prophet: O Muhammad! Why do you command us to do something and then forbid it?*

Maʿārif gives the occasion and the argument in full:

*At first, Muslims used to pray with their faces turned towards Bayt al-Maqdīs at Jerusalem; later on, Allah commanded them to turn towards the Kaʿbah. Similarly, certain other injunctions were abrogated altogether, or replaced by others. This provided the Jews and some of the associators too with an occasion to taunt the Muslims, and to say that such changes were made by the Holy Prophet himself and not by Allah.*

*They used to argue that if everything that Allah revealed was good, as the Muslims affirmed, why should one injunction be replaced by another? For, it would only mean that one of the two injunctions must be good, and the other evil, but no divine revelation can possibly be evil. Putting these two premises together, the Jews tried to draw the conclusion that the Holy Qurʾān could not be a revealed book.*

A real syllogism, and a serious one. Tazkīrul Qurʾān records its effect:

*So intensive had this propaganda campaign become that even some simple-minded Muslims were affected, and started raising the issue with the Prophet.*

**The answer.**

Maʿārif states the reply, and it is the verse's whole argument:

*The present verse refutes this line of argument, and, in effect, points out that abrogation does not mean replacing good with evil, or vice versa, which should imply the possibility of the presence of evil in divine revelation, but that everything that Allah reveals to His prophets is good, and that what has been abrogated is good as much as what abrogated it.*

*What has been abrogated is good as much as what abrogated it.* Both are good. The syllogism assumed one must be bad. It is not.

**What naskh means — and the glosses.**

Ibn Kathīr collects them, and the range is wide:

*Ibn Abī Ṭalḥah said that Ibn ʿAbbās said that "whatever a verse do we nansakh" means, "Whatever an āyah We abrogate." Also, Ibn Jurayj said that Mujāhid said that it means, "Whatever an āyah We erase." Also, Ibn Abī Najīḥ said that Mujāhid said that it means, "We keep the words, but change the meaning." He related these words to the companions of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd.*

*Ibn Abī Ḥātim said that similar statements were mentioned by Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī. Also As-Suddī said that it means, "We erase it."*

Three kinds: abrogate, erase, keep the words and change the meaning.

**Ibn Jarīr's definition, and its limit.**

Ibn Kathīr records the most precise formulation, and it draws a boundary that still holds:

*Ibn Jarīr stated that it means, "Whatever ruling we repeal in an āyah, by making the allowed unlawful and the unlawful allowed." The naskh only occurs with commandments, prohibitions, permissions, and so forth. As for stories, they do not undergo naskh.*

*As for stories, they do not undergo naskh.* A narrative cannot be repealed. Only a ruling can.

*The word "naskh" literally means, "to copy a book." The meaning of naskh in the case of commandments is removing the commandment and replacing it by another. And whether the naskh involves the wordings, the ruling, or both, it is still called naskh.*

**Or cause it to be forgotten.**

*Aw nunsihā.* Al-Jalālayn gives the variants:

*There is a variant reading nunsikh, meaning, "Whatever verse We command you or Gabriel to abrogate," or postpone, so that We do not reveal the judgement contained in it, and We withhold its recital, or retain it in the Preserved Tablet; a variant reading of nunsihā is nunsihā, from "to forget," so "Whatever verse We abrogate, or We make you forget — that is, We erase from your heart."*

*We erase from your heart.* On that reading the forgetting is literal and it happens to the Prophet.

**We replace it with a better or similar one.**

Al-Jalālayn defines both terms:

*The response to the conditional sentence begun with mā is, "We bring in place a better one" — that is, more beneficial for Our servants, either because it is easier to implement, or contains much reward; "or the like of it," in terms of religious obligation and reward.*

*Easier to implement, or contains much reward.* Two ways a replacement can be better.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *We bring one better, We send Gabriel with that which is more profitable and easier to act upon, or the like, in reward, benefit and action.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *He replaces them with something more beneficial for the immediate moment or for later, or with what is similar. Such cases occur because of Allah's wisdom and knowledge.*

*For the immediate moment or for later.* The benefit can be temporal. A ruling suited to one moment is replaced by one suited to another.

**Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything?**

Al-Jalālayn: *do you not know that God has power over all things, including abrogating and substituting verses? — the interrogative here is meant as an affirmative.*

An interrogative that is an affirmation. The same form as verse 91's question.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *You know, O Prophet, that Allah has power over all things. He does as He wills, and rules as He wishes.*

**Tazkīrul on what lay underneath the objection.**

Its account explains why the objection was raised at all, and it is the sharpest comment on the verse:

*One who has discovered the truth by the help of God has to face stiff opposition when he starts to communicate it to others. One reason is that acceptance of truth entails negation of the self. People of high social status always find this hard, and none more so than the People of the Book, who considered prophethood to be their exclusive right.*

*Acceptance of truth entails negation of the self.* That is the obstacle, and it is not intellectual.

*Unable to conceive of a prophet coming amongst people other than them, they tried various ploys to turn people away from the Arab prophet. One of the theological objections that they raised to his teachings was on the subject of abrogation.*

*A theological objection.* The syllogism was sincere in form and instrumental in purpose.

**And the verse's own words.**

*Some of the Quranic injunctions differ from Mosaic law, so they would say, "Does God make mistakes in His revelations, that He sends down one commandment, and then replaces it with another? This shows that what your Prophet Muhammad is teaching is not from God, but is his own creation."*

The answer the verse gives is not that nothing changed. It is that what changed was good before and is good now.

**Why this verse sits here.**

Verse 101 said they cast the Book behind their backs. Verse 102 said what they followed instead. Verse 104 addressed the believers about a word. Verse 105 said Allah gives His bounty to whom He chooses.

Verse 106 completes it: and He takes back what He gave, when He chooses, and replaces it.

The sūrah's argument with the People of the Book has been about a scripture they treated as permanent. Verse 106 says revelation was never a fixed object. It is an act, and the Actor decides.

107.text:
*Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs only to Allah, and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah?*

**The verse that closes the argument on abrogation.**

Verse 106 said Allah replaces what He wills. Verse 107 says why no objection is possible: the kingdom is His.

**The kingdom.**

Al-Jalālayn: *Do you not know that to God belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, doing what He pleases, and that you have none besides God — other than God — neither protector, to safeguard you, nor helper, to keep away His chastisement when it comes?*

*Doing what He pleases.* The kingdom is not merely ownership. It is unrestricted action.

Al-Mukhtaṣar spells out what that means for legislation, and it is the verse's connection to the one before:

*You know, O Prophet, that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and that He rules as He wills. He instructs His servants as He wills, and forbids them from doing what He wills, establishing the sacred law as He wishes, and abolishing what He wishes.*

*Establishing the sacred law as He wishes, and abolishing what He wishes.* That is abrogation stated as a consequence of ownership.

**No guardian or helper.**

*Walī* and *naṣīr.* Al-Jalālayn distinguishes them: a protector, to safeguard you; a helper, to keep away His chastisement when it comes.

Two functions. One prevents harm, the other removes it. Neither is available from anyone else.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and ye have not, O Jews, apart from Allah, from Allah's torment, any friend, anyone close to benefit or protect you, or helper, anyone that can prevent your punishment.*

*Anyone close.* Walī carries proximity. The word implies relationship, not just function.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Your only protector is Allah, Who will take care of you, and you have no other helper to protect you from harm. Allah is the protector and guardian of all, and has power over everything.*

**Who the verse addresses.**

Al-Jalālayn reads it as the believers. Tanwīr al-Miqbās addresses the Jews directly: *and ye have not, O Jews.*

Both readings are in the sources, and neither is marked as preferred. The verse's *you* is open.

**Why this verse follows verse 106.**

Maʿārif's account of the preceding exchange explains the sequence. The objection was that changing a ruling implies one of the two was bad:

*They used to argue that if everything that Allah revealed was good, as the Muslims affirmed, why should one injunction be replaced by another? For, it would only mean that one of the two injunctions must be good, and the other evil, but no divine revelation can possibly be evil.*

Verse 106 answered that both are good. Verse 107 answers the deeper question: who is in a position to object?

Maʿārif's summary of the pair: *the verse declares that if Allah chooses to abrogate an injunction contained in a certain verse, while retaining the verse itself as a part of the Holy Qurʾān, or chooses to remove a verse from the memories of men altogether, there is nothing objectionable in it, for Allah alone knows the wisdom that lies in His choice, and He makes these changes for the good of men.*

*For the good of men.* The changes are not arbitrary. They are also not negotiable.

**Tazkīrul on what the objection was really about.**

Its account of verses 106 to 109 names the real obstacle, and it is not intellectual:

*One reason is that acceptance of truth entails negation of the self. People of high social status always find this hard, and none more so than the People of the Book, who considered prophethood to be their exclusive right.*

*Acceptance of truth entails negation of the self.* The syllogism about abrogation was the form the resistance took. The content was status.

**Why the verse is short.**

Thirty words. A kingdom, an owner, and the absence of anyone else.

The sūrah has been arguing with the People of the Book for sixty-seven verses. Verse 107 does not argue. It states the position that makes argument unnecessary.

Verse 108 turns to the believers, and warns them about a different failure — asking the wrong kind of question.

108.text:
*Or do you, believers, intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before? But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way.*

**The verse that turns the warning onto the believers.**

Verse 107 addressed everyone. Verse 108 addresses the Muslims, and it compares them to the Israelites in a way that is not a compliment.

**Two occasions, both recorded.**

Al-Jalālayn gives the first, and it involves the Quraysh:

*When the Meccans asked the Prophet to enlarge the size of Mecca and make Ṣafā full of gold, the following was revealed: "Or do you desire to question your Messenger, as Mūsā was questioned by his people aforetime?" — when they asked him to show them God openly, among other things.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives the second, and it is about the Jews:

*Or would ye question your messenger — ask him to see your Lord, hear His speech and other similar things — as Moses was questioned, as the Children of Israel asked Moses, before — before the advent of Muhammad?*

Maʿārif records a third:

*Hostility to the Holy Prophet had become so habitual to the Jews that they were always making insolent demands. Once they asked him to bring before them the whole of the Qurʾān all at once, just as the Torah had been revealed.*

Three demands: move a mountain, show us God, send the whole Book at once. The verse covers all of them.

**What Mūsā was asked.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar names the precedent: *as the people of Mūsā questioned their prophet before, like when they said, "Show us Allah openly" (sūrat an-Nisāʾ: 153).*

That is verse 4:153 — the same request the sūrah already described at 2:55, where the seventy were struck by the thunderbolt. The question has been asked before, and the sūrah has already recorded what happened.

**Ibn Kathīr on the prohibition.**

He reads the verse as a rule about questions, and states it precisely:

*In this verse, Allah forbade the believers from asking the Prophet numerous questions about matters that did not occur yet. Similarly, Allah said: "O you who believe! Ask not about things which, if made plain to you, may cause you trouble. But if you ask about them while the Qurʾān is being revealed, they will be made plain to you" (5:101).*

*This verse means, "If you ask about a matter after it is revealed, it shall be duly explained to you. Therefore, do not ask about matters that have not occurred yet, for they might become prohibited, due to your questions."*

*They might become prohibited because of your questions.* The danger is not ignorance. It is that asking creates obligations.

**The ḥadīth that states it.**

Ibn Kathīr records it from the Ṣaḥīḥ:

*"The greatest criminal among the Muslims is the one who asks if a thing is prohibited, which is not prohibited, and it becomes prohibited because of his asking about it."*

*The greatest criminal among the Muslims.* Not for sin. For asking.

**And the example.**

Ibn Kathīr gives the case that illustrates it:

*This is why, when the Messenger of Allah was asked about a husband who finds another man with his wife — if he exposes the adultery, he will be exposing a major incident; if he is quiet about it, he will be quiet about a major matter — the Messenger of Allah did not like such questions. Later on, Allah revealed the ruling of mulāʿanah.*

A genuine dilemma, asked in good faith, and the Prophet disliked the question. Then the ruling came anyway, from 24:6-9.

**The second ḥadīth, and it is the decisive one.**

Ibn Kathīr records it from Muslim:

*The Messenger of Allah said: "Leave me as I leave you; those before you were only destroyed because of their excessive questioning and disputing with their Prophets. Therefore, when I command you with a command, do as much of it as you are able."*

*Those before you were only destroyed because of their excessive questioning.* That is verses 68 to 71 — the three questions about the cow — stated as the cause of a destruction.

And al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah's report: *the Messenger of Allah "forbade saying, 'it was said' and 'he said,' and wasting money and asking many questions."*

**Maʿārif on what the demands were really for.**

He reads the intention, and the reading is the verse's indictment:

*In such cases, the intention of the Jews had never been to seek guidance or to satisfy their doubts or to strengthen their faith, but only to cast aspersions on a prophet, or to question the wisdom of Allah. The verse indicts this behavior as kufr (infidelity).*

*Never been to seek guidance.* The question was not a request for information. It was an attack.

Then his general principle:

*Such demands are improper, because there is a raison d'être for everything Allah does, but divine wisdom alone knows what that is, and the creature has no right to determine the precise mode of his Creator's acts — he should not even ask the why and wherefore of a divine action, but accept it and submit himself to the Divine Will.*

He had said the same at verse 72, about why the cow was needed. The position is consistent: the reasons exist, and they are not ours to demand.

**And the second reading.**

Maʿārif notes it: *If one takes this verse as having been addressed to the Muslims, it would mean that they are being warned against making improper demands on the Holy Prophet.*

Al-Jalālayn takes that reading — the Meccans asking for gold. Tanwīr takes the other. Both stand.

**Whoever trades belief for disbelief.**

Al-Jalālayn explains how questioning becomes apostasy, and the mechanism is specific:

*Whoever exchanges belief for unbelief, taking the latter in place of the former, by refraining from contemplating the clear proofs, and by requesting others instead, has surely strayed from the even way — meaning, he has mistaken the proper path. Al-sawāʾ essentially means al-wasaṭ, "middle way."*

*By refraining from contemplating the clear proofs, and by requesting others instead.* Not rejecting evidence. Demanding different evidence. That is the trade.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Whoever exchanges faith for disbelief has lost the balanced way, the right path.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *He who chooseth disbelief instead of faith, verily he hath gone astray from a plain road, he has relinquished the path of guidance.*

**Why this verse sits here.**

Verses 97 to 107 have been about the People of the Book. Verse 108 turns and says: the failure being described is available to you too.

The Israelites asked three questions about a cow and paid a skin's weight in gold. They asked to see God and were struck. They asked for the whole Book at once.

The believers are told, before they start, that the same door is open to them.

Tazkīrul Qurʾān's instruction at verse 104 covers it: *receptiveness rather than obstinacy was to mark their attitude to his instructions.*

109.text:
*Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you, believers, back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them. Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything.*

**The verse that names the motive and then forbids retaliation.**

Two halves, and they pull in opposite directions. The first says what they want. The second says what to do about it, and it is not what the first half invites.

**What they wish.**

*Yawaddu kathīrun min ahli al-kitāb.* Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar and the motive:

*Many of the People of the Scripture long that — law, "if only that," represents the import of the verbal noun — they might make you disbelievers after you have believed, from the envy — ḥasadan is the object denoting reason — being of their own souls, that is to say, their wicked souls have prompted them to this attitude.*

*Their wicked souls have prompted them.* The envy is not provoked by anything the Muslims did. It originates inside.

Maʿārif makes the same point precisely:

*Some of the Jews, pretending to be the well-wishers of the Muslims, were always inventing new stratagems to make them turn away from Islam, and, in spite of repeated failure in this effort, did not refrain from it.*

*The verse warns the Muslims against their intentions, which are motivated, not by sincerity and friendship, but by envy — which in its turn arises not from anything the Muslims do, but spontaneously from within themselves, even after they have come to understand clearly what the truth is.*

*Not from anything the Muslims do.* There is no grievance to answer. The envy is self-generated.

**Who they were.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names the people on both sides:

*Many of the people of the Scripture — Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, and Finhās ibn ʿAzūrah and his companions — long to make you disbelievers, make you abandon your Religion and become unbelievers, O ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān and Muʿādh ibn Jabal!*

Named agitators, and named targets. Three specific Muslims the effort was directed at.

Ibn Kathīr records the occasion from Ibn Abī Ḥātim:

*ʿAbdullāh ibn Kaʿb ibn Mālik said that Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, who was a Jew and a poet, used to criticize the Prophet in his poems, so Allah revealed, "Many of the People of the Scripture wish that they could turn you away," regarding his matter.*

*A poet.* The campaign was conducted in verse.

**After the truth has been made clear to them.**

Ibn Kathīr records Ibn ʿAbbās on this clause, and it is the sharpest formulation:

*"An unlettered Messenger came to the People of the Scriptures, confirming what they have in their own Books about the Messengers and the āyāt of Allah. He also believes in all of this, just as they believe in it. Yet, they rejected the Prophet out of disbelief, envy and transgression."*

*He also believes in all of this, just as they believe in it.* The Prophet affirmed their own scripture. That is what made the rejection inexplicable.

*Allah said that after He illuminated the truth for them, such that they were not ignorant of any of it, yet their envy made them deny the Prophet. Thus Allah criticized, chastised and denounced them.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *after the Truth hath become manifest unto them, in their Book, that Muhammad and his Book, his description and traits, are true.*

**Pardon and bear with them.**

*Fa-ʿfū wa-ṣfaḥū.* Al-Jalālayn: *yet pardon, leave them be, and be forgiving, stay away and make no encroachments against them, till God brings His command concerning fighting them.*

*Till God brings His command concerning fighting them.* The pardon is temporary, and the verse says so.

Maʿārif draws out what the verse anticipates:

*The verse also asks the Muslims not to give way to their justifiable anger at such misconduct, but to forgive the Jews, and wait till Allah sends a new commandment with regard to such matters. Thus, the verse gives an indication that Allah is soon going to lay down a law for the preservation of peace and order on the earth, which would guide the Muslims in dealing with mischief-makers — the law, of course, being the permission to go to war against the enemies of Islam.*

*Justifiable anger.* Maʿārif does not call the anger wrong. He says the response must wait.

Al-Mukhtaṣar names what the command turned out to be: *God's command came with its ruling, either Islam, or paying the jizyah, or physical intervention.*
