Tanwīr al-Miqbās is the most specific about the historical outcome: *until Allah giveth command, brings His chastisement upon Banū Qurayẓah and Banū an-Naḍīr, through killing, captivity and expulsion.*

The same two tribes from verse 85. The verse's "until" has a date.

**Why the believers are told to wait.**

Maʿārif explains the situation the instruction was given into:

*The Muslims were actually conscious of their own weakness and the strength of their foe, and could have wondered how they would be able to act upon the new law. So, the verse reminds them that Allah's power extends over everything, small or big, ordinary or extraordinary.*

That is why the verse ends where it does.

**Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything.**

Al-Jalālayn: *truly God has power over all things.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās specifies: *Lo! Allah is Able to do all things, to cause their death and expulsion.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *God has power over all things, and they do not affect Him in any way.*

*They do not affect Him.* The opponents are real and the outcome is not in doubt.

**Tazkīrul on the instruction.**

Its account of verses 110 to 112 states the reasoning, and it is the most practical comment on the verse:

*It was only natural that this should provoke the Muslims, but God told them that this was not the time for violent reaction. Muslims should always be patient, since patience prevents one from taking negative retaliatory measures in the heat of the moment.*

*In the heat of the moment.* The pardon is not a principle of weakness. It is a discipline about timing.

**Ibn Kathīr's frame for the passage.**

*Allah warned His believing servants against following the ways of the People of the Book, who publicly and secretly harbor enmity and hatred for the believers, and who envy the believers, while they recognize the virtue of the believers and their Prophet.*

*While they recognize the virtue.* The envy and the recognition are simultaneous. That is what verse 90 called the worst envy there is.

*Allah also commanded His believing servants to forgive them and to be patient with them, until Allah delivers His aid and victory to them.*

**Why the two halves go together.**

The verse names a campaign, identifies the motive as self-generated envy, confirms the truth is already clear — and then says: pardon, and wait.

The reason the wait is possible is the last clause. Allah is capable of everything. The outcome does not depend on the believers acting now.

Verse 110 tells them what to do in the meantime, and it is the same two things verse 83 listed in the covenant.

110.text:
*Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will certainly find its reward with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.*

**What to do while waiting.**

Verse 109 said pardon and wait. Verse 110 says what the waiting consists of — and it is two commands the sūrah has given before.

**Establish prayer and pay alms.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And establish prayer, perfect the five daily prayers, and pay the poor-due, pay the poor what is due from your wealth.*

Al-Jalālayn: *And perform the prayer and pay the alms.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the fullest form: *Establish the prayer with all its parts, both obligatory and recommended aspects, and give zakāh from their wealth to those who deserve it.*

*Both obligatory and recommended aspects.* Not the minimum.

**The same two as verse 83.**

Verse 83 listed the covenant's six duties and ended with *establish prayer and pay alms*. Verse 110 gives the believers the same two.

That is not incidental. The covenant at Sinai and the instruction to Madinah end in the same place.

Ibn Kathīr: *Allah commanded the believers to perform the prayer perfectly, to pay the zakāh, and He encouraged them to preserve the practice of these righteous deeds.*

*To preserve the practice.* The emphasis is on continuation, not initiation.

**Maʿārif on why these two, now.**

He connects the verse to the one before it, and the connection is the verse's real point:

*The next verse asks the Muslims to continue offering their prayers and paying zakāh, and when the new law comes down, they can add the participation in a jihād to these good deeds which they have already been performing.*

*They can add.* Not replace. The prayer and the zakāh continue; something is added to them.

Then he answers an objection the believers might have had:

*Nor should the Muslims suppose that until they can take part in a jihād, mere prayers and fasting will not bring them the spiritual merit they desire; in fact, they shall receive a full reward in the other world for each and every good deed they perform, for Allah knows what people do, and not a particle of one's good deeds shall be lost.*

*Not a particle shall be lost.* The waiting period is not a spiritual hold.

**Whatever good you send forth.**

*Wa mā tuqaddimū li-anfusikum min khayr.* Al-Jalālayn defines the good and the finding:

*Whatever good, in the way of obedience, such as observing kinship and charity, you shall offer for your own souls, you shall find it — that is, its reward — with God.*

*Observing kinship and charity.* Two examples, and both are social rather than ritual.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and whatever of good, of righteous deeds, and the poor-due and charitable works, ye send before for your souls, you save for yourselves, ye will find it, you will find its reward, with Allah, from Allah.*

*You save for yourselves.* Tuqaddimū — to send ahead. The metaphor is of luggage sent on before a journey.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Whatever good action they do in life before death will be a treasure for them: the reward of which they will find with their Lord on the Day of Judgement.*

*A treasure.* The same image, made explicit.

**You will find it with Allah.**

*Tajidūhu ʿinda Llāh.* Not "you will be rewarded." You will *find* it — as something already there, stored.

The verb is the same one verse 62 used for the believers' reward being *with their Lord*, and verse 82's *residents of Paradise*. What is sent ahead is waiting.

**Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās specifies what is seen, and it narrows the verse considerably:

*Lo! Allah is Seer, knows your intentions, of what ye do, of what you spend in charity and the poor-due.*

*Knows your intentions.* The seeing reaches the motive, not just the act.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Allah sees all that you do, and rewards everyone accordingly.*

Al-Jalālayn: *assuredly God sees what you do, and will requite you for it.*

**Tazkīrul on why these two specifically.**

Its account of verses 110 to 112 explains the social logic of both commands, and it is the most substantive comment on the verse:

*They should be steadfast in prayers, for prayer brings one closer to God. They should never fail in the payment of the prescribed alms (zakāh), for a society in which the rich are willing to share with the poor will be based on compassion; there will be a real sense of togetherness among its members.*

*A society in which the rich are willing to share with the poor.* Zakāh is not described as a tax or an offering here. It is described as the condition of a compassionate society.

**Why this verse is so short.**

Verse 109 named a campaign and forbade retaliation. Verse 110 does not explain, argue or threaten. It gives two commands and a promise.

The promise is the point. Whatever you send ahead, you will find. Nothing is lost in the waiting.

And the two commands are the ones the covenant required — which means the believers are being held to the same standard the Children of Israel turned away from.

Verse 111 goes back to the claim the whole address has been answering: that Paradise belongs to one group.

111.text:
*The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, O Prophet, "Show me your proof if what you say is true."*

**The claim, stated by both sides, and answered in three words.**

Verse 94 challenged the Jews to wish for death. Verse 111 challenges both communities to produce evidence.

**Two claims, not one.**

Al-Jalālayn records the occasion, and it was a debate:

*And they say, "None shall enter Paradise except those who are Jews" — hūd is the plural of hāʾid — "or Christians." This is what the Jews of Madinah and the Christians of Najrān said, when they disputed with the Prophet, each party separately claiming Paradise for its members exclusively.*

The Jews of Madinah and the Christians of Najrān. Two delegations, making the same claim about themselves and excluding each other.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And they say, i.e. the Jews: "None entereth Paradise unless he be a Jew," unless he dies as a Jew, allegedly, "or a Christian," as the Christians also claimed.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *The Jews and the Christians each said that Paradise would be for them alone.*

**Ibn Kathīr on where the claim comes from.**

He connects it to the verses already in this sūrah, and the connection matters:

*Allah made the confusion of the Jews and the Christians clear, since they claim that no one will enter Paradise unless he is a Jew or a Christian. Similarly, Allah mentioned their claims in sūrat al-Māʾidah: "We are the children of Allah and His loved ones" (5:18).*

*Allah refuted this false claim and informed them that they will be punished because of their sins. Previously we mentioned their claim that the Fire would not touch them for more than a few days, after which they would be put in Paradise.*

Three claims, now complete: the forty days (2:80), the exclusive Paradise (2:94 and here), and being Allah's children (5:18). The sūrah has been answering the same claim in three forms.

**These are their desires.**

*Tilka amāniyyuhum.* Al-Jalālayn: *Such sayings are their desires, their false passions.*

Ibn Kathīr collects the glosses: *Allah rebuked this baseless claim, and He said: "These are their own desires." Abū al-ʿĀliyah commented, "These are wishes that they wished Allah would answer, without basis." Similar was stated by Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas.*

*Wishes that they wished Allah would answer, without basis.* Not a doctrine. A hope presented as a fact.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās is the most pointed: *These are their own desires, what they wish from Allah, even though it is not in their Books.*

*Even though it is not in their Books.* The claim is not even sourced from the texts they appeal to.

And *amāniyy* is the same word verse 78 used for the unlettered — *except lies*, which Tazkīrul identified as *the mythical tales invented by Jewish scholars* to prove Paradise was reserved for the Jews. The verse uses the scholars' own word for what they produced.

**Show me your proof.**

*Hātū burhānakum.* Ibn Kathīr gives the glosses:

*"Produce your burhān" — meaning, "your proof," as Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid, As-Suddī and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas stated. Qatādah said that the verse means, "Bring the evidence that supports your statement, if you are truthful in your claim."*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās specifies where the proof would have to come from: *Say, O Muhammad, to both parties: "Bring your proofs" — from your own respective Books — "if ye are truthful" in your claim.*

*From your own respective Books.* Not from the Qurʾān. The challenge is internal to each tradition.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Tell them, O Prophet, in reply, to bring proof of what they were claiming if they were telling the truth.*

**Maʿārif on what the claim reveals.**

He diagnoses it, and the diagnosis is the sharpest in the six sources:

*The Jews and the Christians were hostile not only to the Muslims, but also to each other. They had forgotten the essence of religion — that is, adherence to the true and authentic doctrines, and performance of good deeds as laid down by the Sharīʿah — and had identified it with a mere affiliation to a racial or social community.*

*Identified it with a mere affiliation.* Religion reduced to membership. That is what verse 91's *"what was sent down to us"* meant, stated as a diagnosis.

*Each of the two groups claimed that it had the exclusive right to go to the Paradise, without having any argument to substantiate the claim. The Jews read the Torah, while the Christians read the Evangel, and they could have easily seen that the two Books confirm each other. Each party used to assert, in its malice, that the religion of the other was baseless.*

*They could have easily seen.* The evidence was in their hands. That is what verse 101 called casting the Book behind their backs.

*This gave an excuse to the mushrikīn (associators), who, in spite of their ignorance, began to say the same of both the religions.*

The pagans watched two scripture-bearing communities invalidate each other, and concluded neither was true. Verse 113 will state this.

**Maʿārif's answer.**

He gives the principle the sūrah replaces the claim with, and it is the same standard as verse 62:

*It declares that other people too will go to Paradise who have, in their time, been following the Sharīʿah of their own prophet, and who, now that the Holy Qurʾān also has abrogated all the earlier Divine Books, follow the Islamic Sharīʿah.*

*The essence of religion, whether it be Islam or Christianity or Judaism, lies in two things. (1) One should obey Allah in one's belief as well as in one's actions. (2) This obedience should not arise from expediency, but one should surrender oneself to divine commandments in all sincerity.*

Two conditions, and neither mentions a community.

Then the limit he adds, which prevents the principle from becoming formless:

*Moreover, it is not enough to be worthy of Paradise merely to have a sincere intention to obey Allah, and then to invent, according to one's own fancy, the modes and forms of obedience, for it is absolutely essential that the forms of worship and [obedience be as revealed].*

Sincerity is necessary. Invention is not sufficient. The forms come from revelation, not preference.

**Tazkīrul on what the Jews told new converts.**

Its account supplies the social context, and it explains why this verse mattered in Madinah:

*The Jews used to tell new Muslim converts that if they had to forsake their ancestral religion, they should become Jews or Christians. Being the descendants of saints and prophets throughout history, they were the ones who would go to heaven.*

*If you have to forsake your ancestral religion…* The argument offered to a convert was not that Islam was false. It was that there were better options.

Then the answer: *But the Quran tells us that one does not merit entry into heaven by dint of belonging to a certain community. Everyone will be judged according to his own actions. National status is of no significance in the sight of God.*

*National status is of no significance.* That is the whole verse in one sentence.

**Why the verse is a challenge and not a denial.**

The Qurʾān does not say "you are wrong." It says: bring your proof.

The challenge is answerable in principle. If the Torah or the Gospel contained the claim, producing it would settle the matter. The verse's confidence is that they cannot.

Tanwīr says the claim is not in their Books. Maʿārif says they could have seen the two Books confirm each other. Al-Jalālayn calls it a false passion.

Three sources, one conclusion: the claim is not in the texts it appeals to.

**And what follows.**

Verse 112 gives the answer — whoever submits his face to Allah and does good. Verse 113 records what the two communities said about each other.

The sequence is: an exclusive claim, a demand for proof, the actual standard, and then the two claimants contradicting each other in public.

112.text:
*But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.*

**The answer to verse 111's claim.**

Verse 111 demanded proof. Verse 111 does not wait for it. It states the actual standard, and the standard mentions no community.

**But no.**

*Balā.* The same word that opened verse 81's answer to the forty days. Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Nay — it is certainly not as you have claimed.*

Al-Jalālayn supplies what the word denies and what it affirms: *Nay, but others will also enter Paradise.*

*Others will also enter.* The claim was that Paradise was exclusive. The answer is that other people get in.

**Whoever submits their face to Allah.**

*Man aslama wajhahu li-Llāh.* Al-Jalālayn explains the image, and the explanation is the verse's heart:

*Namely, whoever submits his purpose to God — that is, adheres to His commands. Wajh, "face," sc. "purpose," is here mentioned because it is the most noble part of the body, so that when it has submitted, there is all the more reason for the other parts to follow — being virtuous, affirming God's Oneness.*

*The most noble part of the body.* The face is named because it leads. If it submits, the rest follows.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *but whoever surrendereth his purpose to Allah — whoever makes sincere his Religion and works to Allah.*

*Makes sincere his Religion.* Aslama wajhahu as ikhlāṣ — sincerity, not merely compliance.

**And does good.**

*Wa huwa muḥsin.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *while doing good, in words and deeds.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *All those who are sincere in repenting to Allah, doing good, serving Allah and following what the Prophet came with, will enter Paradise, no matter what group they come from.*

*No matter what group they come from.* The phrase that answers verse 111 directly.

**Maʿārif on the principle the verse establishes.**

He states it as a rule that all three traditions share, and it is the most complete formulation in the six sources:

*Verse 112 lays down the general principle in this respect, which is accepted by the followers of all the Divine Books. The essence of religion, whether it be Islam or Christianity or Judaism, lies in two things. (1) One should obey Allah in one's belief as well as in one's actions. (2) This obedience should not arise from expediency, but one should surrender oneself to divine commandments in all sincerity.*

*Whether it be Islam or Christianity or Judaism.* Not a specifically Islamic standard. The common one.

Then the limit he adds, which keeps the principle from becoming formless:

*Moreover, it is not enough to be worthy of Paradise merely to have a sincere intention to obey Allah, and then to invent, according to one's own fancy, the modes and forms of obedience, for it is absolutely essential that the forms of worship and [obedience be as revealed].*

Sincerity is necessary. Invention is not enough. The forms come from revelation.

**And Maʿārif's restriction.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the boundary plainly:

*Regardless of someone's original religious group — whether Jew, Christian, idolater or other — successfully submitting to Allah is only now valid before Him by becoming Muslim, after the arrival of Prophet Muhammad.*

Maʿārif says the same in his commentary on the verse: those who followed the Sharīʿah of their own prophet in their time go to Paradise, *and who, now that the Holy Qurʾān also has abrogated all the earlier Divine Books, follow the Islamic Sharīʿah.*

The principle is universal. Its current form is specific. Both statements are in the sources.

**Their reward with their Lord.**

Al-Jalālayn: *his reward is with his Lord — the reward of his deeds, being Paradise.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *his reward is with his Lord, in Paradise.*

*With their Lord.* Not "from their Lord." The reward is stored, as verse 110 said — whatever you send ahead, you will find it.

**No fear and no grief.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās specifies both directions: *and there shall no fear come upon them, about staying eternally in hell, neither shall they grieve, about the prospect of missing Paradise.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *They will have no fear about what awaits them in the Afterlife, or feel sorrow about what passed them by in their lifetime.*

No fear forward, no grief backward. The same formula as verse 62, and the same as 10:62 and 41:30, which Ibn Kathīr quoted there.

**Tazkīrul on what replaced the claim.**

Its summary of verses 110 to 112 states the substitution:

*But the Quran tells us that one does not merit entry into heaven by dint of belonging to a certain community. Everyone will be judged according to his own actions. National status is of no significance in the sight of God.*

*National status is of no significance.* That is verse 111's claim answered and verse 112's standard given, in two sentences.

Then its definition of the sincerity the verse requires: *To be sincere in one's faith is to become so devoted to God that everything else assumes secondary importance.*

**Why this verse repeats verse 82.**

Verse 82 said: *those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever.*

Verse 112 says the same, with *submits his face* in place of *believes*. The wording changes; the standard does not.

The sūrah has now stated it three times — at verse 62 to the four communities, at verse 82 after the forty days, and here after the two exclusive Paradises. Each time it comes as an answer to a claim of exclusivity.

Verse 113 goes back to the two communities, and records what they said about each other.

113.text:
*The Jews say, "The Christians have nothing to stand on" and the Christians say, "The Jews have nothing to stand on," although both recite the Scriptures. And those pagans who have no knowledge say the same about people of faith. Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute.*

**The verse that records both claims at once.**

Verse 111 gave the claim each made about Paradise. Verse 113 gives the claim each made about the other — and the two together undo both.

**The two statements.**

Al-Jalālayn gives both, with what each denied:

*The Jews say, "The Christians stand on nothing" — that can be used as support for their claims — and they rejected Jesus; and the Christians say, "The Jews stand on nothing" — that can be used as support for their claims — and they rejected Moses.*

The Jews rejected ʿĪsā. The Christians rejected Mūsā. Each denies the other's prophet.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names the delegations again: *And Jews — the Jews of Madinah — say, "Christians follow nothing," as religion from God, and there is no true religion except Judaism, and Christians — the Christians of Najrān — say, "Jews follow nothing," as religion from God, and there is no true religion except Christianity.*

The same two parties from verse 111's debate. The argument continued.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *The Jews said that the Christians were not on the correct path, and the Christians said the same about the Jews.*

**Although both recite the Scriptures.**

*Wa hum yatlūna al-kitāb.* The clause is the verse's pivot, and al-Jalālayn explains why:

*Yet they both groups recite the Scripture revealed to them. In the Scripture of the Jews there is the confirmation of Jesus, and in that of the Christians there is the confirmation of Moses. Yatlūna al-kitāb, "they recite the Scripture," the sentence is a circumstantial qualifier.*

*In the Scripture of the Jews there is the confirmation of Jesus.* Each Book confirms the other's prophet. Each community recites a Book that contradicts its own claim.

That is what makes the verse so economical. It does not need to argue. It points at what they are already reading.

Al-Jalālayn notes the grammar: the clause is circumstantial, not coordinate. They say this *while* reciting. The contradiction is simultaneous.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *though both are readers of the Scripture — both parties read the Book and do not believe in it, and further claim things that are not mentioned therein.*

*Claim things that are not mentioned therein.* The same charge as verse 111's *these are their desires*.

Al-Mukhtaṣar supplies what the Books actually contain: *although they both claimed to read the scriptures that Allah revealed to them, which contain the command to have faith in all the prophets without any distinction between them.*

*Without any distinction between them.* The Books require believing in all the prophets. Each community believes in some.

**And those who have no knowledge say the same.**

Al-Jalālayn identifies them and explains what they say:

*Thus, in the way that these have said, the ignorant from among the Arabs and others say the like of what these say — this last phrase, mithla qawlihim, "the like of what they say," is the explication of dhālika, "that way" — that is to say, to every person of religion they would say, "You have no basis."*

*To every person of religion.* The pagans do not take a side. They apply the same dismissal to everyone.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives a different reading of who they are: *Even thus spoke those who know not, knew the Oneness of Allah through their own forefathers; and it is said this means: they knew the Book of Allah from others.*

Maʿārif explains how they got the argument:

*Each party used to assert, in its malice, that the religion of the other was baseless. This gave an excuse to the mushrikīn (associators), who, in spite of their ignorance, began to say the same of both the religions.*

*Gave an excuse.* The pagans did not reason their way to the conclusion. They watched two scripture-bearing communities invalidate each other and adopted the conclusion.

**Tazkīrul on the shared error.**

Its account of verses 113 and 114 identifies what all three groups had in common, and it is the sharpest comment on the verse:

*To the Israelites the criterion of truth was their association with the prophets and saints. That was why they believed that their community was in the right while other communities were in the wrong. As for the Christians, they considered themselves unique in that God's "beloved son" had been sent to them. Even the polytheists of Makkah thought of themselves as superior to others, basing their claim on the fact that they were the guardians of God's Sacred House.*

*Thus every nation had set its own self-styled religious standards, according to which they themselves inevitably appeared to be in the right, and everyone else in the wrong.*

*Inevitably.* A standard set by a group will always favour that group. That is the verse's diagnosis, and it covers the pagans as much as the two Books.

**Their actions did not match.**

Tazkīrul continues:

*Their actions, however, did not substantiate their claims. For one thing, they had become divided into sects, though all of them swore allegiance to the divine scriptures.*

*Divided into sects.* A community claiming exclusive truth, internally fractured. That is the empirical counter-evidence.

**Allah will judge between them.**

Al-Jalālayn states the outcome, and it is binary: *God shall decide between them on the Day of Resurrection, regarding their differences in religion, and will admit the confirmer into Paradise and the falsifier into the Fire.*

*The confirmer* and *the falsifier*. Not the Jew and the Christian. The one who affirmed and the one who denied.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Allah will judge between them, between the Jews and Christians, on the Day of Resurrection, concerning that wherein they differ.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar draws the lesson for the reader: *In His perfect and fair judgements, Allah tells His servants that there is no success without belief in all that He has revealed.*

*Belief in all that He has revealed.* Not some. That is the answer to both claims.

**Maʿārif on the two Books.**

He makes the point that the verse only implies:

*The Jews read the Torah, while the Christians read the Evangel, and they could have easily seen that the two Books confirm each other.*

*They could have easily seen.* The evidence was not hidden. It was in the text each group already read.

That is the same charge as verse 101 — casting the Book behind their backs — applied to both communities at once.

**Why this verse sits between 112 and 114.**

Verse 111 gave the claim. Verse 112 gave the standard. Verse 113 shows the two claimants destroying each other's case in public, and the pagans adopting the wreckage.

Verse 114 then turns to what all three groups did about places of worship — and it is the same failure in a different form.

114.text:
*Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah's Name from being mentioned in His places of worship and strive to destroy them? Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear. For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter.*

**The verse that names the worst wrong in the sūrah so far.**

Not idolatry. Not killing prophets. Preventing worship and destroying its places.

**The question that is not a question.**

*Wa man aẓlamu mimman manaʿa masājida Llāh.* Al-Jalālayn: *And who does greater evil — that is, none does more evil — than he who bars God's places of worship, so that His Name be not invoked in them, in prayer and praise, and strives to ruin them, through destruction and impeding people from them?*

*None does more evil.* The interrogative is a superlative.

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives both forms of the wrong: *No one does greater wrong than those who stop the name of Allah being said in His Houses of worship, preventing the prayer and remembrance of Allah and the recitation of the Qurʾān in them, trying to destroy and ruin them, through tearing them down or stopping people from worshipping in them.*

*Tearing them down, or stopping people from worshipping in them.* Two ways to ruin a mosque, and the second requires no building work.

**Three occasions, all recorded.**

The sources disagree about which event the verse refers to, and all three are in the tradition.

Al-Jalālayn gives two: *this was revealed to inform of the Byzantines' destruction of the Holy House — that is, Jerusalem — or it was revealed when the idolaters barred the Prophet from entering Mecca in the year of the battle of Ḥudaybiyyah.*

Ibn Kathīr takes the second, and gives the fullest account:

*The Quraysh idolators are those who hindered the people from the Masjids of Allah and wanted to destroy them. Ibn Jarīr reported that Ibn Zayd said that Allah's statement is about the Quraysh idolators, who prevented the Prophet from entering Makkah from al-Ḥudaybiyyah, until he slaughtered the sacrificial animal at Dhī Ṭuwā. He then agreed to a peace treaty with the idolators and said to them, "No one before has ever prevented people from entering the House. One would even see the killer of his father and brother, but would not prevent him from entering the House of Allah."*

*They said, "Whoever killed our fathers at Badr shall never enter it while there is one of us alive."*

*The killer of his father and brother.* The sanctuary had been inviolable even for a murderer. That was the custom, and they broke it over Badr.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim's report, also in Ibn Kathīr: *Ibn ʿAbbās said that the Quraysh prevented the Prophet from praying at the Kaʿbah in al-Masjid al-Ḥarām, so Allah revealed this verse.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās takes the first reading and names the person:

*Then He mentioned Tātūs ibn Asībānūs ar-Rūmī, king of the Christians, who destroyed Jerusalem: "and who doth greater wrong in his disbelief than he who forbideth the approach to the sanctuaries of Allah" — Jerusalem — "lest His name should be mentioned therein, by declaring Allah's Oneness and calling to prayer, and striveth for their ruin," in the ruin of Jerusalem, by throwing carrions in it. And this lasted until the reign of ʿUmar.*

*By throwing carrions in it.* And *until the reign of ʿUmar* — the verse's disgrace had a historical endpoint the early Muslims knew.

**Maʿārif's account of all three.**

He sets them out together, and the list is the clearest available:

*In order to understand these two verses, one should keep in mind three different incidents connected with the three groups hostile to Islam, all of which were, in one way or another, guilty of preventing people from worshipping Allah in mosques and of laying them waste.*

*(1) When Allah changed the qiblah — that is to say, commanded the Muslims to turn towards the Kaʿbah in their ṣalāh, and not towards Bayt al-Maqdīs — the Jews raised all kinds of objections to it, and tried to produce in the minds of the Muslims doubts and misgiving which, had they taken root, would have led to the denial of the Holy Prophet and to the giving up of prescribed ṣalāh, thus laying waste the mosque of the Holy Prophet.*

*(2) The Romans had once invaded Jerusalem, and the ignorant among them had polluted Bayt al-Maqdīs, which naturally prevented people from performing ṣalāh in this mosque. The Christians in a way looked upon the Romans as their ancestors; moreover, the humiliation of the Jews was in itself pleasing to them. Thus, in refusing to condemn this misdeed of the Romans, the Christians too were being indirectly responsible for laying waste the mosque.*

*(3) At the time of the peace of Ḥudaybiyyah, the mushrikīn did not allow the Holy Prophet to enter Makkah and to perform the Ḥajj. So, this group too was guilty of the same sin.*

Three groups, three methods — argument, pollution, exclusion — and one charge.

Then he records the scholarly disagreement and declines to settle it:

*According to the blessed Companion ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās, verse 114 refers to the second of these three incidents — the commentator Ibn Jarīr too accepts this view. But the commentator Ibn Kathīr follows Ibn Zayd in preferring the third as being the occasion on which this verse was revealed. The Holy Qurʾān, however, speaks in general terms of the mosques of Allah, so as to lay down a regular [rule].*

*Speaks in general terms.* The verse is not limited to its occasion. That is the reason to keep all three readings.

**Except with fear.**

*Illā khāʾifīn.* Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar and then turns it into an instruction:

*Such men might never enter them save in fear. Illā khāʾifīna is a predicate also functioning as a command — that is to say, "Frighten them by threats of waging war against them, so that not one of them shall enter it feeling secure."*

*Not one of them shall enter it feeling secure.* On this reading the clause is not a description. It is a ruling.

Al-Mukhtaṣar reads it as the state they deserve: *Those who try to destroy them should not enter Allah's places of worship, except fearfully and with trembling hearts, after their disbelief and having stopped people worshipping in them.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *it was never meant that they should enter them, Jerusalem, except in fear, hiding from the believers for fear of being killed, for they would be killed if found.*

**Disgrace in this world.**

Al-Jalālayn names the forms: *for them, in this world, is degradation — debasement through being killed, taken captive and forced to pay the jizyah; and in the Hereafter a mighty chastisement, namely the Fire.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names the cities: *Theirs in the world is ignominy, a chastisement in that their cities — Constantinople, Amorium and Rome — would be ruined, and theirs in the Hereafter is an awful doom, more severe than the punishment they were subjected to in this world.*

Constantinople, Amorium and Rome. Three named cities, and the verse was read as predicting their fate.

**Maʿārif's rulings drawn from the verse.**

He extracts the jurisprudence, and it is the most practically consequential commentary in the six sources:

*All the mosques in the world are equally worthy of respect. Just as it is a great sin to desecrate in any way Bayt al-Maqdīs, or the mosque attached to the Kaʿbah, or the mosque of the Holy Prophet, the same prohibition holds good with regard to all other mosques.*

*All the mosques in the world are equally worthy of respect.* The three have a superior rank, but the prohibition is general.

Then the second ruling, and its examples are the useful part:

*It is forbidden to prevent people, in any form or manner possible, from offering their prayers or "remembering" Allah in a mosque. An obvious form of such interference is not to allow someone to enter a mosque or to offer his prayers or to read the Holy Qurʾān there. A less explicit form is to produce some kind of a noise in the mosque itself or play music nearby, and thus to disturb people in their prayers. Similarly, if one starts reciting the Holy Qurʾān or "remembering" Allah loudly so as to disturb the people who are offering supererogatory prayers or themselves reading…*

*Play music nearby.* And *reciting loudly so as to disturb*. The prohibition covers the quiet forms of prevention too.

**Tazkīrul on the contradiction.**

Its observation is the sharpest on the verse:

*They took every opportunity to deny others the right to enter places of worship, though they would say that they were doing this to protect the sanctity of these places. In fact they were ruining them, for places of worship become derelict when people are denied the right of worship there.*

*Places of worship become derelict when people are denied the right of worship there.* Exclusion is not preservation. It is the ruin the verse describes.

Then the test it proposes: *If a worshipper has the correct attitude, he will never deny the right to worship to those who come to do so; he will never persecute those who come to serve the Lord. When one is truly conscious of God's greatness and one's own helplessness before Him, one's humility will show in one's dealings with others.*

**Why this verse follows verse 113.**

Verse 113 recorded three groups each claiming exclusive truth. Verse 114 says what all three did about the places where that truth is worshipped.

The connection is exact. Each group claimed to protect religion. Each prevented someone else from praying.

And the verse says none does more wrong.

115.text:
*To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn you are facing towards Allah. Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.*

**The verse that answers the dispute about direction.**

Verse 114 was about places of worship. Verse 115 is about which way to face in them — and it arrives because that question had just become urgent.

**The occasion: the qiblah changed.**

Ibn Kathīr gives the history, and it is the clearest account available:

*This ruling brought comfort to the Messenger of Allah and his Companions, who were driven out of Makkah and had to depart from the area of al-Masjid al-Ḥarām. In Makkah, the Messenger of Allah used to pray in the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis, while the Kaʿbah was between him and the qiblah. When the Messenger migrated to al-Madīnah, he faced Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, and then Allah directed him to face al-Kaʿbah in prayer.*

*The Kaʿbah was between him and the qiblah.* In Makkah he prayed north, toward Jerusalem, with the Kaʿbah behind him. The two were in the same line.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah's report from Ibn ʿAbbās, also in Ibn Kathīr, adds what the Prophet wanted:

*"The first part of the Qurʾān that was abrogated was about the qiblah. When the Messenger of Allah migrated to al-Madīnah, which was inhabited by the Jews, he was at first commanded to face Bayt al-Maqdis. The Jews were happy, and the Messenger of Allah faced Bayt al-Maqdis for some ten months. However, the Messenger of Allah liked to face the qiblah of Ibrāhīm — al-Kaʿbah at Makkah — and he used to look to the sky and supplicate."*

*The Jews were happy.* They had been pleased by the arrangement. That is why the change provoked them.

*"So Allah revealed, 'Verily, We have seen the turning of your face towards the heaven,' until, 'turn your faces in prayer in that direction' (2:144)."*

*The Jews were disturbed by this development and said, "What made them change the direction of the qiblah that they used to face?" Allah revealed: "Say: To Allah belong both, east and the west," and, "So wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah."*

The verse is the answer to a specific question, asked by specific people, at a specific moment.

**Two other occasions.**

Al-Jalālayn gives both: *The following was revealed either when the Jews criticised the change of the direction of prayer, or concerning the supererogatory prayers on animal-back during journeys, which one may pray in any direction.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās takes the second and names the incident:

*This verse was revealed about a group of Companions of the Prophet who prayed whilst travelling in the wrong direction, after doing their best to determine the correct direction.*

Prayed in the wrong direction, having tried their best. The verse answers that case too.

Al-Mukhtaṣar covers it generally: *Whether He instructs you to face Jerusalem or the Kaaba, or you make a mistake in the direction of prayer or are not sure of it, then it is not an issue, because to Allah belongs every direction.*

**To Allah belong the east and the west.**

Al-Jalālayn explains why those two directions stand for everything: *To God belong the East and the West — that is, the entire earth, because these two directions represent both sides of it.*

*Both sides of it.* East and west are not two of many. They are the whole.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives a second reading: *it is also said that "Unto Allah belong the East and the West" means: the people of the East and the people of the West have one direction of prayer, which is the Sacred Precinct.*

**Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah.**

*Fa-thamma wajhu Llāh.* Al-Jalālayn: *whithersoever you turn your faces in prayer, by His command, there is the Face of God — the direction of prayer with which He is pleased.*

*By His command.* The turning is not arbitrary. It is directed, and the direction is His to set.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and whithersoever ye turn your faces in prayer, after ascertaining the direction, there is Allah's Countenance, that prayer is performed in Allah's pleasure.*

*After ascertaining the direction.* The effort is still required.

**Maʿārif on the connection to verse 114.**

He explains why the two verses sit together, and the explanation is the qiblah dispute:

*When Allah changed the qiblah, the Jews raised all kinds of objections to it, and tried to produce in the minds of the Muslims doubts and misgiving which, had they taken root, would have led to the denial of the Holy Prophet and to the giving up of prescribed ṣalāh, thus laying waste the mosque of the Holy Prophet.*

*Thus laying waste the mosque.* The objection to the qiblah was, on Maʿārif's reading, an attempt at the ruin verse 114 describes — carried out by argument rather than by destruction.

**Tazkīrul on the error underneath.**

Its comment on verses 115 to 119 names the misconception, and it is the sharpest observation on the verse:

*Another error into which they fell was to liken God to man. A human being, for instance, cannot be in two places at the same time, and, in consequence, people think that God is also to be found only in some particular place. But God is everywhere.*

*True, He has prescribed a direction for us to face when we worship, but this is a purely organizational requirement for prayer; it does not mean that God is to be found in only one direction and not in any other.*

*A purely organizational requirement.* The qiblah is not a location of God. It is an arrangement for a community praying together.

Then the connection it draws forward: *Another outcome of this basic misconception of God's nature is people's attributing a son to Him. But only those who have needs beget sons, and God is above all such imperfections and limitations. He is complete in Himself. Such beliefs do not stem from God; man has invented them himself.*

The qiblah dispute and the claim of a son come from the same error — measuring God by human limits.

**All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.**

*Wāsiʿun ʿalīm.* Al-Jalālayn: *Lo! God is Embracing, His bounty embracing all things, Knowing, how to manage His creation.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Lo! Allah is All-Embracing, regarding the direction of prayer, All-Knowing, of their intentions.*

*Of their intentions.* The direction may be wrong. The intention is seen.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Allah is vast in His blessings; He covers His creation with His mercy and ease. He knows their intentions and everything that they do.*

*Mercy and ease.* Wāsiʿ as spaciousness, and the spaciousness is experienced as relief.

**Why this verse is a comfort.**

Ibn Kathīr says so directly: *This ruling brought comfort to the Messenger of Allah and his Companions, who were driven out of Makkah.*

They had lost the Kaʿbah. They were praying toward Jerusalem in a city full of people who objected to it. And then the direction changed, and the objection became louder.

The verse says: the directions are His. All of them. Wherever you turn, you are facing Him.

Verse 116 turns to the other claim that came from measuring God by human limits — that He has a son.

116.text:
*They say, "Allah has offspring." Glory be to Him! In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth—all are subject to His Will.*

**Three claims, one answer.**

The verse reports a statement made by three different groups, and refutes all of them in two clauses.

**Who said it.**

Al-Jalālayn names all three: *And they — the Jews and the Christians, and those that claim that the angels are God's daughters — say, read wa-qālū or simply qālū, "God has taken to Himself a son."*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names the two sons: *Then Allah mentions the claims of the Jews and Christians that ʿUzayr and Jesus are the sons of Allah: "And they, the Jews and Christians, say: Allah hath taken unto Himself a Son" — ʿUzayr and the Messiah.*

Maʿārif gives the full picture: *As the Holy Qurʾān reports in some other verses, some of the Jews called the Prophet ʿUzayr (Ezra) the son of God, as did the Christians in the case of Sayyidunā ʿĪsā (Jesus), and most of them still do, while the mushrikīn of Makkah considered the angels to be the daughters of God.*

*Most of them still do.* Maʿārif notes the claim was current, not historical.

Three groups, three different offspring, one structure.

**Glory be to Him.**

*Subḥānah.* Ibn Kathīr: *meaning, He is holier and more perfect than such claim.*

Al-Jalālayn: *God says, "Glory be to Him!" as a way of exalting Himself above this.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Be He glorified! He is far exalted to have a son or partner.*

The refutation begins with an exclamation rather than an argument. The claim is not answered first. It is excluded.

**Then the argument.**

Ibn Kathīr states it, and it is the verse's real content:

*Nay, to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and on earth — meaning, the truth is not as the disbelievers claimed, rather, Allah's is the kingdom of the heavens and earth, and whatever and whoever is in, on and between them. Allah is the Supreme Authority in the heavens and earth, and He is the Creator, Provider and Sustainer, Who decides all the affairs of the creation as He wills.*

*All creatures are Allah's servants and are owned by Him. Therefore, how could one of them be His son?*

*How could one of them be His son.* The argument from ownership. Everything is already His. A son would be a second category, and there is no second category.

Then the reasoning that closes it:

*The son of any being is born out of two comparable beings. Allah has no equal or rival sharing His grace and greatness, so how can He have a son when He has no wife?*

Then the verse he uses: *"He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth. How can He have children when He has no wife? He created all things and He is the Knower of everything" (6:101).*

**Maʿārif's rational argument.**

He sets it out as a dilemma, and it is the most careful treatment in the six sources:

*These two verses show the absurdity of such assertions. For, even on rational grounds, it is totally impossible that God should have offspring. Were it at all possible, the situation would necessarily involve either of the two alternative characteristics — the offspring would belong either to the same genus as the father does, or to a different genus.*

*If it belongs to a different genus, that obviously is a defect, while God should, in order to be God, be free of all defects.*

*If the offspring belongs to the same genus, that too is a contradiction in terms, for God has no equal, and no existent can belong to the same genus as He does.*

Then the metaphysics behind the second horn:

*God alone is the Necessary Being, and hence necessarily carries within Himself the Attributes of Perfection which are peculiar to Him alone and which cannot exist in any one other than God. Now, if we deny a necessary attribute to a certain being, we automatically deny the existence of that being. So, no one other than God can be a necessary being.*

*Hence, it would be a plain and simple contradiction in terms to claim that anyone other than God can belong to the same genus.*

Both horns close. Different genus means defect. Same genus means a second necessary being, which is impossible.

**All are subject to His Will.**

*Kullun lahu qānitūn.* Al-Jalālayn explains the word and the emphasis:

*Nay, to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and the earth, as possessions, creatures and servants — and this sovereignty contradicts having a child, and is expressed by the particle mā, "all that," in order to include all creation that is not rational; all obey His will, submitting to that which is required from each one of them — here the emphasis is on rational beings.*

*This sovereignty contradicts having a child.* Ownership and sonship are mutually exclusive. That is the verse's logic in one line.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Nay, it is not as they say, but whatsoever is in the heavens and the earth, of creation, is His, are His servants. All are subservient unto Him, linked to Him by the bond of servitude and the declaration of His Oneness.*

*The bond of servitude.* Qunūt as the relationship, and it is the only one available.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *He is far above and beyond such a thing, because He has no need of His creation, and no one has a son unless he is needy; and to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. All created beings are His servants, in submission to Him, glory be to Him! They are His servants and He deals with them as He wills.*

*No one has a son unless he is needy.* The argument from need. Offspring answers a want. Allah has none.

**Tazkīrul on where the claim comes from.**

Its diagnosis connects this verse to the one before it, and it is the sharpest comment on the passage:

*But only those who have needs beget sons, and God is above all such imperfections and limitations. He is complete in Himself. Such beliefs do not stem from God; man has invented them himself.*

*Man has invented them himself.* Not a misreading of revelation. An invention, produced by the same habit of measuring God by human limits that produced the qiblah objection.

**Why the verse is so short.**

A claim from three groups, an exclamation, an argument from ownership, and a statement that everything is already a servant.

The sūrah does not engage the claim at length here. Verse 117 will add the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who says "Be" and it is.

**And what the verse establishes.**

Verse 115 said the directions are Allah's. Verse 116 says everything is Allah's.

The two verses answer the two claims with the same move: the thing being disputed is already His, entirely, and there is nothing left over for a rival or a son.

That is the sūrah's answer to exclusivity in every form — the exclusive Paradise of verse 111, the exclusive direction of verse 115, and the exclusive offspring here.
